confirmedFindings.title: getJwtExpirySeconds and getRefreshTokenTtlSeconds lack NaN guards (unlike token-service copies)
confirmedFindings.description: The auth-service has its own local copies of getJwtExpirySeconds() (line 871) and getRefreshTokenTtlSeconds() (line 876) that use parseInt() without any NaN check. If OP_JWT_EXPIRY_SECONDS or OP_REFRESH_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS is set to a non-numeric string, parseInt returns NaN. This NaN propagates into token expiry calculations (line 259: expiresIn becomes NaN) and session expiry (line 226: Date.now() + NaN * 1000 = NaN -> Invalid Date inserted into Postgres). The token-service versions of these same helpers (lines 177-201) already have isNaN guards that throw on invalid values, but the auth-service copies were never updated. This means the auth-service will silently issue tokens with NaN expiry or try to insert invalid dates into the database.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Add the same isNaN/non-positive guards that token-service.ts has: if the parsed value isNaN or <= 0, throw an error with a descriptive message.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The finding is confirmed in full. The auth-service has local copies of getJwtExpirySeconds() (line 871) and getRefreshTokenTtlSeconds() (line 876) that call parseInt() without any NaN guard. The token-service versions of these same helpers (lines 177-201) were explicitly patched (comment "V6-124") to include isNaN checks that throw on invalid values, but the auth-service copies were never updated.

The unguarded NaN would propagate into: (1) Postgres session inserts with Invalid Date at lines 226 and 374, (2) API responses with NaN expiresIn at lines 259 and 418, and (3) Redis SET EX calls with NaN TTL at lines 671 and 764. These are all real failure modes that would corrupt data or cause runtime errors.

However, the severity should be adjusted to MEDIUM because the bug only triggers when OP_JWT_EXPIRY_SECONDS or OP_REFRESH_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS is set to a non-numeric string. In normal operation these are either unset (defaults apply safely) or set to valid integers. This is a configuration-error scenario, not something that can be triggered by user input or an attacker. It is a genuine code quality gap (the token-service was patched but the auth-service copy was missed), but the practical impact is limited to misconfiguration scenarios.

confirmedFindings.title: API key service getBcryptRounds lacks NaN guard, could produce invalid hashes
confirmedFindings.description: getBcryptRounds() (line 79-82) parses OP_BCRYPT_ROUNDS with parseInt but has no NaN check. If the env var is set to a non-numeric value, parseInt returns NaN, which is then passed to bcrypt.hash(fullKey, NaN). Depending on the bcrypt library version, this could throw an unhandled error during key creation or produce a hash with unpredictable cost factor. The password-service.ts version (lines 15-32) properly validates and rejects values below the minimum threshold, but this copy does not.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Add the same validation as password-service.ts: check isNaN(parsed) and parsed < 10, throwing an error for invalid values. Better yet, import and reuse the resolveRounds function from password-service.ts to avoid the duplication.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The code exists exactly as described: getBcryptRounds() at lines 79-82 of api-key-service.ts parses OP_BCRYPT_ROUNDS with parseInt but has no NaN guard, while the equivalent resolveRounds() in password-service.ts (lines 15-32) properly validates with isNaN check and minimum threshold enforcement.

However, the described severity and impact are significantly overstated. Testing with the actual bcrypt library (v5.1.1) installed in this project shows that bcrypt.hash(key, NaN) does NOT throw an unhandled error and does NOT produce invalid or unpredictable hashes. Instead, bcrypt silently falls back to a cost factor of 10 (as confirmed by examining the cost prefix in the generated hash: "$2b$10$..."). The resulting hash is fully valid and verifiable with bcrypt.compare().

The real impact: if an operator sets OP_BCRYPT_ROUNDS to a non-numeric string (an operational error), API key hashes will silently use cost 10 instead of the intended default of 12. This is slightly weaker but still within secure bounds. It also bypasses the project's policy (established in password-service.ts) of rejecting rounds below MIN_BCRYPT_ROUNDS=10, though NaN falling to 10 happens to meet that threshold anyway.

This is a real code quality/consistency issue -- the validation present in password-service.ts is missing from api-key-service.ts -- but the actual security impact is minimal (silent cost reduction from 12 to 10 under an already-erroneous configuration), not the "unhandled error" or "unpredictable cost factor" claimed. Adjusting severity to LOW.

confirmedFindings.title: OAuth service getJwtExpirySeconds and getRefreshTokenTtlSeconds lack NaN guards
confirmedFindings.description: The OAuth service has its own copies of getJwtExpirySeconds() (line 528) and getRefreshTokenTtlSeconds() (line 533) that parse environment variables with parseInt but do not check for NaN. If the env var contains a non-numeric string, these return NaN, causing the OAuth login flow to issue tokens with NaN expiry values and create sessions with invalid expiry dates. This is the same pattern as the auth-service copies but in a separate code path.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Add NaN and non-positive guards identical to the token-service versions, or better yet, extract this helper into a shared utility to eliminate the duplication across four copies.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The finding is confirmed as real. The oauth-service.ts file contains getJwtExpirySeconds() (line 528) and getRefreshTokenTtlSeconds() (line 533) that use parseInt without NaN guards. This is provably an inconsistency because two other copies of these exact same functions in the same codebase DO have NaN guards:

1. token-service.ts (lines 177-198) - has NaN guards, explicitly tagged with "V6-124: Guard against NaN from malformed env var values"
2. bootstrap-service.ts (lines 357-378) - has NaN guards with the same pattern
3. auth-service.ts (lines 871-878) - MISSING NaN guards (same bug)
4. oauth-service.ts (lines 528-536) - MISSING NaN guards (the reported bug)

If OP_JWT_EXPIRY_SECONDS or OP_REFRESH_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS is set to a non-numeric string, parseInt returns NaN. This causes: (a) new Date(Date.now() + NaN * 1000) = Invalid Date, which would be inserted as the session expires_at in PostgreSQL, and (b) expiresIn: NaN returned to the OAuth callback handler. Both would break the OAuth login flow.

The severity is appropriately HIGH because it affects a security-critical code path (OAuth authentication/session creation), though it requires a misconfigured environment variable to trigger. Downgrading to MEDIUM because env vars are typically set by operators and validated during deployment, but the inconsistency with the fixed copies (V6-124) confirms this was a recognized risk that was partially remediated.

confirmedFindings.title: User role update does not validate that assigned roles exist in the tenant
confirmedFindings.description: When updating a user's roles via PUT /api/v1/users/:id (line 232), the route validates against privilege escalation (platform-admin assignment) but does NOT validate that the requested roles actually exist in the tenant's role registry. The POST /api/v1/users (create) route properly validates roles against roleRepository.findByTenantId (lines 63-69), but the PUT route skips this validation entirely. An admin could assign nonexistent role names to users, which would grant no permissions but could cause confusing behavior, and more critically, if a role with that name is later created, the user would retroactively gain those permissions without any audit trail of the permission change.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Add the same role existence validation that the POST /api/v1/users route has: query roleRepository.findByTenantId(user.tenantId), check that all requested roles exist in the result set, and throw a ValidationError for unknown roles.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning: The finding is confirmed. The PUT /api/v1/users/:id route (line 232) accepts arbitrary role names without validating they exist in the tenant's role registry, while the POST /api/v1/users route (lines 63-69) properly validates roles via roleRepository.findByTenantId(). The asymmetry is clear in the code: POST has a "V6-103" comment block that builds a knownRoleNames set and throws ValidationError for unknown roles, but the PUT route only checks for platform-admin privilege escalation. There is no database-level protection either -- the roles column is TEXT[] with no foreign key to auth.roles (impossible for array columns in PostgreSQL). The repository layer also performs no validation, writing whatever strings it receives. The retroactive permission gain scenario is plausible: assigning a nonexistent role name that is later created would silently grant those permissions. However, the severity should be adjusted to MEDIUM because: (1) exploitation requires users:manage scope (already a privileged operation), (2) the immediate impact is no-op (nonexistent roles grant nothing), and (3) the retroactive scenario requires a subsequent role creation that happens to match, which is unlikely to be accidental and would be visible in role creation logs. It is a real consistency/correctness bug with a theoretical security implication, not an immediate privilege escalation.

confirmedFindings.title: Billing webhook config lacks authorization scope check
confirmedFindings.description: The POST, GET, and DELETE endpoints for /api/v1/billing/webhook-config only check that the user is authenticated (has a tenantId) but do not verify any specific scope or role. Any authenticated user within a tenant can create, view, or delete the billing webhook configuration, including setting arbitrary webhook URLs and thresholds. In contrast, other sensitive admin operations (rate limits, data residency, transfer rules) require the 'admin' scope. This allows a low-privilege user to configure billing webhooks that fire to an attacker-controlled endpoint and receive internal usage data.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Add an admin scope check like the other admin routes: if (!user.scopes.includes('admin')) throw new ForbiddenError('Admin role required.');
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The code in `/home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/services/gateway/src/routes/billing.ts` exactly matches the finding's description. The POST, GET, and DELETE handlers for webhook-config only check `user?.tenantId` (authentication) but perform no scope or role check. This is inconsistent with every other sensitive endpoint in the gateway: webhooks.ts requires `webhooks:manage`/`webhooks:read`, admin.ts requires `admin` scope, data.ts requires `data:read`/`data:write`, lineage.ts requires `lineage:read`, and data-residency.ts requires `admin` scope for mutations.

However, there is an important mitigating factor: the `createBillingRoutes` function is imported in `index.ts` (line 55) but **never called or mounted**. No `app.route("/api/v1/billing", ...)` line exists. The `billingWebhookConfigRepo` is only passed to the metering service, not to any route handler. This means the endpoints are not currently reachable in the running application.

The finding is real at the code level -- the authorization gap genuinely exists and is inconsistent with established patterns. When these routes are eventually mounted (the infrastructure is clearly being prepared: the import exists, the repo is instantiated), any authenticated user would be able to manage billing webhook configurations without admin privileges. This would allow a low-privilege user to set a webhook URL to an attacker-controlled endpoint and receive internal usage/billing data.

Severity is adjusted from HIGH to LOW because the routes are currently dead code that is not mounted on the application. The vulnerability cannot be exploited today, but it represents a latent authorization defect that would become HIGH severity the moment the routes are wired up.

confirmedFindings.title: Billing webhook HMAC signing uses raw secret_encrypted ciphertext instead of decrypted secret
confirmedFindings.description: In checkAndDeliverThresholds, the code sets 'const secret = config.secret_encrypted' and passes it directly to deliverBillingWebhook as the HMAC signing key. The comment says 'the config upsert route handles encryption before storage', but the billing route upsert does NOT pass any secret_encrypted value (it defaults to null in the repository). If a secret were stored, it would be AES-256-GCM ciphertext, not the raw secret. The HMAC would be computed over ciphertext rather than the actual shared secret, making signature verification impossible for webhook consumers. This means billing webhook signatures are either absent (null secret) or cryptographically meaningless (signing with ciphertext).
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: If a signing secret is intended, the billing webhook config should store an encrypted secret (like webhook-service does with masterKey), and checkAndDeliverThresholds should decrypt it with the masterKey before passing it to deliverBillingWebhook. The billing route should also accept a 'secret' field in the request body, encrypt it, and pass it to the repository.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The finding is confirmed as real but should be adjusted in severity. The code at line 493 of metering-service.ts does exactly what the finding describes: `const secret = config.secret_encrypted;` passes the raw `secret_encrypted` column value directly to `deliverBillingWebhook` without decryption. This contrasts with the regular webhook service (webhook-service.ts line 291) which properly decrypts via `await decrypt(webhook.secret_encrypted, masterKey)` before HMAC signing.

However, the practical impact is limited because the billing route's upsert endpoint (billing.ts lines 57-65) never passes a `secret_encrypted` value — the Zod validation schema does not even include a secret field. The repository defaults it to null (usage-event-repository.ts line 190: `data.secret_encrypted ?? null`). When secret is null, `deliverBillingWebhook` skips HMAC signing entirely (line 123: `if (secret !== null)`).

So the current real-world consequence is that billing threshold webhooks are always sent unsigned — consumers cannot verify authenticity. The ciphertext-as-HMAC-key scenario described in the finding is hypothetical since no code path populates `secret_encrypted` for billing configs. If someone manually inserted an encrypted secret into the database, the HMAC would indeed be computed over ciphertext rather than the decrypted secret, making verification impossible for consumers. This is a genuine code-level bug (missing decryption step) combined with an incomplete feature (no API to set the signing secret), but the severity is lower than HIGH because the practical impact is unsigned webhooks rather than actively broken signatures.

confirmedFindings.title: HMAC verification bypass via truncated signature
confirmedFindings.description: The HMAC verification copies the incoming hex-decoded signature into a fixed-size buffer via Buffer.copy, which silently truncates to the expected length. The subsequent timingSafeEqual compares only the first N bytes. The length check `incomingHex.length === expectedHmac.length` is performed AFTER timingSafeEqual, but the order of the `&&` operator means timingSafeEqual must pass first. However, the real issue is that `Buffer.from(incomingHex, 'hex')` on a string shorter than expectedHmac produces a shorter buffer that is zero-padded by Buffer.alloc. If the attacker sends a signature that happens to match the first few bytes of the expected HMAC when zero-padded, timingSafeEqual would pass. While the subsequent length check would catch this, the comparison `incomingHex.length === expectedHmac.length` compares the *hex string* lengths, not the raw buffer lengths. An attacker sending the correct hex characters plus extra non-hex characters (which Buffer.from('hex') silently ignores) could potentially make incomingHex.length match expectedHmac.length while the actual decoded bytes are different. For example, 'abcdzz' has length 6 but Buffer.from('abcdzz','hex') produces only 2 bytes (0xab, 0xcd). This could allow forgery if an attacker crafts a hex string with the right length but invalid hex characters after the valid prefix.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Validate the incoming signature strictly before comparison: check that incomingHex matches /^[0-9a-f]+$/ and that its length equals expectedHmac.length before doing the timingSafeEqual. Alternatively, compare raw byte lengths of both decoded buffers and reject immediately if they differ.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The code exists exactly as described at lines 262-268 of webhook-receive-service.ts. The finding correctly identifies a genuine defensive coding flaw in the HMAC verification logic:

1. Buffer.from(incomingHex, 'hex') silently stops parsing at the first non-hex character (confirmed experimentally: Buffer.from('abcdzz', 'hex') produces only [0xab, 0xcd]).
2. Buffer.alloc(expectedBuf.length) zero-fills the remaining bytes.
3. The length check (incomingHex.length === expectedHmac.length) compares string lengths, not decoded buffer lengths.
4. An attacker COULD craft a string like "ab" + "z".repeat(62) that passes the string length check (length 64 = SHA-256 hex length) while only decoding to 1 byte.

However, the severity is vastly overstated. For the attack to succeed, timingSafeEqual must ALSO pass, which requires the expected HMAC to have 0x00 in all positions not covered by the attacker's valid hex prefix. For SHA-256, this means most of the 32-byte HMAC must be zero -- probability approximately 2^-248 even in the best case. The attacker also does not know the HMAC value (it depends on a secret key they lack), making it impossible to craft even the valid hex prefix correctly.

The proper fix would be to validate hex input or check decoded buffer length rather than string length, but exploitation is cryptographically infeasible. This is a code hygiene issue, not a practically exploitable vulnerability. Downgrading from HIGH to LOW.

confirmedFindings.title: Race condition in batch progress tracking causes lost progress updates
confirmedFindings.description: In processBatchJob, the progress is read from Redis, incremented, and written back without any atomicity guarantees. When multiple batch jobs run concurrently (concurrency is set to 10 for the batch worker), two jobs can read the same progress state, each increment completedBatches by 1, and write back, resulting in only one increment being recorded instead of two. This causes completedBatches and processedRecords to be under-counted, and the sync may never show as fully complete in the progress tracker even after all batches finish.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Use a Redis MULTI/EXEC transaction or a Lua script to atomically read-modify-write the progress JSON. Alternatively, use Redis HINCRBY on individual numeric fields instead of reading and rewriting the entire JSON blob.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The race condition is confirmed. The code at lines 894-901 of sync-service.ts performs a non-atomic read-modify-write on the Redis progress key: it calls getSyncProgress (Redis GET + JSON.parse), increments completedBatches and processedRecords in memory, then calls writeProgress (JSON.stringify + Redis SET). The batch worker runs with concurrency=10 (index.ts line 286), so multiple batch jobs process simultaneously. Two concurrent workers can read the same progress state, each increment by 1, and write back, losing one increment.

However, the finding's claim that "the sync may never show as fully complete" is incorrect. The sync status is set to "success" by processSyncJob (line 742) independently of the batch workers' progress updates. The waitForCompletion polling loop (internal.ts line 131-138) checks progress.status, not completedBatches. So functional completion is not affected.

The real impact is: (1) completedBatches and processedRecords counters will be under-counted, leading to inaccurate progress reporting via the API; (2) the rowsIngested value returned to callers of the internal trigger-sync endpoint (internal.ts line 143) may be incorrect. This is a genuine concurrency bug, but its impact is limited to monitoring/reporting accuracy rather than functional sync completion. The fix would be to use Redis HINCRBY or a Lua script for atomic increments.

Adjusting severity from HIGH to MEDIUM because the sync completes successfully regardless -- only the progress counters are affected.

confirmedFindings.title: Webhook signature header lookup ignores the receiver's configured headerName
confirmedFindings.description: The webhook receive route (webhooks.ts line 38) hardcodes the signature header lookup to check only 'X-Webhook-Signature', 'x-hub-signature-256', and 'x-signature'. The receiver's configured headerName (stored in the DB as header_name, configurable per receiver) is completely ignored. If a receiver is configured with a custom headerName like 'X-Custom-Sig', the signature will never be found, HMAC verification will fail (empty string vs expected), and all events from that sender will be silently dropped. This effectively makes the headerName configuration field non-functional.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: The route handler should not hardcode which headers to check. Instead, pass all headers to receiveEvent and let the service look up the correct header based on the receiver's configured headerName. The receiveEvent method should read receiver.header_name and use that to extract the signature from the incoming headers.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The bug is confirmed and real. The route handler at `/home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/services/ingestion/src/routes/webhooks.ts` lines 38-40 hardcodes three header names for signature extraction: `X-Webhook-Signature`, `x-hub-signature-256`, and `x-signature`. The receiver's configurable `header_name` field (stored in the DB, settable via the management API with a default of `"X-Webhook-Signature"`) is never consulted during the receive path.

The `receiveEvent` method in `webhook-receive-service.ts` accepts the already-extracted `signatureHeader` parameter and never accesses HTTP request headers directly. The receiver lookup happens INSIDE the service (line 199-212), but by then the header has already been extracted in the route layer without knowledge of the receiver's configuration.

If a receiver is configured with a custom `headerName` (e.g., `"X-Custom-Sig"`), the route will never look for that header. The `signatureHeader` will be `undefined`, which becomes `""` at line 251 (`const rawSignature = signatureHeader ?? ""`), causing HMAC verification to always fail, and the event will be silently dropped (logged as WEBHOOK_HMAC_FAILED but returning 200 OK to the sender).

This makes the `headerName` configuration field completely non-functional for any value other than the three hardcoded defaults. The schema allows any string for `headerName`, and the management API dutifully stores it, but the receive path ignores it entirely. This is a genuine architectural gap between the configuration model and the receive implementation.

confirmedFindings.title: Missing tenant isolation on draft confirm endpoint
confirmedFindings.description: The POST /api/v1/ontology/drafts/:id/confirm endpoint calls draftRepo.confirm(id, userId) without verifying that the draft belongs to the authenticated user's tenant. A user from tenant A could confirm a draft belonging to tenant B by guessing or enumerating draft IDs. The draftRepo.confirm() method updates the draft by ID without scoping to tenant_id.
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet:
const confirmed = await draftRepo.confirm(c.req.param("id"), user.userId);
if (!confirmed) throw new NotFoundError("Draft not found or already processed.");
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Before calling draftRepo.confirm(), fetch the draft via draftRepo.findById() and verify draft.tenant_id === user.tenantId, similar to the pattern used in the GET /drafts/:id endpoint. Alternatively, add a tenantId parameter to draftRepo.confirm() and include it in the WHERE clause.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The finding is confirmed as a real cross-tenant authorization vulnerability. The evidence is conclusive:

1. The code exists exactly as described at /home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/services/ontology/src/routes/drafts.ts line 65: `draftRepo.confirm(c.req.param("id"), user.userId)` passes only the draft ID and user ID, never the tenant ID.

2. The repository method `confirm()` at /home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/services/ontology/src/repositories/draft-repository.ts lines 66-75 executes `UPDATE ontology.draft_ontologies SET ... WHERE id = $2 AND status = 'draft'` -- filtering only by ID and status, with no tenant_id constraint.

3. The same file demonstrates the correct pattern: the GET /drafts/:id endpoint on line 44 explicitly checks `draft.tenant_id !== user.tenantId`, but neither the confirm nor reject endpoints perform this check.

4. Other route files (migrations.ts, mapping-rules.ts) consistently check tenant_id before allowing mutations, confirming this is an omission rather than a design choice.

5. No database-level Row Level Security exists on the draft_ontologies table, and no middleware enforces tenant scoping on queries. The RLS in ddl-builder.ts is for dynamically created tenant data tables, not system tables.

6. The reject endpoint (line 82) has the same vulnerability: `draftRepo.reject(c.req.param("id"))` also lacks tenant scoping.

A user from tenant A can confirm (or reject) any draft belonging to tenant B by providing that draft's ID. This is a genuine multi-tenant isolation failure.

confirmedFindings.title: Missing tenant isolation on draft reject endpoint
confirmedFindings.description: The POST /api/v1/ontology/drafts/:id/reject endpoint calls draftRepo.reject(id) without verifying the draft belongs to the authenticated user's tenant. A user from tenant A could reject a draft belonging to tenant B.
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet:
const rejected = await draftRepo.reject(c.req.param("id"));
if (!rejected) throw new NotFoundError("Draft not found or already processed.");
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Fetch the draft via draftRepo.findById() first and verify draft.tenant_id === user.tenantId before calling draftRepo.reject().
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning: The finding is confirmed as a real bug. The POST /api/v1/ontology/drafts/:id/reject endpoint (line 75-85 of drafts.ts) calls draftRepo.reject(c.req.param("id")) without any tenant isolation check. The repository's reject method (line 77-85 of draft-repository.ts) executes an UPDATE query filtered only by id and status='draft' — no tenant_id filter is applied. By contrast, the GET /drafts/:id endpoint correctly fetches the draft then checks draft.tenant_id !== user.tenantId before returning data. This tenant check pattern is absent from both the reject and confirm mutation endpoints. There is no middleware, database-level row security, or other mechanism providing tenant isolation for these mutation paths. A user from tenant A who knows or guesses a draft UUID belonging to tenant B can reject that draft cross-tenant. The confirm endpoint (line 59-73) has the same vulnerability but the finding specifically calls out reject, which is accurately reported.

confirmedFindings.title: Missing tenant isolation on migration confirm endpoint
confirmedFindings.description: The POST /api/v1/ontology/migrations/:id/confirm endpoint passes the migration ID directly to migrationService.confirmMigration() without verifying the migration belongs to the authenticated user's tenant. A user from tenant A could confirm a migration for tenant B, triggering schema changes on another tenant's data. The confirmMigration service method also does not check tenant ownership.
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet: const confirmed = await migrationService.confirmMigration(c.req.param("id"), user.userId);
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Add tenant isolation to the confirm route: look up the migration first, verify migration.tenant_id === user.tenantId, and return 404 if it does not match. Alternatively, pass user.tenantId into confirmMigration and scope the lookup.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The finding is confirmed as a real cross-tenant authorization bypass vulnerability. Here is the evidence:

1. The code exists exactly as described. In `/home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/services/ontology/src/routes/migrations.ts` at line 84, the confirm endpoint calls `migrationService.confirmMigration(c.req.param("id"), user.userId)` without passing `user.tenantId`.

2. The `confirmMigration` method in `/home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/services/ontology/src/services/migration-service.ts` (line 165-225) fetches the migration by ID alone via `migrationRepo.findById(migrationId)`, which queries `WHERE id = $1` with no tenant filter. It never compares `migration.tenant_id` against the authenticated user's tenant.

3. Other endpoints in the same file DO enforce tenant isolation properly:
   - GET /:id (line 58): checks `migration.tenant_id !== user.tenantId`
   - GET /:id/status (line 112): checks `migration.tenant_id !== user.tenantId`
   - GET /migrations (line 27): queries by `user.tenantId`
   
   This inconsistency confirms it is an oversight, not a design choice.

4. The rollback endpoint (line 92-103) has the identical missing tenant check.

5. The consequence is severe: a user from tenant A who knows or guesses a migration ID belonging to tenant B could confirm that migration, causing the service to execute DDL statements (create union views, alter schemas) on tenant B's database schema via `tenantSchemaName(migration.tenant_id)`. This is a direct cross-tenant data integrity violation.

confirmedFindings.title: Missing tenant isolation on migration rollback endpoint
confirmedFindings.description: The POST /api/v1/ontology/migrations/:id/rollback endpoint passes the migration ID to migrationService.rollbackMigration() without verifying tenant ownership. A user from tenant A could roll back a migration belonging to tenant B, corrupting another tenant's data by restoring old rows from shadow tables.
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet: await migrationService.rollbackMigration(c.req.param("id"));
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Before calling rollbackMigration(), look up the migration via migrationRepo.findById() and verify migration.tenant_id === user.tenantId. Return 404 if there is no match.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning: The finding is confirmed as a real security vulnerability. The POST /api/v1/ontology/migrations/:id/rollback route handler (line 92-103 of migrations.ts) passes only the migration ID to migrationService.rollbackMigration() without any tenant ownership verification. The service layer (migration-service.ts line 294-370) also performs no tenant check -- it calls migrationRepo.findById(migrationId) which queries only by ID with no tenant filter, then operates directly on the migration's tenant schema. This is clearly inconsistent with the GET endpoints in the same file: both GET /migrations/:id (line 58) and GET /migrations/:id/status (line 112) explicitly verify migration.tenant_id !== user.tenantId. A user from Tenant A who knows or guesses a migration UUID belonging to Tenant B can invoke the rollback, which would delete rows from and restore old rows into Tenant B's data tables, corrupting their data. The same vulnerability also affects the confirm endpoint (line 84), but rollback is the more destructive operation. This is a genuine cross-tenant isolation failure.

confirmedFindings.title: SQL injection via unvalidated number default value in DDL generation
confirmedFindings.description: formatDefaultValue() for 'number' field types does String(value) and directly interpolates the result into DDL SQL. The Zod schema for defaultValue is z.unknown().optional(), allowing any type to be passed. If an attacker supplies a string like '0; DROP TABLE important_data;--' as the defaultValue for a number-typed field, it will be directly interpolated into ALTER TABLE or CREATE TABLE DDL statements without sanitization.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Validate that the value is actually a finite number before using it in DDL: if (typeof value !== 'number' || !Number.isFinite(value)) throw new Error('Default value for number field must be a finite number'). Alternatively, use a parameterized query or cast the value through Number() and verify it's not NaN.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning: The vulnerability is confirmed. The code at ddl-builder.ts line 77-79 does exactly `return String(value)` for number field types, directly interpolating the result into DDL SQL without any sanitization. The Zod schema uses `z.unknown().optional()` for defaultValue, allowing any JSON type (including strings) to pass validation. The generated DDL is executed directly via `client.query()` without parameterization. There is no intermediate validation anywhere in the pipeline that checks whether defaultValue is actually numeric when fieldType is "number". An authenticated user with ontology:write scope could supply a malicious string as defaultValue for a number-typed field, which would be interpolated into CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE statements. While PostgreSQL's client.query() typically executes a single statement (limiting semicolon-based injection), SQL subquery injection (e.g., using parenthesized SELECT expressions) remains viable and could lead to data exfiltration or DDL manipulation. Severity is HIGH because it requires authentication with ontology:write scope, but any tenant user with that scope could exploit it.

confirmedFindings.title: Entity metadata update outside transaction in patchEntity
confirmedFindings.description: In patchEntity's backward-compatible path, entityRepo.updateOptimistic() is called which uses the db pool directly (db.query), not the checked-out transaction client. This means the entity metadata update (name, description, isPublic, version bump) is NOT part of the BEGIN/COMMIT transaction that wraps the DDL changes (ADD COLUMN). If the DDL fails and the transaction rolls back, the entity metadata update will already be committed, leaving the entity in an inconsistent state where the version was bumped but the schema change did not apply.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Pass the transaction client to the repository method, or execute the UPDATE directly via client.query() within the transaction block instead of going through the pool.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The bug is confirmed. In `patchEntity`'s backward-compatible path (entity-service.ts lines 411-521), a transaction client is checked out and BEGIN is issued on it. However, `entityRepo.updateOptimistic()` (line 421) calls `db.query()` on the pool (entity-repository.ts line 85), not the transaction client. Similarly, `fieldRepo.update()` (line 474) also calls `db.query()` on the pool (field-repository.ts line 128). Both of these operations execute on separate auto-committing connections, completely outside the transaction.

Meanwhile, the field INSERT statements (line 444) and DDL operations like ADD COLUMN (line 463) correctly use `client.query()` and are part of the transaction.

If the DDL fails (e.g., ADD COLUMN encounters an error), the transaction rolls back the field INSERT and DDL, but the entity metadata update (name, description, is_public, version bump) and field metadata updates (validation_rules, is_indexed, etc.) have already been auto-committed on separate connections. This leaves the entity in an inconsistent state: the version is bumped but the schema change was never applied.

There is no compensating logic or retry mechanism anywhere in the code to handle this scenario. The repository methods do not accept an optional client parameter (unlike `fieldRepo.create` which does accept an optional client), so there is no way to pass the transaction client to them as currently designed.

Note: the `fieldRepo.update()` call (line 474) has the same problem as `entityRepo.updateOptimistic()`, making the scope of the bug even wider than described in the finding.

confirmedFindings.title: Field metadata updates outside transaction in patchEntity
confirmedFindings.description: In patchEntity's backward-compatible path, fieldRepo.update() is called for each updateFields entry. The fieldRepo.update() method uses the pool (db.query) rather than the checked-out transaction client. If any subsequent operation within the transaction block fails and triggers a ROLLBACK, these field metadata updates will already be committed, leaving fields in an inconsistent state.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Either pass the transaction client to fieldRepo.update() (which would require adding a client parameter to the update method), or execute the UPDATE SQL directly via client.query() within the transaction.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The finding is confirmed as a real data integrity bug. Here is the evidence:

1. **fieldRepo.update() uses the pool, not the transaction client.** In `/home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/services/ontology/src/repositories/field-repository.ts`, the `update()` method (lines 101-135) calls `db.query()` where `db` is the `pg.Pool`. It does NOT accept an optional `client` parameter, unlike the `create()` and `createMany()` methods which do. Every call to `fieldRepo.update()` acquires its own connection from the pool and auto-commits immediately.

2. **patchEntity calls fieldRepo.update() inside a transaction block that uses a different connection.** In `entity-service.ts` lines 469-481, within a `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` block running on a checked-out `client`, the code calls `fieldRepo.update(field.id, {...})` which goes through the pool, not through `client`. These updates are immediately visible and committed, completely outside the transaction boundary.

3. **entityRepo.updateOptimistic() has the same problem.** At line 421, `entityRepo.updateOptimistic()` is called, and checking `entity-repository.ts` line 85-86 confirms it also uses `db.query()` (the pool), not the transaction client. So even the entity version bump happens outside the transaction.

4. **The addFields path correctly uses the transaction client.** Lines 444-459 of `entity-service.ts` use `client.query()` directly for field inserts within addFields. This contrast demonstrates the developers intended transactional consistency but failed to achieve it for the updateFields and entity update paths.

5. **Failure scenario is realistic.** If `patchEntity` is called with both `updateFields` and `addFields`, and a DDL statement for addFields fails (e.g., column already exists, type conflict), the ROLLBACK on `client` would undo the addFields inserts done via `client.query()`, but the field metadata updates from `fieldRepo.update()` and the entity version bump from `entityRepo.updateOptimistic()` would remain committed. The entity version would be incremented with field metadata partially updated, while no schema changes were applied -- a clear inconsistent state.

The fix would be to either: (a) make `fieldRepo.update()` accept an optional `client` parameter like `create()` does, and pass the transaction client; or (b) use `client.query()` directly in patchEntity for the field updates, similar to how addFields handles its inserts. The same fix is needed for `entityRepo.updateOptimistic()`.

confirmedFindings.title: Advisory lock acquired on pooled connection is effectively leaked
confirmedFindings.description: confirmMigration acquires a session-level advisory lock via pg_try_advisory_lock on a connection checked out from the pool. The connection is then released back to the pool in the finally block. Session-level advisory locks are bound to the PostgreSQL session (connection), NOT the transaction. When completeMigration or rollbackMigration later tries to release the lock, they acquire a DIFFERENT connection from the pool, so pg_advisory_unlock has no effect -- the lock remains held on the original connection. The lock is only released when the original connection happens to be closed or recycled by the pool.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Use pg_try_advisory_xact_lock instead, which is automatically released when the transaction ends. This requires running the lock acquisition and the subsequent operations within a single transaction. Alternatively, keep the connection reference somewhere accessible so the same connection can be used for the unlock.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The bug is confirmed and real. The code at /home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/services/ontology/src/services/migration-service.ts works exactly as the finding describes.

In `confirmMigration` (lines 188-224), a connection is checked out from `db.connect()`, a session-level advisory lock is acquired via `pg_try_advisory_lock(hashtext($1))` on that connection, and then the connection is released back to the pool in the `finally` block (line 223). The lock remains held on that pooled connection.

In `completeMigration` (lines 242-247), `failMigration` (lines 274-281), and `rollbackMigration` (lines 360-367), a NEW connection is checked out from the pool and `pg_advisory_unlock` is called on it. Since PostgreSQL session-level advisory locks are bound to the specific connection (session) that acquired them, calling `pg_advisory_unlock` on a different connection has no effect -- it silently returns false, and the return value is never checked.

The practical consequence is significant: after a migration completes (or fails, or rolls back), the advisory lock remains held on whichever pooled connection originally acquired it. Since PostgreSQL advisory locks are server-wide, any subsequent `pg_try_advisory_lock` call for the same entity (from any connection other than the original one) will return false, causing a spurious `MigrationInProgressError`. This effectively blocks all future migrations for that entity until the pool recycles the specific connection that holds the orphaned lock.

There is no other code in the codebase that compensates for this issue -- no connection affinity mechanism, no lock cleanup background job, and no alternative unlock path.

confirmedFindings.title: Timer leak in evaluateWithTimeout — setTimeout never cleared on success
confirmedFindings.description: The evaluateWithTimeout function uses Promise.race between the jsonata evaluation and a setTimeout-based timeout. When the evaluation completes successfully (the normal path), the setTimeout timer is never cleared. This happens for every webhook body template evaluation and every responseMapping evaluation. Over many pipeline runs, this creates thousands of orphaned timers that each hold closures referencing the reject function and potentially large data.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Store the timeout handle and clear it in a finally block, similar to how evaluateConditional at line 511 already does correctly: wrap in try/finally, assign the setTimeout to a variable, and clearTimeout it after the race resolves.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The finding is confirmed as a real bug. The `evaluateWithTimeout` function (lines 188-198) uses `Promise.race` with a `setTimeout` but never clears the timer on the success path. The same file contains `evaluateConditional` (lines 500-523) which correctly stores the timeout handle and clears it in a `finally` block -- proving the authors intended this cleanup pattern but missed it in `evaluateWithTimeout`. The function is called on lines 733 and 768 for webhook body template and responseMapping evaluations respectively.

However, the severity should be downgraded from HIGH to LOW. The timeout is only 5 seconds (`JSONATA_WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT_MS = 5_000`), meaning each leaked timer self-resolves after at most 5 seconds. The `reject` call on an already-resolved promise is a no-op. This means timers cannot accumulate unboundedly -- at any point in time, only timers from the last 5 seconds of webhook step evaluations exist. The finding's claim of "thousands of orphaned timers" holding large data indefinitely is overstated. This is a real code quality issue (missing cleanup that the adjacent function handles correctly), but the practical impact is minimal -- short-lived timers that self-expire, with no permanent resource leak.

confirmedFindings.title: SSE subscription leak — unsubscribe never called on client disconnect for non-terminal executions
confirmedFindings.description: When a client connects to the SSE stream for a running execution and then disconnects before the execution completes, the event listener registered via executionTracker.subscribe() is never removed. The code comments acknowledge this problem at lines 217-227 but leave it unresolved. For long-running pipelines (wait steps up to 24h, approval steps), this means every client disconnect leaks an event listener on the EventEmitter, and each listener holds a reference to the ReadableStream controller and encoder, preventing garbage collection.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Use the ReadableStream's cancel callback to call unsubscribe on client disconnect: pass a cancel function in the ReadableStream constructor options: new ReadableStream({ start(controller) { ... }, cancel() { unsubscribe(); } }). Alternatively, hook into the request AbortSignal if available.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The finding is confirmed as real. The code at /home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/services/pipeline/src/routes/executions.ts lines 207-228 matches the description exactly. When a client connects to the SSE stream and then disconnects before the execution reaches a terminal state, the event listener registered via executionTracker.subscribe() is never removed until the execution eventually completes.

Key evidence:

1. The unsubscribe() function is only called inside the "execution:complete" event handler (line 212). There is no cleanup on client disconnect.

2. The code comments at lines 217-227 explicitly acknowledge this as a known unresolved problem. The comment even suggests the fix (c.req.raw.signal.addEventListener("abort", unsubscribe, { once: true })) but states it is not implemented because "Hono does not expose the raw AbortSignal in all environments."

3. The "void unsubscribe;" at line 228 is a no-op statement that does nothing to clean up.

4. While completeExecution() in execution-tracker.ts (line 416) eventually deletes the tracked execution from activeExecutions, removing the emitter reference, this only happens when the execution finishes. Between client disconnect and execution completion, the leaked listener: (a) receives and processes every subsequent step event, wasting CPU on JSON serialization; (b) calls controller.enqueue() on a disconnected ReadableStream, which will throw; (c) holds references to the controller and encoder, preventing GC.

5. For long-running pipelines with wait steps (up to 24h) or approval steps, multiple client connect/disconnect cycles would accumulate listeners on the emitter, each attempting to push data to dead streams on every event.

Severity is appropriately HIGH rather than CRITICAL because: (a) the leak is bounded by execution lifetime -- once completeExecution fires, activeExecutions.delete() makes the emitter and all its listeners eligible for GC; (b) the MAX_ACTIVE_EXECUTIONS cap of 5000 provides an outer bound; (c) this is primarily a resource waste issue rather than a data corruption or security issue. However, for production deployments with long-running pipelines and many SSE clients, this could cause meaningful resource degradation and uncaught exceptions.

confirmedFindings.title: SSRF bypass via IPv4 literal 0.0.0.0 and bare IP addresses
confirmedFindings.description: The assertHostnameResolvesToPublicIp function returns early for bare IPv4 literals (line 161: `if (/^\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/.test(hostname)) return;`), trusting that the URL regex patterns have already blocked them. However, 0.0.0.0 is not matched by any of the BLOCKED_URL_PATTERNS regexes and is not in the BLOCKED_IPV4_RANGES list (0.0.0.0/8 is the unspecified address range). A sandbox user calling context.fetch('http://0.0.0.0:3005/...') could hit the execution service itself or other services bound to all interfaces. This was verified: `isUrlBlocked('http://0.0.0.0:3005')` returns false, and `isIpv4Blocked('0.0.0.0')` returns false.
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet: if (/^\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/.test(hostname)) return;
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Add 0.0.0.0/8 to BLOCKED_IPV4_RANGES: `[0x00000000, 0xff000000]` and do NOT return early for bare IPv4 literals — instead, run them through isIpv4Blocked() before returning. Alternatively, add a regex pattern for 0.0.0.0 to BLOCKED_URL_PATTERNS.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The bug is confirmed and verified by tracing the actual code path and running the validation functions.

The security flow for `context.fetch('http://0.0.0.0:3005')` is:

1. `isUrlBlocked()` (line 238): Returns `false` because none of the `BLOCKED_URL_PATTERNS` regexes match `0.0.0.0`. The patterns cover `127.x.x.x`, `10.x.x.x`, `172.16-31.x.x`, `192.168.x.x`, `169.254.x.x`, `localhost`, and `.service` hostnames, but NOT the `0.0.0.0/8` range.

2. URL parsing (line 250): Succeeds, protocol is `http:` -- passes the scheme check.

3. `assertHostnameResolvesToPublicIp()` (line 266): Called with the parsed URL. On line 161, the hostname `0.0.0.0` matches the bare IPv4 regex `/^\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/`, causing an immediate `return` with no IP-level validation. The code comment says "Bare IP literals pass through the regex checks above; no DNS lookup needed" -- but the regex checks above did NOT block `0.0.0.0`.

4. The fetch proceeds to `0.0.0.0:3005`.

On Linux, `0.0.0.0` resolves to the local machine for services bound to all interfaces (INADDR_ANY). A sandbox user could use this to reach the execution service itself or any co-located service (gateway, auth, etc.) on their known ports, constituting an SSRF vulnerability.

Additionally confirmed: `isIpv4Blocked('0.0.0.0')` returns `false` because `0.0.0.0/8` is not in `BLOCKED_IPV4_RANGES`. Even if the early return were removed, the IP-level check would still not catch it. There are no tests for this case, no middleware layer providing additional protection, and no other code in the execution service handling `0.0.0.0`.

confirmedFindings.title: SSRF bypass via IPv6 literal URLs (e.g. http://[::1], http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1])
confirmedFindings.description: IPv6 literal hostnames in URLs (like http://[::1] or http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]) are not caught by the BLOCKED_URL_PATTERNS regexes, AND assertHostnameResolvesToPublicIp returns early for them at line 162 (`if (hostname.startsWith('[') || hostname.includes(':')) return;`). The code assumes the regex patterns have already handled them, but the regexes only match IPv4 and hostname patterns. Verified: `isUrlBlocked('http://[::1]')` returns false. This allows sandbox code to reach the loopback interface via `context.fetch('http://[::1]:3005/...')`. The ::ffff:N.N.N.N mapped form bypasses all checks for any internal IPv4 address.
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet: if (hostname.startsWith("[") || hostname.includes(":")) return; // IPv6 literal
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Do not return early for IPv6 literals. Instead, strip brackets from the hostname, then check against isIpv6Blocked(). For ::ffff:-prefixed addresses (IPv4-mapped IPv6), extract the IPv4 part and also check it against isIpv4Blocked(). Add regex patterns for IPv6 literals to BLOCKED_URL_PATTERNS as well.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The SSRF bypass via IPv6 literal URLs is a confirmed, real vulnerability. The code path is:

1. `isUrlBlocked('http://[::1]:3005/path')` returns false -- none of the BLOCKED_URL_PATTERNS regexes match IPv6 bracket notation (they only cover IPv4 dotted-decimal and hostname patterns).

2. `assertHostnameResolvesToPublicIp` receives hostname `[::1]` from `new URL(...)`. At line 162, it checks `hostname.startsWith("[") || hostname.includes(":")` and returns early, skipping all DNS resolution and IP validation. The comment says "IPv6 literal" -- the assumption is that regex patterns already caught these, but they did not.

3. The `isIpv6Blocked` function (line 137) exists and correctly identifies `::1` as blocked, but it is NEVER invoked for direct IPv6 URL literals. It is only called in the DNS resolution branch (lines 193-199), which is entirely skipped by the early return on line 162.

4. The fetch then proceeds to `http://[::1]:3005/path`, reaching the loopback interface.

5. IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses like `::ffff:10.0.0.1` present a double bypass: they skip the early-return path AND are not caught by `isIpv6Blocked` since `::ffff:` is not in `BLOCKED_IPV6_PREFIXES`.

6. No IPv6-related test cases exist in the test file, confirming this was an oversight.

This allows sandbox code to reach any internal service via `context.fetch('http://[::1]:PORT/...')` or `context.fetch('http://[::ffff:INTERNAL_IP]:PORT/...')`, defeating the SSRF protection that is the sole outbound proxy security layer (the sandbox itself has no direct network access, per the code comments).

confirmedFindings.title: Cross-app role modification via missing app_id check in updateRole/deleteRole
confirmedFindings.description: The updateRole and deleteRole methods verify that the authenticated user's tenant owns the specified appId (via assertAppAccess), but then pass only the roleId to the repository without verifying the role actually belongs to that app. An attacker who owns app A can modify or delete roles belonging to app B (owned by a different user in the same or different tenant) by sending PATCH /apps/{ownAppId}/roles/{victimRoleId}. The assertAppAccess passes because ownAppId is valid, then permRepo.updateRole(victimRoleId, input) updates the victim's role since the SQL WHERE clause only filters by id, not app_id.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Use permRepo.findRoleByAppAndId(appId, roleId) to verify the role belongs to the app before updating/deleting, or change the repository methods to include app_id in the WHERE clause: UPDATE app.roles SET ... WHERE id = $1 AND app_id = $2
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The vulnerability is confirmed through end-to-end code analysis across three layers:

1. **Route handler** (apps.ts:352-381): Extracts `appId` from `:id` URL param and `roleId` from `:roleId` URL param, passes both to the service.

2. **Service layer** (permission-service.ts:113-132): Both `updateRole` and `deleteRole` call `assertAppAccess(tenantId, appId)` to verify the tenant owns the app, but then pass ONLY `roleId` to the repository methods `permRepo.updateRole(roleId, input)` and `permRepo.deleteRole(roleId)`, without verifying the role belongs to the specified app.

3. **Repository layer** (permission-repository.ts:68-105): `updateRole` SQL is `UPDATE app.roles SET ... WHERE id = $N` and `deleteRole` SQL is `DELETE FROM app.roles WHERE id = $1` - both filter only by role ID, not by app_id.

The attack is straightforward: an attacker who owns app A sends `PATCH /apps/{appA_id}/roles/{victimRoleId}` or `DELETE /apps/{appA_id}/roles/{victimRoleId}`. The `assertAppAccess` passes because appA belongs to the attacker's tenant, then the repository modifies/deletes the victim's role since the SQL WHERE clause has no app_id constraint.

Notably, the repository already has a `findRoleByAppAndId(appId, id)` method that correctly filters by both columns, but the service never uses it for update/delete. Also, other operations like `deleteEnvVar` correctly pass `appId` to the repository (WHERE app_id = $1 AND key = $2), highlighting that the role operations are inconsistently implemented.

This is a cross-tenant/cross-app privilege escalation that allows arbitrary role modification and deletion across application boundaries.

confirmedFindings.title: isOriginAllowed never matches because Origin header includes scheme but patterns do not
confirmedFindings.description: The isOriginAllowed function compares the raw HTTP Origin header (e.g., 'https://example.com') against allowedOrigins patterns that are bare hostnames (e.g., 'example.com'). The schema validation (originPattern regex) ensures origins are stored as hostnames without a scheme prefix. Since browsers always send the Origin header with a scheme (e.g., 'https://example.com'), the exact match (pattern === requestOrigin) will never succeed for non-wildcard entries, and the suffix match for wildcards (*.example.com) also fails because 'https://sub.example.com' does not end with '.example.com' when the actual suffix check is against '.example.com' without scheme. This means all legitimate cross-origin embed requests are rejected with 403.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Parse the requestOrigin to extract the hostname (new URL(requestOrigin).hostname) before comparing against the allowedOrigins patterns, or store allowedOrigins with scheme prefixes and compare against the full Origin header.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The bug is real for the exact-match case but the finding overstates the wildcard case.

**Confirmed evidence:**

1. The `originPattern` regex in `/home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/services/app/src/schemas/index.ts` (line 171) enforces that stored origins are bare hostnames without a scheme (e.g., `example.com`, not `https://example.com`).

2. In `/home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/services/app/src/routes/embed.ts` (line 236), the raw `Origin` header is read directly: `c.req.header("Origin") ?? ""`. No normalization is performed. Browsers always send the Origin header with a scheme (e.g., `https://example.com`).

3. In `isOriginAllowed` (embed-service.ts line 332), the exact match `pattern === requestOrigin` compares `"example.com"` against `"https://example.com"`, which is always `false`. Verified with Node.js.

4. The `buildFrameAncestors` function in the same file correctly prepends `https://` to bare hostnames when building CSP frame-ancestors (line 322-324: `https://${o}`), confirming the system knows the origins are stored as bare hostnames but `isOriginAllowed` fails to account for this.

5. The tests (embed-service.test.ts line 392) test with bare hostnames on both sides (`isOriginAllowed("example.com", ["example.com"])`), which does not reflect real browser behavior.

**Partial correction to the finding:** The wildcard suffix match (`*.example.com`) actually DOES work with scheme-prefixed origins by accident: `"https://sub.example.com".endsWith(".example.com")` returns `true`. This was verified with Node.js. So the finding's claim that wildcard matching also fails is incorrect.

**Impact:** Any user who configures exact hostname origins (e.g., `["example.com"]`) will find that all legitimate cross-origin embed requests from `https://example.com` are rejected with 403. Only the `*` wildcard and `*.domain.com` patterns will work. This is a meaningful bug since exact hostname matching is the most common use case for origin restrictions.

Severity adjusted to MEDIUM because: (a) wildcard patterns still work, (b) the `*` catch-all still works, (c) only exact hostname patterns are broken, and (d) the CSP frame-ancestors header (generated by `buildFrameAncestors`) provides a second layer of origin enforcement that IS correct.

confirmedFindings.title: CSP blocks inline script in app serving HTML shell, breaking app config injection
confirmedFindings.description: The app serving HTML shell at /apps/:slug/ contains an inline <script> tag that sets window.__OP_APP_CONFIG__. However, the Content-Security-Policy header sets script-src to only 'self' without 'unsafe-inline' or a nonce. This causes the browser to block the inline script, preventing the app from receiving its configuration. The embed serve route correctly handles this by generating a per-request nonce, but the main app serving route does not. Without the config, the app SDK cannot initialize (appId, tenantId, etc. are not available).
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Generate a per-request nonce (like the embed route does), add it to the <script> tag as a nonce attribute, and include 'nonce-{value}' in the script-src CSP directive. Alternatively add 'unsafe-inline' to script-src, though the nonce approach is more secure.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The finding is confirmed as a real bug. The evidence is clear:

1. The code at lines 559-592 of /home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/services/app/src/index.ts generates an HTML shell with an inline script tag (line 580-582) that sets window.__OP_APP_CONFIG__, but the CSP header on line 591 specifies script-src 'self' without 'unsafe-inline' or a nonce. This means CSP-compliant browsers will block the inline script execution.

2. The embed serve route in /home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/services/app/src/routes/embed.ts (lines 268-304) correctly handles this same pattern by generating a per-request nonce with randomBytes(16), attaching it to the script tag as a nonce attribute, and including 'nonce-${nonce}' in the CSP script-src directive. This proves the developers were aware of the issue for embeds but missed it on the main app serving route.

3. The impact is significant: without the config object (appId, tenantId, appSlug, bffOrigin), the app SDK cannot initialize. The external bundle.js will load (it matches 'self'), but the config it depends on will not be available, causing the app to fail at runtime.

The fix is straightforward: apply the same nonce pattern from the embed route to the main app serving route - generate a nonce, add nonce="..." to the inline script tag, and add 'nonce-${nonce}' to the CSP script-src directive.

confirmedFindings.title: Entity path parameter not encoded in upstream URL allows SSRF path traversal
confirmedFindings.description: In the BFF data proxy routes (GET/POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE /bff/data/:entity), the entity parameter from the URL path is interpolated directly into the upstream execution service URL without encoding: `${executionServiceUrl}/internal/data/${user.tenantId}/${appId}/${entity}`. If entity contains URL-encoded path traversal characters (e.g., '..%2F..%2Fadmin'), the Hono router decodes the path parameter, and the resulting entity value with slashes/dots is concatenated raw into the upstream URL. While the itemId is properly encoded with encodeURIComponent in PATCH/PUT/DELETE routes, entity is never encoded in any of the data proxy routes.
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet: const upstreamUrl = `${executionServiceUrl}/internal/data/${user.tenantId}/${appId}/${entity}${queryParams ? `?${queryParams}` : ""}`;
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Apply encodeURIComponent(entity) when constructing the upstream URL, or validate that entity matches an expected pattern (e.g., /^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$/) before forwarding the request.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The vulnerability is confirmed through code review and empirical testing. The entity path parameter extracted by Hono (e.g., from /bff/data/:entity) decodes URL-encoded characters like %2F to /, so a request to /bff/data/..%2F..%2F..%2F..%2Fsome-endpoint yields entity="../../../../some-endpoint". This value is interpolated directly into the upstream URL string without encodeURIComponent, and when fetch() parses the resulting URL, path normalization resolves the .. segments, allowing traversal out of the intended /internal/data/{tenantId}/{appId}/ prefix.

Empirical test confirmed: entity="../../../../other-service-endpoint" resolves to http://execution-service:3005/other-service-endpoint, completely escaping the intended path hierarchy. The RBAC check (assertEntityPermission) is bypassable when a user holds a role with wildcard entity "*". No gateway or middleware-level path normalization exists to prevent this.

The inconsistency is stark: itemId IS properly encoded with encodeURIComponent (lines 342, 391, 439), and the gateway's own gRPC data service also correctly uses encodeURIComponent for entityType, confirming this was an oversight specifically in the BFF data proxy routes. The finding correctly identifies a real SSRF path traversal vulnerability that allows an authenticated user to make the app service issue internal requests (carrying a valid service token) to arbitrary paths on the execution service.

confirmedFindings.title: SQL syntax error when cursor is used without any filter conditions
confirmedFindings.description: In LogEventRepository.query(), when a cursor is provided but all filter parameters (tenantId, service, level, traceId, search, from, to) are undefined, the whereClause is an empty string but cursorClause starts with 'AND'. The resulting SQL is 'FROM logging.events  AND (created_at, id) < ...' which is a SQL syntax error. This is reachable by admin users calling GET /api/v1/logs?cursor=xxx with no other filters, or by the internal query route (POST /internal/logging/query) with only cursor and limit in the body.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: When conditions is empty but cursorClause is non-empty, the cursorClause should use WHERE instead of AND. confirmedFindings.title: Auth middleware does not handle wildcard (*) glob patterns in publicRoutes

confirmedFindings.title: createApp does not pass jwtPublicKey to authMiddleware, blocking EdDSA user token verification
confirmedFindings.description: The CreateAppConfig interface (line 77) has no jwtPublicKey field, and createApp (line 185-193) does not pass jwtPublicKey when constructing the authMiddleware config. 2. `createApp` (app.ts lines 185-193) calls `authMiddleware()` with only `jwtSecret`, `redis`, `validateApiKey`, and `publicRoutes` -- it never passes `jwtPublicKey`.

3. `AuthMiddlewareConfig` (middleware/auth.ts lines 24-39) does declare `jwtPublicKey?: string` as an optional field and fully implements EdDSA verification when provided (lines 62-74 parse the key at startup, lines 144-163 use it for verification).

4. When `jwtPublicKey` is absent, the middleware explicitly rejects EdDSA tokens with a 401: "EdDSA token received but no public key is configured" (middleware/auth.ts lines 147-158).

5. The auth service's token-service.ts (lines 115-122, 290-330) fully supports `OP_JWT_ALGORITHM=EdDSA` and will issue EdDSA-signed tokens.

7. The EdDSA tests in auth-eddsa.test.ts exercise `authMiddleware` directly, not through `createApp`, so they pass -- but they don't cover the integration gap.

confirmedFindings.title: API key prefix leaked in error message
confirmedFindings.description: When an invalid API key is provided, the error message exposes the first 8 characters of the key: `apiKey.slice(0, 8)`. Since valid keys start with 'op_live_' or 'op_test_' (exactly 8 characters), the slice reveals the entire prefix plus nothing useful for debugging. But for keys that don't match the expected prefixes, this leaks 8 characters of what might be a secret token from a different system that was accidentally passed here. Error messages can end up in logs, Sentry, or user-facing error pages.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Remove the key prefix from the error message entirely, or only show the first 3-4 characters, or only show the characters if they match an expected prefix pattern. For example: `Received key starting with: "${apiKey.slice(0, 3)}..."`

When an API key does not start with "op_live_" or "op_test_", the error message includes `apiKey.slice(0, 8)`, leaking the first 8 characters of whatever string was passed. If a user accidentally passes a secret from another system (e.g., a Stripe key, AWS key, or other credential), those 8 characters would be exposed in error messages that can end up in logs, Sentry, CI output, or error responses. There is no redaction or sanitization elsewhere in the error pipeline. The fix is trivial: remove the slice from the error message since the message already tells users what valid prefixes look like. confirmedFindings.title: Transport unwraps {data: T} envelope incorrectly - falsy data values silently dropped
confirmedFindings.description: The envelope unwrapping logic at lines 470-476 checks `if (envelope.data !== undefined && envelope.data !== null)` and returns envelope.data when truthy. But when the server returns `{data: 0}`, `{data: false}`, or `{data: ""}` (legitimate responses for count endpoints, boolean toggles, etc.), the check passes for 0 and false and empty-string since they are not undefined/null, so those are returned correctly. However, the same logic exists in `executeMultipartRequest` (line 347) and the two copies could diverge. More importantly, if the server response has no `data` key at all (e.g. `{items: [...], nextCursor: null}`) the code falls through to `return parsed as T`, which works. But if the server returns `{data: null}` to explicitly mean 'no result', the code falls through and returns the entire envelope `{data: null}` as type T instead of returning null. Callers expecting `T | null` get an object with a data property instead.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: When `envelope.data === null`, return `null as T` explicitly instead of falling through to return the raw envelope. Change the logic to: `if (envelope.data !== undefined) return envelope.data as T; return parsed as T;` -- this correctly returns null when data is explicitly null, and only falls through to the raw parse when there is no data key at all.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The code exists exactly as described at lines 467-476 (and the identical copy at lines 345-348 for multipart). The `{data: null}` unwrapping defect is real: when the server returns `{data: null}` to indicate "no result", the check `envelope.data !== undefined && envelope.data !== null` evaluates to false, causing the code to fall through to `return parsed as T`, which returns the entire `{data: null}` envelope object instead of `null`. The comment on lines 468-469 explicitly acknowledges this case ("some server responses set data: null to indicate 'no result'") but the implementation fails to handle it correctly.

Confirmed server endpoints that return `{data: null}`: billing.ts line 83 (`c.json({ data: null })`) and reconciliation.ts line 105 (`c.json({ data: report ?? null })`).

However, the severity should be reduced from HIGH to LOW because:
1. No existing SDK resource method currently uses a nullable type parameter (`request<T | null>`), so the bug is latent.
2. The two server endpoints returning `{data: null}` do not have corresponding SDK resource modules yet.
3. The finding's other sub-claims are weak: falsy values (0, false, "") are handled correctly by the `!== undefined && !== null` check (the finding itself admits this); the "two copies could diverge" concern is speculative maintenance risk, not a bug.
4. When SDK resources are added for these endpoints, the bug would manifest, making this a real but currently latent correctness issue.

confirmedFindings.title: ESM bundle source embedded in vm.Script context fails to populate exports
confirmedFindings.description: The wrappedSource string directly embeds the raw bundle source (which is ESM format per the scaffold's esbuild --format=esm) into a vm.Script context that uses CommonJS-style `exports[__entrypoint]` access. ESM syntax (`export const foo = ...`) is not valid inside vm.Script and will either throw a SyntaxError or silently fail to populate the `exports` object. This means `op plugin simulate-hook` will always fail with 'Bundle does not export ...' for any ESM plugin bundle. In contrast, pack.ts correctly handles this by calling toBundleCjs() before running in vm.Script.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Convert the bundleSource from ESM to CJS before embedding it in the vm.Script context, the same way pack.ts does with its toBundleCjs() helper. Import and call toBundleCjs(bundleSource) before constructing wrappedSource, then reference the CJS exports.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The bug is confirmed real. The evidence is clear:

1. **Code exists as described**: `simulate-hook.ts` lines 257-277 embed the raw `bundleSource` directly into a `vm.Script` wrapper that expects CommonJS-style `exports[__entrypoint]` access.

2. **Bundles are ESM format**: Both the scaffold template (`scaffold.ts` line 673: `--format=esm`) and the pack build step (`pack.ts` line 279: `"--format=esm"`) produce ESM-format bundles. esbuild ESM output uses `export { ... }` syntax, which is a module-level declaration not valid in script mode.

3. **vm.Script cannot execute ESM syntax**: `vm.Script` uses V8's classic script evaluator, not the ES module evaluator. ESM `export` declarations will throw a `SyntaxError` because they are only valid at the top level of a module, not inside a script context.

4. **pack.ts correctly handles this, simulate-hook.ts does not**: `pack.ts` has a `toBundleCjs()` function (lines 491-503) that uses esbuild's `transform` API to convert ESM to CJS before running in `vm.Script`. Both `verifyEntrypoint()` and `verifyMetadataType()` call `toBundleCjs()` first. `simulate-hook.ts` skips this conversion entirely.

5. **Practical impact**: Every plugin scaffolded by `op plugin init` will produce an ESM bundle via `npm run build`. Running `op plugin simulate-hook` on that bundle will always fail with a `SyntaxError` from the `export` statements in the ESM bundle, making the simulate-hook command completely broken for the default project setup. The fix would be to add a `toBundleCjs()` call (or equivalent) before embedding the source in the vm.Script wrapper.

confirmedFindings.title: Insecure file permission check allows overly-permissive credentials files
confirmedFindings.description: checkCredentialsPermissions() uses `mode > SECURE_MODE` (numeric comparison: `mode > 0o600`) to determine if the file is insecurely permissive. This is a numeric comparison on the raw permission bits, which gives incorrect results. For example, 0o440 (r--r-----) is numerically less than 0o600 (rw-------) but is a group-readable file -- arguably insecure since the credentials are readable by the group. More critically, 0o060 (---rw-----, group read/write) is numerically less than 0o600 and would pass the check without warning, despite granting group access to the credentials file. The correct approach is to check if any bits outside owner-read-write are set: `(mode & 0o177) !== 0`.
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet:
const mode = stats.mode & 0o777;
if (mode > SECURE_MODE) {
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Replace `if (mode > SECURE_MODE)` with `if ((mode & 0o177) !== 0)` to correctly detect any permissions granted to group or others (any bits beyond owner rw).
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The bug is confirmed real. The code at line 188 uses `mode > SECURE_MODE` (i.e., `mode > 0o600` which is `mode > 384` in decimal) to detect insecure permissions. This numeric comparison fails to detect permission patterns where group or other bits are set but the total numeric value is below 384. Verified examples: 0o440 (owner+group read, decimal 288) passes the check silently despite being group-readable; 0o060 (group rw, decimal 48) passes despite granting group full read-write; 0o004 (world-readable, decimal 4) passes despite being readable by everyone. The correct check would be `(mode & 0o177) !== 0` to catch any bits outside owner read-write.

However, the practical severity should be adjusted downward from HIGH to MEDIUM for several reasons: (1) this is a warning-only check that never blocks operations -- it only prints to stderr, so the security boundary does not depend on it; (2) writeCredentialsFile always enforces chmod 600 on write, so under normal operation permissions are always correct; (3) the most dangerous missed patterns (0o060, 0o004) are unrealistic because the file owner couldn't read the file either, making the CLI non-functional; (4) the most realistic missed case is 0o440 (group-readable), which requires deliberate external permission changes. It is a genuine logic error in a security-relevant check, but the defense-in-depth design limits its practical impact.

confirmedFindings.title: Silent fallback to machine-id decryption when keychain entry is missing -- masks credential theft
confirmedFindings.description: In decryptEntry(), when a credential was stored with keyDerivation='keychain' but the keychain entry is missing (e.g., deleted or on a different machine), the code silently falls through to machine-id derivation (line 240-241). Since the credential was encrypted with a random 32-byte key stored in the keychain, decrypting with the machine-id derived key will always fail with a crypto error. However, the intent to silently fall through means no warning is issued about the missing keychain entry. Worse, if an attacker replaces the credentials.json and changes keyDerivation to 'machine-id' while copying the file to a machine where they control machine-id, the fallback would successfully decrypt without any warning. The fallback should either not exist for keychain-encrypted credentials, or should at minimum issue a clear warning.

The fallback will almost certainly fail anyway (wrong key), but silently attempting it hides the real problem from the user.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning: The code exists exactly as described at lines 225-242 of /home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/packages/cli/src/lib/credentials.ts. The silent fallthrough from keychain to machine-id derivation is real and does lack any warning message. However, the severity is overstated. The "credential theft" scenario described in the finding is not practically exploitable: (1) If a credential was encrypted with a random keychain key and the attacker changes keyDerivation to "machine-id", decryption will still fail because AES-256-GCM authentication tag verification will reject the wrong key - AES-GCM is an authenticated cipher, so you cannot silently decrypt with the wrong key.
