confirmedFindings.title: Open redirect via backslash-to-slash normalization bypass in safeRedirect
confirmedFindings.description: The safeRedirect function blocks protocol-relative URLs starting with '//' but allows paths like '/\evil.com' through. Many browsers normalize backslashes to forward slashes in URL contexts, so when the returned value is assigned to window.location.href (as done in CallbackPage.tsx line 54 and LoginPage.tsx line 49), '/\evil.com' becomes '//evil.com' -- a protocol-relative URL that redirects the user to an attacker-controlled domain. This is a classic open redirect bypass.
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet: if (raw.startsWith("/") && !raw.startsWith("//")) return raw;
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Add a check for backslash after the leading slash: if (raw.startsWith("/") && !raw.startsWith("//") && !raw.startsWith("/\\")) return raw; -- or more robustly, replace all backslashes with forward slashes first and re-validate, or use new URL(raw, window.location.origin) and verify the origin matches.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The vulnerability is confirmed through code review and programmatic verification:

1. The code exists exactly as described in auth-utils.ts line 13: `if (raw.startsWith("/") && !raw.startsWith("//")) return raw;`

2. The bypass is real: An attacker supplies `/%5Cevil.com` (URL-encoded backslash) as the redirect parameter. `safeRedirect` sees `/\evil.com` which starts with `/` but not `//`, so it passes validation and is returned unchanged.

3. The sink is confirmed: Both CallbackPage.tsx (line 54) and LoginPage.tsx (line 49) assign the result directly to `window.location.href`.

4. Browser normalization confirms the exploit: The WHATWG URL spec (which all modern browsers implement) normalizes backslashes to forward slashes in "special scheme" URLs. Node's WHATWG-compliant URL parser confirms: `new URL('/\\evil.com', 'https://app.example.com')` resolves to `https://evil.com/`. This means `/\evil.com` becomes `//evil.com` (protocol-relative), redirecting the user to the attacker's domain.

5. No other mitigations exist between safeRedirect and window.location.href assignment.

This is a classic open redirect bypass via backslash normalization. The fix should also reject paths where the second character is a backslash, e.g. checking `!raw.startsWith("/\\")` alongside the `//` check.

confirmedFindings.title: topologicalSort is documented as Kahn's algorithm but is plain BFS, producing incorrect step order
confirmedFindings.description: The topologicalSort function computes in-degree for every node (lines 199-206) but never uses it. It performs a simple BFS from the entry node, adding neighbors to the queue as soon as they are discovered. Kahn's algorithm requires decrementing in-degree when processing an edge and only enqueuing a node when its in-degree reaches 0. Without this, steps can appear before their dependencies in the output. For example, with edges A->B, A->C, C->B, the function returns [A, B, C] instead of the correct [A, C, B]. When this result is sent to graphToPipelineDefinition and saved to the API, pipeline steps will be in the wrong execution order.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Implement actual Kahn's algorithm: seed the queue with all nodes that have in-degree 0, and when processing outgoing edges, decrement the in-degree of each neighbor. Only enqueue the neighbor when its in-degree reaches 0. Remove the visited set and use the in-degree map for cycle detection (if result.length < nodes.length, there is a cycle).
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The bug is confirmed by reading the actual source at /home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/packages/frontend/src/components/pipeline-editor/graph-converter.ts.

1. The code exists exactly as described. The `topologicalSort` function (lines 194-233) computes `inDegree` on lines 199-206 but never references it again. The actual traversal (lines 209-225) is a plain BFS using a `visited` set, enqueuing neighbors as soon as they are discovered rather than when their in-degree reaches zero.

2. The bug is real. Kahn's algorithm requires decrementing in-degree when processing edges and only enqueuing nodes when in-degree reaches 0. This code does neither. I traced the finding's example (edges A->B, A->C, C->B) and confirmed the function returns [A, B, C] when the correct topological order is [A, C, B], because C must precede B due to the C->B edge.

3. This matters in practice because `graphToPipelineDefinition` (line 134) uses the topological sort result to determine the order of steps in the output `ConvertibleDefinition`. The `buildEdgesFromDefinition` function derives edges from sequential array order, so round-tripping a pipeline with conditional branches (which create convergent DAG patterns) through graph and back could corrupt step ordering. Specifically, conditional steps with `thenStepId`/`elseStepId` create diamond-shaped subgraphs where BFS can visit a merge node before all its predecessors, producing an incorrect execution order in the saved pipeline definition.

confirmedFindings.title: Auth credentials stored in plain text in serializable handle metadata
confirmedFindings.description: The connect() method stores the raw auth header value (bearer token, API key, or base64-encoded username:password) directly in ConnectorHandle.metadata. The ConnectorHandle interface's JSDoc states 'the platform may checkpoint this between calls', meaning this metadata is serialized and persisted (likely to a database). This means raw credentials are written to durable storage in plain text. The auth header field contains the literal bearer token, literal API key, or the base64-encoded password -- all of which are trivially reversible or directly usable by anyone with access to the checkpoint storage.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Do not store credentials in handle metadata. Instead, re-resolve credentials from context.credentials.get() at the start of each fetchBatch() call. The credentials accessor is available on every PluginContext, and the platform manages secure credential storage and rotation. This also handles credential rotation between fetchBatch() calls, which the current design misses.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The code exists exactly as described. The `connect()` method at lines 509-524 of `/home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/plugins/connector-rest-api/src/index.ts` stores raw auth credentials (bearer tokens, API keys, base64-encoded username:password) in `HandleMetadata.authHeader`, which is placed in `ConnectorHandle.metadata`.

The `ConnectorHandle` interface JSDoc (line 29 of `packages/plugin-sdk/src/types/connector.ts`) explicitly states: "Must be JSON-serializable (the platform may checkpoint this between calls)." This is a documented contract that metadata may be persisted.

However, the current platform implementation does NOT actually checkpoint handle metadata to durable storage. The sync service (`services/ingestion/src/services/sync-service.ts`) calls the Execution Service via HTTP for each `fetchBatch`, passing `config`, `credentialBundleId`, and `cursor` -- not the handle metadata. The `ConnectorRunRequestSchema` in the execution service does not include a handle/metadata field. The `connect()` and `fetchBatch()` calls happen within the same sandbox execution, so the handle remains in-memory only and is discarded when the sandbox terminates.

Additionally, the platform already has a proper encrypted credential system (`PluginContext.credentials`), which the connector uses to retrieve credentials. The credentials are encrypted at rest via the credential service. The connector correctly uses this system to obtain credentials but then copies the raw values into handle metadata, which is a design-level violation of the credential isolation pattern.

The finding is real as a security design flaw: (1) it violates the credential isolation principle by copying decrypted secrets into a structure the interface explicitly warns may be checkpointed, (2) it exposes credentials in sandbox memory longer than necessary, and (3) it creates a latent risk that would become critical if checkpointing is ever implemented. The postgres-cdc-connector correctly avoids this by storing only non-sensitive connection metadata. However, the severity should be adjusted downward from HIGH to MEDIUM because in the current implementation, the metadata is never actually persisted to durable storage -- the risk is latent rather than actively exploitable.

confirmedFindings.title: Link-header pagination follows arbitrary URLs without origin validation (SSRF vector)
confirmedFindings.description: When paginationType is 'link', the connector blindly follows the URL extracted from the Link header on subsequent requests. The cursor.nextUrl is used directly as the fetch URL without validating that it belongs to the same origin as the configured baseUrl. A malicious or compromised API could return a Link header pointing to an internal network address (e.g., http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ for cloud metadata, or http://localhost:6379/ for Redis). The FetchProxy does enforce a URL allowlist, but the manifest declares 'https://**' which allows any HTTPS URL, so a redirect to any external HTTPS endpoint would also succeed.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Before using cursor.nextUrl, validate that its origin (protocol + hostname + port) matches the configured baseUrl origin. For example: `const nextOrigin = new URL(cursor.nextUrl).origin; const baseOrigin = new URL(meta.baseUrl).origin; if (nextOrigin !== baseOrigin) throw new PluginDataError('Link header next URL origin does not match baseUrl');`
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The finding is confirmed as a real security issue, though the severity should be adjusted downward based on the existing mitigations.

**Code exists as described:** Yes. In `/home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/plugins/connector-rest-api/src/index.ts`, lines 660-666, the `buildRequestUrl` method for "link" pagination directly uses `cursor.nextUrl` without any origin validation:
```
case "link": {
  if (cursor?.nextUrl !== undefined) {
    return { url: cursor.nextUrl, isLinkFollowRequest: true };
  }
```
The `nextUrl` comes from `parseNextLinkHeader()` (line 373), which extracts the raw URL from the Link header with no origin checking. This URL is then stored in the cursor and used directly in `context.fetch.fetch(url, ...)` on the next batch call.

**What the finding gets right:**
1. There is no origin validation - the connector does not compare the Link header URL's origin against the configured `baseUrl`.
2. A malicious or compromised API could return a Link header pointing to an arbitrary URL.
3. The manifest declares `"requiredExternalUrls": ["https://**"]` which is maximally permissive.

**What the finding gets partially wrong about mitigations:**
The finding states "The FetchProxy does enforce a URL allowlist" but in reality, the `requiredExternalUrls` allowlist is NOT enforced at all - there is zero code in the execution service's `context-call-handler.ts` that checks the manifest's `requiredExternalUrls`. The fetch handler only enforces a blocklist.

**Existing mitigations that reduce severity:**
1. The execution service's `handleFetch` blocks RFC 1918, localhost, link-local (169.254.x.x), and internal `.service` hostnames via regex patterns (lines 92-108).
2. DNS rebinding protection via `assertHostnameResolvesToPublicIp` resolves hostnames and checks IPs against blocked CIDR ranges (lines 113-119), blocking cloud metadata endpoints even through DNS tricks.
3. Redirect handling uses `redirect: "manual"` and validates each redirect hop's destination.
4. Only http/https schemes are permitted.

So the cloud metadata attack vector (http://169.254.169.254) mentioned in the finding is actually blocked by the execution service. Internal Redis (localhost:6379) is also blocked. However, a malicious API could still redirect the connector to any arbitrary external HTTPS endpoint (e.g., exfiltrating auth headers to an attacker-controlled server), which is a real concern. The connector sends its authentication headers (API key, bearer token, basic auth) to whatever URL the Link header specifies, since `buildHeaders` applies auth unconditionally.

The core issue is real: the connector should validate that Link header URLs share the same origin as `baseUrl` before following them, to prevent credential leakage to attacker-controlled external servers. The SSRF-to-internal-network angle is largely mitigated by the execution service, but the credential-forwarding-to-external-attacker angle is not.

confirmedFindings.title: Incremental sync skips rows with duplicate cursor values at batch boundaries
confirmedFindings.description: In fetchBatchIncremental, the cursor is set to the last row's incrementalColumn value (line 657). The proxy is expected to filter with 'WHERE incrementalColumn > cursor_value' (strictly greater, as stated in the comment on line 636-637). If multiple rows share the same incrementalColumn value and the batch boundary falls in the middle of that group, subsequent rows with that value are permanently skipped. For example, if batchSize=2 and three rows all have updated_at='2024-01-01T00:00:00Z', the first batch returns two of them and sets cursor to '2024-01-01T00:00:00Z'. The next fetch uses '> 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z', skipping the third row entirely. This is silent data loss.
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet: nextCursor = encodeCursor({ mode: "incremental", lastValue: String(colValue) });
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Use a compound cursor that includes both the incrementalColumn value and a tiebreaker (e.g., the primary key). Alternatively, use '>=' (greater-than-or-equal) with deduplication by sourceId, or switch to keyset pagination using (incrementalColumn, primaryKey) as the composite sort key to guarantee unique ordering.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The finding is confirmed as a real bug. The code at line 657 sets the cursor to the last row's incrementalColumn value (e.g., updated_at). The proxy contract, explicitly documented at line 16 ("WHERE incrementalColumn > cursor") and line 73 ("Only rows with a strictly greater value are returned"), uses strict greater-than filtering. No proxy implementation exists in this codebase to check -- it is external -- but the contract is unambiguous.

The problem: if multiple rows share the same incrementalColumn value and a batch boundary falls within that group, the cursor is set to that shared value. The next fetch uses "> that_value", permanently skipping any remaining rows with the same value. This is a classic cursor-based pagination bug with non-unique cursor columns.

This is realistic because: (1) the typical incrementalColumn is a timestamp like "updated_at" which can easily have duplicate values from batch updates, ORM defaults, or limited precision; (2) there is no secondary sort key or tie-breaking mechanism; (3) there is no >= filtering with deduplication; (4) the tests only exercise cases with unique cursor values and never test the duplicate-value scenario.

The severity is appropriately rated HIGH because this causes silent, permanent data loss -- rows are skipped without any error or warning.

confirmedFindings.title: Manifest configSchema marks 'table' as required, blocking customQuery-only usage
confirmedFindings.description: Both the manifest configSchema (line 15) and the CONNECTOR_METADATA configSchema (src/index.ts line 378) declare 'required: ["proxyUrl", "table"]'. However, the implementation in parseConfig (line 191-201) explicitly supports configs with only 'customQuery' and no 'table'. The platform validates incoming config against the manifest's JSON Schema before the plugin code runs. Since 'table' is required in the schema, any config using customQuery without table will be rejected at the platform level, making the entire customQuery feature dead code that can never be used.
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet: "required": ["proxyUrl", "table"]
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Change the required array to only ["proxyUrl"] in both the manifest configSchema and CONNECTOR_METADATA.configSchema. Add a custom validation note or use JSON Schema oneOf/anyOf to express the 'table OR customQuery' constraint, or leave the mutual-exclusion validation to parseConfig which already handles it.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The finding is confirmed as a real bug through direct code inspection of three files:

1. The manifest at `plugins/connector-postgres/plugin.manifest.json` line 15 declares `"required": ["proxyUrl", "table"]`.

2. The CONNECTOR_METADATA in `plugins/connector-postgres/src/index.ts` line 378 also declares `required: ["proxyUrl", "table"]`.

3. The `parseConfig` function in the same file (lines 191-201) intentionally supports configs where only `customQuery` is provided and `table` is absent -- it throws only if BOTH are missing.

4. Critically, the platform's `InstanceService` in `services/plugin/src/services/instance-service.ts` (lines 305-313) validates incoming config against the manifest's `configSchema` using Ajv BEFORE the plugin code runs. The `createInstance` method calls `validateConfigAgainstSchema(config, configSchema)` and throws `ConfigValidationFailedError` if validation fails. The same validation is applied in `patchInstance` (lines 353-364).

This means any config with `customQuery` but without `table` will be rejected by Ajv at the platform level (because `table` is listed in `required`), before the plugin's `parseConfig` ever executes. The entire customQuery-only code path -- including `fetchBatchCustomQuery`, the connect method's customQuery-mode branch (lines 433-441), and the customQuery handling in `fetchBatch` (lines 472-474) -- is dead code that can never be reached through the normal platform flow.

The fix is straightforward: remove `table` from the `required` array in both the manifest and CONNECTOR_METADATA, keeping only `["proxyUrl"]`. The plugin's own `parseConfig` already validates that at least one of `table` or `customQuery` is provided.

confirmedFindings.title: Incremental sync loses high-water mark on final batch, causing duplicate re-ingestion on next run
confirmedFindings.description: When the last batch of an incremental sync is returned (isLastPage === true because records.length < batchSize), nextCursor is set to null and hasMore is set to false. This means the high-water mark from the final batch is discarded. On the next ingestion run, the platform resumes with cursor=null (or the cursor from the previous-to-last batch), causing the connector to re-fetch rows that were already ingested in the final batch. Compare with the Postgres connector (line 657) which always persists the cursor on the last incremental batch: 'nextCursor = encodeCursor({ mode: "incremental", lastValue: String(colValue) })'. The MySQL connector should encode a cursor with the high-water mark even when hasMore=false, so the next ingestion run can filter with WHERE incrementalColumn > lastSeenValue.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
This is a confirmed real bug. The analysis traces the full data flow:

1. In the MySQL connector (line 739-742), when the final batch is returned (records.length < batchSize), `nextCursor` is set to `null` and `hasMore` is set to `false`. The high-water mark from the incremental column in the final batch's rows is completely discarded.

2. In the ingestion sync service (lines 716-723), the cursor is only persisted to sync_state when it is non-null: `if (cursor !== null) { await syncStateRepo.updateCursor(connectorId, cursor); }`. So the null cursor from the final batch is never written.

3. The final status update (lines 736-740) also conditionally includes the cursor: `...(cursor !== null ? { last_cursor: cursor } : {})`, so `last_cursor` remains at whatever value was set by the previous-to-last batch (or null if there was only one batch).

4. On the next incremental sync run (line 567-569), the service reads `cursor = syncState?.last_cursor ?? null`, which will be the stale value from the penultimate batch, causing the final batch's rows to be re-fetched.

5. The Postgres connector (lines 653-657) explicitly fixes this exact pattern with a comment referencing bug V5-116: "Always persist the cursor so a partial (final) batch saves its position. Without this, restarting after a partial batch would re-fetch rows that were already processed." It always encodes a cursor with the high-water mark regardless of whether hasMore is true or false.

The MySQL connector needs to compute and encode the high-water mark cursor even when isLastPage is true, identical to the Postgres connector's approach. This would cause duplicate re-ingestion of the final batch's rows on every subsequent incremental sync run.

confirmedFindings.title: Incremental sync combines offset pagination with WHERE filter, causing rows to be skipped
confirmedFindings.description: When using incremental sync across multiple batches within a single run, the cursor carries both an incrementing offset AND a high-water mark (since). On the second batch, the query becomes: SELECT * FROM table WHERE incrementalColumn > ? ORDER BY incrementalColumn ASC LIMIT ? OFFSET 2. The OFFSET is relative to the filtered result set, but the high-water mark (since) may have already changed to the max value of the first batch. This means the WHERE clause already excludes previously-seen rows, making the OFFSET redundant and actively harmful -- it skips rows. For example: if batch 1 returns rows with updated_at='2024-01-01' and '2024-01-02', the next query uses WHERE updated_at > '2024-01-02' OFFSET 2, skipping the first 2 rows that match updated_at > '2024-01-02'.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The bug is confirmed by tracing through the actual code at /home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/plugins/connector-mysql/src/index.ts.

The fetchBatch method (line 682) decodes the cursor into {offset, since} (line 697-698). On non-last-page batches, it computes nextOffset = offset + records.length (line 745) and nextSince = findHighWaterMark(...) (line 746-748), encoding both into the next cursor.

The buildTableQuery function (line 461) uses both values simultaneously: when since is non-null, it adds WHERE incrementalColumn > ? (line 476-478), and it always appends LIMIT ? OFFSET ? (line 489-490).

The problem: The offset is a running total of rows fetched across all batches, but the WHERE clause changes the result set size. On the second batch of an incremental sync, the query filters to only rows with incrementalColumn > highWaterMark, but then also applies OFFSET 1000 (or whatever the running total is). Since the WHERE clause already excludes previously-seen rows, the OFFSET is both redundant and harmful -- it skips rows from the filtered result set that should be returned.

Example: First batch (offset=0, since=null) returns 1000 rows, the max updated_at is '2024-01-10'. Next cursor has offset=1000, since='2024-01-10'. The second batch query becomes: SELECT * FROM table WHERE updated_at > '2024-01-10' ORDER BY updated_at ASC LIMIT 1000 OFFSET 1000. If there are 2000 rows with updated_at > '2024-01-10', this skips 1000 of them. Those 1000 rows are never fetched.

The fix would be to reset offset to 0 whenever since changes, since the WHERE filter already handles excluding previously-processed rows.

confirmedFindings.title: String comparison for high-water mark produces wrong results for numeric incremental columns
confirmedFindings.description: findHighWaterMark converts all values to strings and compares them lexicographically (asString > highest). For numeric auto-increment IDs or numeric timestamps, this produces incorrect results: String(9) > String(10) is true because '9' > '1' lexicographically, so the high-water mark would be set to '9' instead of '10'. The comment on line 569 acknowledges this but claims 'String comparison is safe for ISO 8601 timestamps and numeric IDs (MySQL returns numerics as numbers)' -- this claim is incorrect. While ISO 8601 timestamps do sort correctly as strings, numeric IDs emphatically do not when they differ in digit count.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The bug is confirmed and real. The `findHighWaterMark` function at lines 572-591 of `/home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/plugins/connector-mysql/src/index.ts` converts all values to strings via `String(value)` and compares them lexicographically (`asString > highest`). This produces incorrect results for numeric values that cross digit-count boundaries. Verified empirically: `String(9) > String(10)` evaluates to `true` in JavaScript because `'9' > '1'` lexicographically, so the high-water mark would be set to `'9'` instead of `'10'`.

The comment on lines 567-569 acknowledges the comparison approach but incorrectly claims "String comparison is safe for ISO 8601 timestamps and numeric IDs (MySQL returns numerics as numbers)." While ISO 8601 timestamps do sort correctly as strings (fixed-width, left-padded), numeric IDs do not. The fact that MySQL returns numbers doesn't help -- `String()` converts them to variable-width decimal strings which sort incorrectly across digit boundaries (9 vs 10, 99 vs 100, etc.).

There is no mitigation elsewhere in the code. The results are ORDER BY incrementalColumn ASC, so the function could simply take the last row's value, but instead it does a max-scan with broken string comparison. The incorrect high-water mark is stored in the cursor's `since` field and used in subsequent `WHERE incrementalColumn > ?` clauses, which could cause data to be re-processed or (depending on how MySQL casts the string parameter) other subtle issues with incremental sync correctness.

This is a data integrity bug affecting any incremental sync on a numeric column (like auto-increment IDs) whenever values cross digit-count boundaries within a batch.

confirmedFindings.title: Lone carriage return (\r without \n) causes infinite loop in CSV parser
confirmedFindings.description: In parseRow(), the unquoted field inner while loop stops when it encounters a \r character (line 164). The subsequent if/else chain (lines 169-179) checks for EOF, the delimiter, CRLF (\r\n), and LF (\n), but has no branch for a bare \r (classic Mac line ending). When none of these conditions match, execution falls through without advancing pos or breaking. The outer while loop re-enters at the same position, creating an infinite loop that will hang the plugin sandbox and eventually the ingestion worker. Old Mac-style CSV files (pre-OS X) and files with stray \r characters will trigger this. The quoted field branch has a similar secondary effect: after a quoted field, a lone \r hits the else/break path (line 157-159) which breaks the row but leaves pos pointing at the \r, so the next parseRow call starts at \r and enters the unquoted infinite loop.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Add a final else branch to handle bare \r as a line terminator: else if (text[pos] === '\r') { pos += 1; break; }. Apply the same fix after the quoted field delimiter/newline checks (lines 148-160). Alternatively, normalize all \r to \n in a preprocessing step before parsing.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The bug is confirmed real and reproducible. In parseRow() at line 164, the unquoted field inner while loop stops on \r. The subsequent if/else chain (lines 169-178) handles EOF, delimiter, CRLF (\r\n), and LF (\n), but has NO branch for a lone \r (bare carriage return without following \n). When a lone \r is encountered, none of the conditions match, there is no else clause, no break, and pos is not advanced. The outer while loop (line 135) re-enters at the same position, creating an infinite loop. This was confirmed empirically by running the actual parsing logic with a lone \r input -- the process hangs and must be killed.

The quoted field branch (lines 148-160) has a secondary path to the same bug: a lone \r after a closing quote hits the else/break at line 158-159, which breaks out of parseRow but leaves pos pointing at the \r. The next parseCSV iteration calls parseRow starting at the \r, which enters the unquoted branch and triggers the same infinite loop.

Old Mac-style CSV files (pre-OS X, which used \r as line ending), files generated by certain legacy tools, or files with stray \r characters will trigger this. Since this runs in the plugin sandbox during ingestion, it would hang the ingestion worker thread indefinitely. The severity is appropriately rated as CRITICAL because it causes a complete hang with no recovery path other than killing the process.

confirmedFindings.title: Bearer token read from config instead of context.credentials, bypassing encrypted credential storage
confirmedFindings.description: The manifest (plugin.manifest.json line 46-52) declares bearerToken as a requiredCredential and lists 'credentials' in requiredApis. The platform's credential management system encrypts and manages these values. However, extractConfig() reads bearerToken from the raw config object (raw['bearerToken'] at line 269) instead of calling context.credentials.get('bearerToken'). This means: (1) if the admin provisions the token through the proper credentials system as the manifest instructs, the connector will never see it; (2) if the user puts the token in plaintext config, it bypasses encryption; (3) the token is then stored in handle.metadata (line 365) which the platform may checkpoint to persistent storage in plaintext per the ConnectorHandle interface contract.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Read the bearer token from context.credentials instead of config. In connect(), call: const available = await context.credentials.list(); let bearerToken: string | undefined; if (available.includes('bearerToken')) { bearerToken = await context.credentials.get('bearerToken'); }. Pass it to fetchBatch via a closure or re-fetch from credentials in fetchBatch rather than storing it in handle.metadata. Remove bearerToken from the configSchema properties (it is a credential, not a config value).
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning: The finding is confirmed as a real security bug. The plugin.manifest.json declares bearerToken as a requiredCredential (lines 46-52) and lists "credentials" in requiredApis (line 55), indicating the platform's encrypted credential management should be used. However, the extractConfig() function (line 269) reads bearerToken from the raw config object (raw["bearerToken"]) rather than calling context.credentials.get("bearerToken"). The PluginContext interface provides a CredentialAccessor with get(name) that "returns the decrypted credential value" and explicitly warns "Never store it in the plugin's cache." The sibling connector-rest-api plugin correctly uses context.credentials.list() and context.credentials.get("bearerToken") (lines 197-201), proving the correct pattern. Three consequences are real: (1) credentials provisioned through the proper system will never reach the connector, (2) tokens placed in plaintext config bypass encryption, and (3) the token is stored in handle.metadata (line 365) which the ConnectorHandle interface documents "the platform may checkpoint this between calls" -- persisting the token in plaintext to durable storage.

confirmedFindings.title: Bearer token persisted in plaintext in ConnectorHandle metadata
confirmedFindings.description: The bearer token is stored in handle.metadata at line 365. The ConnectorHandle interface explicitly states that metadata 'Must be JSON-serializable (the platform may checkpoint this between calls)'. This means the bearer token can be written to the platform's checkpoint storage (likely a database) in plaintext. If the checkpoint table is compromised, or if checkpoint data appears in logs or debug endpoints, the token is exposed. Even if the credential-reading bug above is fixed, the architecture of passing the token through metadata is fundamentally unsafe.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Do not store the bearer token in handle.metadata. Instead, fetch it from context.credentials.get('bearerToken') in each fetchBatch call. The credential accessor caches within an execution, so repeated calls are cheap. Remove the bearerToken field from the metadata object entirely.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The code exists exactly as described: line 365 of `/home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/plugins/connector-csv/src/index.ts` stores `bearerToken: cfg.bearerToken ?? null` in `ConnectorHandle.metadata`. The `ConnectorHandle` interface at `/home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/packages/plugin-sdk/src/types/connector.ts` (line 28) explicitly documents: "Must be JSON-serializable (the platform may checkpoint this between calls)."

The only thing the sync service checkpoints between batches is the cursor string (via `syncStateRepo.updateCursor`), not the handle metadata. confirmedFindings.title: hasMore=true with nextCursor=null when all page records are skipped
confirmedFindings.description: When all payloads in a page are skipped (failed HMAC verification or TTL-expired), lastSuccessfulId remains null (initialized on line 547, only updated on line 548 for successfully mapped records). The nextCursor is computed as 'hasMore ? lastSuccessfulId : null' on line 617. If hasMore is true (there are more IDs beyond this page in the original index) but every record in this page was skipped, nextCursor becomes null despite hasMore being true. This violates the BatchResult contract (documented in connector.ts line 40: 'Set to true if there are more records after this batch (i.e., nextCursor is non-null)'). The ingestion service, seeing nextCursor=null, will either stop fetching (causing data loss of remaining valid payloads) or restart from the beginning (causing an infinite retry loop if the same payloads keep failing).
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet: const nextCursor = hasMore ? lastSuccessfulId : null;
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Track the last processed payload ID separately from the last successfully mapped ID. Use the last entry in processedIds (or the last entry in pageIds) as the cursor value, since the cursor's purpose is to mark the position in the index, not to indicate successful mapping. For example: 'const nextCursor = hasMore ? (pageIds[pageIds.length - 1] ?? null) : null;'. However, because the index is mutated by removing processed IDs (the cursor won't be found in the next read), consider using an index-based cursor or removing the cursor entirely and always starting from position 0 of the (already-mutated) index.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The code at line 617 does exactly what the finding describes: `const nextCursor = hasMore ? lastSuccessfulId : null;`. When all records in a page are skipped (HMAC failure or TTL expiry), `lastSuccessfulId` remains null (initialized on line 547, only set on line 592 for successful mappings), so `nextCursor` becomes null even when `hasMore` is true. This violates the BatchResult contract documented in connector.ts line 44: "Set to true if there are more records after this batch (i.e., nextCursor is non-null)."

However, the severity should be reduced from HIGH to LOW because the finding's claimed consequences (data loss or infinite retry loop) do NOT actually occur, thanks to compensating logic:

1. No data loss: Lines 603-609 remove all processed/skipped IDs from the pending index before returning. When the ingestion service loops back (line 716-717 sets cursor=null, hasMore=true), the next fetchBatch call with cursor=null starts from index 0 of the now-pruned list (line 519-520), which contains only the remaining unprocessed IDs. These remaining valid payloads are correctly fetched.

2. No infinite loop: Each call removes skipped IDs from the index (line 604-605), so the index shrinks monotonically. Eventually all IDs are either successfully processed or skipped and removed.

3. Crash recovery works: If a crash occurs, the persisted cursor (which was not updated since nextCursor was null, per sync-service.ts line 721-723) may reference an ID no longer in the index. Line 523-525 handles this by resetting startIndex to 0 when the cursor ID is not found.

The bug is real -- it is a genuine contract violation that could confuse monitoring, logging, or any future consumer of BatchResult that relies on the hasMore/nextCursor invariant. But the practical runtime impact is negligible because the index cleanup creates a self-correcting mechanism.

confirmedFindings.title: Cursor-based pagination is broken because processed IDs are removed from the index
confirmedFindings.description: The pagination design is fundamentally inconsistent. fetchBatch removes processed IDs from the index (line 605) after each batch, but uses the cursor (a payload ID) to find its position in the index via indexOf on the next call (line 523). Since the cursor ID was already removed from the index in the previous batch, indexOf always returns -1, and the code falls back to startIndex=0 (line 525). This means the cursor mechanism is entirely non-functional -- every call effectively starts from position 0 of the remaining index. While this happens to produce correct results for the simple sequential case, it breaks if: (1) multiple consumers process the same connector instance concurrently (they will re-process already-claimed payloads), (2) the ingestion service retries a batch with the same cursor (it will skip to different payloads than the original attempt since the index was already mutated), or (3) the ingestion service uses the cursor for checkpoint/resume after a crash (the cursor points to a non-existent entry).
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Choose one pagination strategy and implement it consistently. Option A: Keep cursor-based pagination but do NOT remove processed IDs from the index during fetchBatch. Instead, let the caller manage index cleanup after acknowledging successful processing. Option B: Remove cursor-based pagination entirely. Since the index is mutated after each batch (processed IDs removed), always start from index 0 and set nextCursor to a sentinel like 'continue' when hasMore is true. The ingestion service would treat any non-null cursor as 'call again'. Option C: Use a numeric offset cursor instead of a payload ID cursor, and do not mutate the index until the full drain is complete.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The finding is confirmed. The code at lines 519-526 and 602-609 exists exactly as described. The cursor-based pagination is indeed fundamentally broken:

1. `fetchBatch` removes processed IDs from the index (line 604-605) after processing each batch.
2. On the next call, the cursor ID (which was the last processed ID) is looked up via `allIds.indexOf(cursor)` (line 522) against the updated index.
3. Since the cursor ID was already removed from the index, `indexOf` always returns -1, and `startIndex` falls back to 0.

In the simple sequential single-consumer happy path, this accidentally works correctly because index 0 of the pruned list is the next unprocessed item. However, the cursor is semantically non-functional -- it never actually serves its purpose of marking a resume point.

The finding's failure scenarios are valid:
- **Retry after crash:** If the ingestion service successfully calls fetchBatch (which removes IDs from the index and deletes payloads from cache) but then crashes before persisting the records, those payloads are permanently lost. The cursor cannot be used to re-fetch them because both the index entries and the cached payloads have been eagerly deleted.
- **Concurrent consumers:** Without locking, two consumers read the same index, process the same payloads, and both mutate the index -- classic race condition. The cursor provides no protection here.
- **Retry with same cursor:** If the caller retries with the same cursor expecting to re-receive the same batch, the index has already been mutated and the payloads deleted, so different (or no) data is returned.

The core issue is that deletion of processed entries happens eagerly within fetchBatch itself, rather than being deferred until the caller confirms successful processing (an acknowledgment pattern). This makes the cursor a vestigial mechanism that provides a false sense of checkpoint/resume capability. I'm adjusting severity to MEDIUM because the happy path (sequential, single consumer, no crashes) works correctly by coincidence, but the design is genuinely flawed for any production scenario involving retries, crashes, or concurrency.

confirmedFindings.title: Client secret cached with same TTL as JWKS, becomes unavailable during long sessions
confirmedFindings.description: The client secret is cached in initialize() with a TTL of jwksCacheTtlSeconds (default 3600 seconds / 1 hour). After this TTL expires, handleCallback() and refreshToken() will fail with 'OIDC client secret not available' because there is no mechanism to re-populate the cached secret. The discovery document and JWKS are re-fetched on cache miss, but the client secret cannot be re-resolved because AuthContext (used by handleCallback and refreshToken) does not provide a CredentialAccessor -- it was deliberately removed from the AuthContext interface. This means after 1 hour of uptime, all logins and token refreshes will fail until the plugin is re-initialized.
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet: await context.cache.set(CLIENT_SECRET_CACHE_KEY, clientSecret, this.config.jwksCacheTtlSeconds);
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Either set the client secret cache TTL to the maximum allowed value (86400 seconds) independent of jwksCacheTtlSeconds, or implement a re-initialization mechanism. Alternatively, since AuthContext actually DOES include a credentials field (as seen in the auth-provider.ts interface definition at line 79), use context.credentials.get('clientSecret') directly in handleCallback() and refreshToken() instead of relying on the cache.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The bug is real but the finding's explanation of the root cause is partially wrong.

WHAT IS TRUE:
1. The client secret is cached in `initialize()` at line 432 with TTL of `this.config.jwksCacheTtlSeconds` (default 3600s / 1 hour).
2. The code comment at line 301 claims "TTL of 86400s" but the actual code uses `jwksCacheTtlSeconds` which defaults to 3600s -- a doc/code mismatch.
3. In `handleCallback()` (line 530-534) and `refreshToken()` (line 707-711), when the cache returns null, the code throws an error instead of re-fetching the secret.
4. After 1 hour of uptime (default TTL), the cached client secret expires and all logins and token refreshes will fail.

WHAT IS FALSE IN THE FINDING:
The finding claims "AuthContext does not provide a CredentialAccessor -- it was deliberately removed from the AuthContext interface." This is factually wrong. The `AuthContext` interface at `/home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/packages/plugin-sdk/src/types/auth-provider.ts` line 79 clearly includes `credentials: CredentialAccessor`. The `handleCallback` and `refreshToken` methods receive `context: AuthContext` which HAS credentials access. The bug is that the code does not USE `context.credentials.get("clientSecret")` as a fallback when the cache miss occurs, not that credentials are unavailable.

THE FIX IS TRIVIAL:
Replace the throw-on-null pattern with a fallback: `const clientSecret = await context.cache.get(CLIENT_SECRET_CACHE_KEY) ?? await context.credentials.get("clientSecret");` and optionally re-populate the cache entry.

SEVERITY ASSESSMENT:
The bug is real and would cause a complete authentication outage after the cache TTL expires (default 1 hour). However, since the fix is a one-line fallback to an already-available API, and the finding's root cause analysis was incorrect (claiming credentials are unavailable when they are), I adjust severity to MEDIUM. It is a real operational issue but not as dire as described -- it does not require architectural changes, just using the credentials accessor that is already present on the context.

confirmedFindings.title: handleCallback ignores AuthContext.credentials and reads secret from cache despite AuthContext having credentials
confirmedFindings.description: The code comment says 'AuthContext deliberately omits FetchProxy' and 'AuthContext methods cannot access credentials directly'. However, examining the AuthContext interface in the plugin-sdk (auth-provider.ts lines 55-86), AuthContext DOES include both a 'credentials: CredentialAccessor' field and a 'fetch: FetchProxy' field. The implementation caches the client secret and FetchProxy during initialize() instead of using them from the context, creating a stale-data bug. If credentials are rotated by the platform after initialize(), the plugin continues using the old secret from cache.
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet: const clientSecret = await context.cache.get<string>(CLIENT_SECRET_CACHE_KEY);
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Use context.credentials.get('clientSecret') directly in handleCallback() and refreshToken() instead of reading from the cache. This ensures credential rotation is respected and eliminates the TTL expiry problem.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The finding is confirmed as a real bug through examination of three source files:

1. The OIDC plugin (index.ts line 530) reads the client secret from cache (`context.cache.get(CLIENT_SECRET_CACHE_KEY)`) instead of from `context.credentials.get("clientSecret")`. The same pattern appears in `refreshToken()` at line 707.

2. The AuthContext interface (auth-provider.ts lines 55-86) clearly includes both `credentials: CredentialAccessor` (line 79) and `fetch: FetchProxy` (line 72). The code comments in the OIDC plugin stating "AuthContext deliberately omits FetchProxy" (line 332) and "AuthContext methods cannot access credentials directly" (line 428) are factually incorrect.

3. The CredentialAccessor documentation in context.ts (lines 63-64) explicitly states: "Never store it in the plugin's cache -- the platform rotates credentials and will deliver updated values automatically." The OIDC plugin directly violates this contract by caching the secret with `context.cache.set(CLIENT_SECRET_CACHE_KEY, clientSecret, ...)` in `initialize()` and reading it from cache in `handleCallback()` and `refreshToken()`.

The stale-data scenario is real: if the platform rotates the OIDC client secret after `initialize()` but before the cache entry expires (default TTL = 3600 seconds), all `handleCallback()` and `refreshToken()` calls will send the old secret to the identity provider's token endpoint, causing "invalid_client" errors and authentication failures for all users.

Severity is appropriately HIGH: credential rotation is a security-critical operation (e.g., after a suspected secret compromise), and this bug would cause it to silently fail for up to an hour.

confirmedFindings.title: Whitespace-only password bypasses empty-password check, enabling anonymous LDAP bind
confirmedFindings.description: The password validation checks `password === ""` (exact empty string) but the username validation uses `username.trim() === ""`. A password consisting entirely of whitespace (e.g., " " or "\t") passes this check and is sent to the LDAP proxy as the bind password. Many LDAP servers treat whitespace-only passwords the same as empty passwords, performing an anonymous bind that succeeds without credential verification. This is a credential bypass vulnerability: an attacker who knows a valid username can authenticate by supplying a whitespace-only password.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Change the check to `if (password.trim() === "")` to reject whitespace-only passwords, matching the treatment already applied to the username field.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The code asymmetry is confirmed: at line 674, username is validated with `username.trim() === ""` (catching whitespace-only usernames), while at line 678, password is validated with `password === ""` (only catching the exact empty string). A password of " " or "\t" passes the check and is sent to the LDAP proxy as the bind password.

However, the severity should be downgraded. The finding claims "many LDAP servers treat whitespace-only passwords the same as empty passwords, performing an anonymous bind." This is inaccurate. Per RFC 4513, anonymous bind (unauthenticated authentication) occurs when the password is a zero-length string. At the LDAP wire protocol level, a whitespace-only password is a non-empty OCTET STRING and standard LDAP servers (OpenLDAP, Active Directory, 389DS) will attempt to verify it against the stored credential hash, which will fail. The anonymous bind bypass described in the finding would not work against any standard LDAP implementation.

The bug is real in the sense that: (1) the developer clearly intended to block empty-like passwords as shown by the trim-based username check and the comment about anonymous bind; (2) the inconsistency is an oversight; (3) it represents a defense-in-depth gap. But the practical exploitability is very low because standard LDAP servers do not equate whitespace with empty at the protocol level. A custom or misconfigured LDAP proxy that trims passwords before binding could make this exploitable, but that is a speculative scenario. The severity should be MEDIUM (real code defect with defense-in-depth implications) rather than HIGH (the described attack does not work against standard LDAP servers).

confirmedFindings.title: Unhandled PluginAuthError from getGroupMembership in validateToken causes 500 instead of valid=false
confirmedFindings.description: The validateToken method wraps the initial proxySearch call in a try/catch that converts PluginAuthError to {valid: false}, but the subsequent call to this.getGroupMembership (line 827) is NOT wrapped. getGroupMembership calls searchGroupsExplicitly which calls proxySearch, which can throw PluginAuthError (e.g., if the LDAP server is temporarily unavailable for the group search). The AuthProvider interface contract states: 'Do not throw for invalid tokens -- return valid=false.' and 'throws PluginAuthError only for unrecoverable errors (e.g., provider unreachable)'. A group search failure during token validation should return valid=false, not crash the calling Auth Service with an unhandled exception.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Wrap the getGroupMembership call (and the rest of the post-search logic) in the same try/catch block, or add a separate try/catch around getGroupMembership that returns {valid: false, error: err.message} for PluginAuthError.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The bug is confirmed. In validateToken (line 777), the first proxySearch call (line 799) is wrapped in a try/catch that converts PluginAuthError to {valid: false, error: err.message} (lines 810-813). However, the subsequent call to this.getGroupMembership (line 827) is NOT wrapped in any try/catch.

getGroupMembership (line 1016) delegates to searchGroupsExplicitly (line 1046) when cfg.groupSearchBase is configured, which calls proxySearch (line 1060). proxySearch can throw PluginAuthError in two places: line 399 (non-JSON response from proxy) and line 407 (LDAP search failure / non-OK HTTP status). It can also throw PluginTimeoutError (line 392).

The inconsistency is clear: the developer intentionally catches PluginAuthError from the first proxySearch and returns {valid: false}, but the identical error type from the group search proxySearch call propagates uncaught. If the LDAP server fails the group search (e.g., permissions error on the group search base, intermittent failure, or malformed proxy response), the PluginAuthError will propagate up as an unhandled exception.

The AuthProvider interface contract (line 166) states: "Do not throw for invalid tokens -- return valid=false." The first catch block shows the developer's intent to follow this contract, but the getGroupMembership call path was missed.

The practical impact: when groupSearchBase is configured (non-null) and the LDAP group search fails during token validation, the Auth Service receives an unhandled PluginAuthError, which would result in a 500 error to the client instead of gracefully returning valid=false or valid=true with empty groups. This is a real inconsistency bug, though the severity depends on how often the group search fails independently of the user search. Adjusting to MEDIUM because: (1) both searches use the same LDAP server, so if the first succeeds the second usually will too, (2) only affects configurations where groupSearchBase is explicitly set, and (3) the interface contract does allow throwing PluginAuthError for "unrecoverable errors" -- the ambiguity is whether a group search failure qualifies.

confirmedFindings.title: App service reads wrong MinIO env var names, always falls back to hardcoded 'minioadmin' credentials
confirmedFindings.description: The app-service reads MINIO_ACCESS_KEY and MINIO_SECRET_KEY env vars (lines 734-735 and build-service.ts lines 243-244), but docker-compose.yml injects OP_MINIO_USER and OP_MINIO_PASSWORD. Because the env var names do not match, the nullish coalescing operator always triggers the fallback to the hardcoded string 'minioadmin'. This means the app-service connects to MinIO with the default 'minioadmin' credentials regardless of what production credentials are configured. Unlike the gateway service (which has an explicit NODE_ENV=production guard for this), the app-service has no such guard, so it will silently use the weak default credential in production.
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet:
minioAccessKey: process.env["MINIO_ACCESS_KEY"] ?? "minioadmin",
minioSecretKey: process.env["MINIO_SECRET_KEY"] ?? "minioadmin",
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Change the env var names to match what docker-compose.yml injects: use process.env["OP_MINIO_USER"] and process.env["OP_MINIO_PASSWORD"] instead of MINIO_ACCESS_KEY / MINIO_SECRET_KEY. Also add a NODE_ENV=production guard (like the gateway has) that refuses to start if the values are still the dev defaults.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The finding is confirmed as a real bug. The app service reads MINIO_ACCESS_KEY and MINIO_SECRET_KEY (index.ts lines 734-735, build-service.ts lines 243-244), but docker-compose.yml injects OP_MINIO_USER and OP_MINIO_PASSWORD to the app-service container (lines 568-569). The service-entrypoint.sh does not translate these env var names. Therefore, the nullish coalescing operator always triggers the fallback to the hardcoded string "minioadmin" for both access key and secret key.

This is provably a mismatch: the gateway service correctly reads OP_MINIO_ACCESS_KEY with a fallback to OP_MINIO_USER (lines 494-495 of gateway/src/index.ts), demonstrating the correct pattern. The app service uses a completely different, non-OP-prefixed naming convention that nothing in the deployment infrastructure provides.

The practical impact is significant: the MinIO root password defaults to "oneplatform_minio_dev_2024" (not "minioadmin"), so the app service would fail to authenticate against MinIO in a standard deployment. In production where credentials are changed from defaults, the app service would always try "minioadmin"/"minioadmin" and fail entirely, or worse, if someone set the MinIO root user to "minioadmin"/"minioadmin" to make things work, it would silently use weak default credentials. The gateway has a NODE_ENV=production guard rejecting default credentials; the app service lacks this safeguard.

confirmedFindings.title: Build service independently reads wrong MinIO env vars with hardcoded 'minioadmin' fallback
confirmedFindings.description: The build-service.ts independently reads MINIO_ACCESS_KEY and MINIO_SECRET_KEY (lines 243-244) with a fallback to 'minioadmin'. This is a second code path (separate from index.ts) that uses the wrong env var names. Even if index.ts is fixed, this code path will continue using the insecure default. The build service uses these credentials to upload and manage app artifacts in MinIO, meaning arbitrary artifacts could be read or written by anyone who discovers the default credentials.
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet:
const minioAccessKey = process.env["MINIO_ACCESS_KEY"] ?? "minioadmin";
const minioSecretKey = process.env["MINIO_SECRET_KEY"] ?? "minioadmin";
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Change to use OP_MINIO_USER / OP_MINIO_PASSWORD env vars to match docker-compose.yml, or accept the credentials as constructor parameters passed from index.ts rather than reading env vars independently.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The finding is confirmed. Lines 243-244 of build-service.ts read `MINIO_ACCESS_KEY` and `MINIO_SECRET_KEY` with fallbacks to `"minioadmin"`. The same wrong env var names are used in index.ts (lines 734-735). However, Docker Compose passes `OP_MINIO_USER` and `OP_MINIO_PASSWORD` to the app-service container, and the service-entrypoint.sh does NOT remap these to `MINIO_ACCESS_KEY`/`MINIO_SECRET_KEY`. The gateway service gets this right by reading `OP_MINIO_ACCESS_KEY` with a fallback to `OP_MINIO_USER`.

This means in production/dev deployments, the app service will ALWAYS fall through to the hardcoded `"minioadmin"` fallback because the expected env vars are never set. Two consequences: (1) If MinIO is configured with non-default credentials (as in the project's own docker-compose where the password is `oneplatform_minio_dev_2024`), build artifact uploads will fail silently with auth errors. (2) If MinIO happens to use its own default `minioadmin` credentials (or someone misconfigures it to do so), the hardcoded fallback creates an insecure credential situation.

The finding correctly identifies that build-service.ts independently reads these wrong env vars, creating a duplicate code path that will persist even if index.ts is fixed. Both need to be updated to read `OP_MINIO_USER`/`OP_MINIO_PASSWORD` (or `OP_MINIO_ACCESS_KEY`/`OP_MINIO_SECRET_KEY`) to match what Docker Compose actually provides. I am adjusting severity to MEDIUM because: while the env var mismatch is real, the practical impact is that builds will fail (credentials won't match), which is a functionality bug more than a direct security exploit. The insecure default is only exploitable if someone independently configures MinIO with its own defaults, which is a narrower scenario than stated.

confirmedFindings.title: App service uses SERVICE_KEYS_DIR (no OP_ prefix) while all other services use OP_SERVICE_KEYS_DIR
confirmedFindings.description: The app service reads process.env["SERVICE_KEYS_DIR"] for the service keys directory, while execution, ontology, pipeline, and plugin services all read process.env["OP_SERVICE_KEYS_DIR"]. Docker Compose does not set either variable, so all services fall back to the same default "/data/service-keys". However, if an operator sets OP_SERVICE_KEYS_DIR in production, the app service will ignore it and use the default, failing to load service keys for inter-service JWT verification.
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet: serviceKeysDir: process.env["SERVICE_KEYS_DIR"] ?? "/data/service-keys",
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Change to process.env["OP_SERVICE_KEYS_DIR"] to match all other services.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning: The finding is confirmed. Line 738 of /home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/services/app/src/index.ts reads process.env["SERVICE_KEYS_DIR"] (without the OP_ prefix), while all four other services that use this variable (execution, plugin, pipeline, ontology) consistently read process.env["OP_SERVICE_KEYS_DIR"]. Neither variable is set in any Docker Compose or .env file, so all services currently fall back to the same default "/data/service-keys" and the bug is latent. However, if an operator sets OP_SERVICE_KEYS_DIR in production to customize the service keys path, the app service would ignore it, continue using "/data/service-keys", and fail to load service public keys for inter-service JWT verification. This is a real naming inconsistency. The severity is appropriately rated as MEDIUM rather than HIGH because: (1) the bug is latent -- it only manifests when someone explicitly sets OP_SERVICE_KEYS_DIR, which currently nobody does, (2) the fix is a trivial one-character change (add "OP_" prefix), and (3) in the default Docker deployment everything works correctly.

confirmedFindings.title: App service uses MINIO_* env vars while all other services use OP_MINIO_* or OP_S3_*
confirmedFindings.description: The app service reads MINIO_ENDPOINT, MINIO_ACCESS_KEY, MINIO_SECRET_KEY, MINIO_REGION (no OP_ prefix). Docker Compose only sets OP_MINIO_USER and OP_MINIO_PASSWORD for services, not the unprefixed MINIO_* variants. The gateway uses OP_MINIO_ENDPOINT/OP_MINIO_ACCESS_KEY/OP_MINIO_SECRET_KEY, the plugin service uses OP_S3_ENDPOINT/OP_S3_ACCESS_KEY/OP_S3_SECRET_KEY. The app service's MinIO defaults (minioadmin/minioadmin) differ from the gateway's (minioadmin/oneplatform_minio_dev_2024), potentially causing authentication failures.
confirmedFindings.codeSnippet:
minioEndpoint: process.env["MINIO_ENDPOINT"] ?? "http://minio:9000",
minioAccessKey: process.env["MINIO_ACCESS_KEY"] ?? "minioadmin",
minioSecretKey: process.env["MINIO_SECRET_KEY"] ?? "minioadmin",
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Standardize MinIO env vars across all services. Use OP_MINIO_ENDPOINT, OP_MINIO_ACCESS_KEY, OP_MINIO_SECRET_KEY, and OP_MINIO_REGION consistently. The app service's default secret key 'minioadmin' also differs from the gateway and docker-compose default of 'oneplatform_minio_dev_2024'.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
Confirmed real bug. The app service at /home/ubuntu/topics/oneplatform/services/app/src/index.ts (lines 733-736) reads MINIO_ENDPOINT, MINIO_ACCESS_KEY, MINIO_SECRET_KEY, and MINIO_REGION -- all without the OP_ prefix used by every other service. Docker Compose (docker/docker-compose.yml) only passes OP_MINIO_USER and OP_MINIO_PASSWORD to the app-service container. The service-entrypoint.sh does not translate these to unprefixed variants. Since the unprefixed env vars are never set, the code always falls back to its hardcoded defaults.

The critical issue is the secret key default: the app service defaults to "minioadmin" for MINIO_SECRET_KEY, but the MinIO server's root password (MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD in docker-compose.yml line 150) defaults to "oneplatform_minio_dev_2024". This credential mismatch means every signed S3 request from the app service to MinIO will fail with an authentication error. This directly breaks the app-serving route at /apps/:slug/* which proxies bundle.js and other build artifacts from MinIO (lines 600-619).

The gateway service correctly handles this by falling through: OP_MINIO_SECRET_KEY -> OP_MINIO_PASSWORD -> "oneplatform_minio_dev_2024" (line 495). The app service has no such fallback chain and uses a completely different, non-matching env var naming convention.

confirmedFindings.title: Core health.ts readyz returns "not-ready" (hyphen) while all custom health routes return "not_ready" (underscore)
confirmedFindings.description: The core package's readyz() function returns status: "not-ready" (with a hyphen) while the custom health routes in app, execution, gateway, ingestion, pipeline, and plugin services all return status: "not_ready" (with an underscore). Auth, ontology, and logging use the core healthz/readyz directly, so they return "not-ready". Any monitoring tool or orchestrator parsing the readyz response to check service readiness will get inconsistent values depending on which service it queries.
confirmedFindings.suggestedFix: Standardize on one format. Since 6 out of 9 services use "not_ready" (underscore), update core/health.ts line 55 to use "not_ready" to match the majority pattern. Alternatively, migrate all services to use the core healthz/readyz functions.
confirmedFindings.verificationReasoning:
The inconsistency is confirmed in the source code. Core `packages/core/src/health.ts` line 55 uses `"not-ready"` (hyphen), while all six custom health routes in app, execution, gateway, ingestion, pipeline, and plugin services use `"not_ready"` (underscore). Three services (auth, ontology, logging) import the core readyz and thus return "not-ready", while the other six return "not_ready". This is a genuine inconsistency.

However, the severity should be adjusted downward. No code within the codebase currently parses the readyz status string for comparison. Docker healthchecks use `/healthz` (not `/readyz`) and check only the HTTP exit code, not the response body. The HTTP status codes (200 for ready, 503 for not ready) are consistent across all implementations. The inconsistency would only matter if an external monitoring tool or future code string-compared the status field value, which is plausible but not currently happening. This is a code quality / consistency issue rather than an active bug causing failures.

mediumLowFindings.title: Redis INCR + EXPIRE for refresh rate limiting has a TOCTOU race window
mediumLowFindings.description: The refresh rate limiter (lines 50-61) uses a non-atomic sequence: redis.incr(key) then redis.expire(key, ttl) when count === 1. If the process crashes between INCR and EXPIRE, the key persists without a TTL and the rate limiter for that IP becomes permanently stuck, blocking all future refresh requests from that IP. The guest-session-service.ts correctly handles this same pattern using an atomic Lua script (lines 66-74 of guest-session-service.ts). The bootstrap route also acknowledges this exact problem in its comment (redis-store.ts lines 156-158).
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Replace the INCR + conditional EXPIRE with an atomic Lua script like the guest-session-service does: `local count = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1]); if count == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end; return count`

mediumLowFindings.title: Token verification accepts any unknown algorithm as HS256, enabling potential algorithm confusion
mediumLowFindings.description: In verifyAccessToken (line 388-389), the algorithm detection code defaults any unrecognized algorithm to HS256: `tokenAlgorithm = header.alg === 'EdDSA' ? 'EdDSA' : 'HS256'`. If an attacker forges a token with alg='none' or any other value, it will be processed as HS256. While jose's jwtVerify with algorithms:['HS256'] rejects 'none' algorithm attacks, the code comment claims there's 'no algorithm confusion risk' but silently treating arbitrary algorithm values as HS256 is not defensive. A token with alg:'RS256' in its header would be processed with the HS256 symmetric key, which is exactly the textbook JWT algorithm confusion attack pattern.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Explicitly check for 'HS256' and 'EdDSA' only, returning null for any other algorithm value: `if (header.alg === 'EdDSA') tokenAlgorithm = 'EdDSA'; else if (header.alg === 'HS256') tokenAlgorithm = 'HS256'; else return null;`

mediumLowFindings.title: In-memory refresh rate limiter Map grows unboundedly without cleanup
mediumLowFindings.description: The in-memory fallback rate limiter for the refresh endpoint (line 46: `const refreshAttempts = new Map<string, ...>()`) has no cleanup mechanism. While entries have a window-based check that resets on access (lines 64-66), IPs that make a single request and never return will have their entries persist in the Map forever. Under sustained traffic from many distinct IPs, this Map grows without bound. The bootstrap-service.ts handles this same concern correctly with a periodic cleanup timer (lines 67-84 of bootstrap-service.ts), but the refresh rate limiter lacks any equivalent.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add a periodic cleanup interval similar to bootstrap-service.ts that iterates the Map and deletes entries whose window has elapsed. Unref the timer so it does not prevent graceful shutdown.

mediumLowFindings.title: CSS sanitization regex for url() does not handle nested parentheses or escaped characters
mediumLowFindings.description: The url() stripping regex `/url\s*\([^)]*\)/gi` (line 119) uses `[^)]*` which does not match nested parentheses. A payload like `url(data:text/css;base64,...)` works fine, but `url(calc(1))` or CSS containing escaped closing parens like `url(foo\)bar)` would leave partial content. More critically, the expression() stripping (line 125) has the same limitation: `expression(nested(evil))` would only strip `expression(nested(evil)` leaving a dangling `)`. While these are edge cases, for security-critical sanitization they represent bypasses.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Use a more robust approach that handles nesting: either use a recursive regex or a parser-based approach. At minimum, replace `[^)]*` with a pattern that handles nested parens or match greedily up to the last closing paren on the line. Consider using a dedicated CSS sanitization library like DOMPurify with CSS support.

mediumLowFindings.title: Role rename updates users and role in separate non-transactional operations, risking inconsistency
mediumLowFindings.description: When a role is renamed (lines 143-159), the code first updates the role name via roleRepository.update(id, ...) and then updates all users' roles arrays via a separate db.query(). These two operations are not wrapped in a transaction. If the process crashes or the second query fails after the first succeeds, the role will have its new name but users will still reference the old name, leaving them with a role that no longer exists. This means those users would lose all permissions associated with that role until manually corrected.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Wrap both the roleRepository.update() and the user roles update in a single database transaction using db.connect() + BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK, similar to how other operations in the codebase handle multi-table updates.

mediumLowFindings.title: OAuth callback schema requires code even when error is present
mediumLowFindings.description: The oauthCallbackQuery schema (line 283) defines `code: z.string()` as required and `error: z.string().optional()`. When an OAuth provider denies consent, it redirects back with `?error=access_denied` but without a `code` parameter. The schema validation will fail because code is required, preventing the route from reaching the error-handling logic (lines 60-64 of oauth.ts) that converts provider-side denials into a proper error response. The user would see a generic 'Invalid OAuth callback query' validation error instead of the meaningful 'OAuth provider returned an error' message.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Make code optional in the schema: `code: z.string().optional()`. Then add a runtime check in the route handler that verifies code is present when error is absent, or use z.union with two schemas (one for success with code required, one for error with error required).

mediumLowFindings.title: CSV export vulnerable to CSV injection via unescaped tenant_id and type fields
mediumLowFindings.description: The /api/v1/usage/export endpoint generates CSV output by directly interpolating ev.tenantId and ev.type into quoted CSV fields without escaping embedded double quotes. While these fields are less likely to contain injection payloads than user-supplied data, the metadata field's JSON stringification replaces double quotes with two double-quotes but the tenantId and type values are not escaped. More critically, if any field value starts with =, +, -, or @ characters, it could trigger formula injection when the CSV is opened in spreadsheet applications. The metadata field escaping only handles double quotes but not formula injection characters.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Escape all CSV field values consistently: (1) double any embedded double-quote characters in tenantId and type, (2) prefix any value starting with =, +, -, or @ with a single quote to prevent CSV formula injection.

mediumLowFindings.title: Non-atomic read-and-delete in metering flush allows data loss between HGETALL and DEL
mediumLowFindings.description: The flush code claims to perform an 'atomic GETDEL via MULTI/EXEC' but actually uses a pipeline (redis.pipeline()), not a transaction (redis.multi()). A Redis pipeline sends commands in a batch for network efficiency but does NOT guarantee atomicity. Between the HGETALL and DEL commands, new increments from concurrent requests can be written to the counter hash. These increments will be deleted by the DEL command without being captured by the preceding HGETALL, resulting in lost metering data. The comment explicitly warns about this scenario but the implementation does not prevent it.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Replace redis.pipeline() with redis.multi() to create an actual Redis MULTI/EXEC transaction, which guarantees that no other commands can interleave between HGETALL and DEL. Alternatively, use a Lua script (like the rate limiter does) to atomically read and delete in a single operation.

mediumLowFindings.title: Bucket name regex is too permissive, allowing path traversal-adjacent characters
mediumLowFindings.description: The BUCKET_NAME_RE regex (/^[a-zA-Z0-9._-]{1,63}$/) allows dots in bucket names. While the assertBucketBelongsToTenant check provides tenant isolation, the dot character in bucket names combined with the URL construction in storage-service.ts could lead to unexpected path resolution. More importantly, the regex does not enforce S3's actual naming rules: S3 bucket names cannot start or end with a dot, cannot contain consecutive dots, and must be lowercase. Passing invalid bucket names to the S3 backend could cause confusing errors or unexpected behavior.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Tighten the regex to enforce actual S3 bucket naming rules: /^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9.-]{0,61}[a-z0-9]$/ and add a check to reject consecutive dots (..).

mediumLowFindings.title: SSE connection limit check has TOCTOU race despite comment claiming otherwise
mediumLowFindings.description: The comment on line 49 says 'Increment immediately after all validation passes, closing the TOCTOU window', but the check on line 34 reads the current count and the increment on line 52 sets it non-atomically. Between two concurrent requests both reading currentConnections as e.g. 9 (with max 10), both could pass the check and both increment to 10 and 11 respectively, exceeding the limit. The in-memory Map has no synchronization primitive. While Node.js is single-threaded for synchronous code, the async operations between the check (line 34) and the set (line 52) include validation that yields the event loop, allowing interleaving.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Move the increment to occur immediately after the limit check, before any async validation. The current code already tries to do this but there is async work (sseQuery.safeParse is synchronous so this specific case may be safe, but the pattern should be audited). Alternatively, use a compare-and-set pattern or move the check-and-increment into a single synchronous block with no intervening await.

mediumLowFindings.title: Webhook listing pagination uses 'id > cursor' which is incompatible with UUID ordering
mediumLowFindings.description: The findByTenantId method with cursor-based pagination uses 'id > $2' for keyset pagination, but the ORDER BY is 'created_at ASC, id ASC'. UUIDs (v4) are not lexicographically ordered by creation time, so using 'id > cursor' does not correctly implement keyset pagination with this ordering. A webhook created later could have a UUID that sorts before an earlier one. This means the cursor-based pagination can skip rows or return duplicates, producing inconsistent results for callers paginating through webhook lists.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Change the cursor to encode both created_at and id (like the GDPR request repository does with 'requested_at|id' format), and use a compound keyset comparison: WHERE (created_at, id) > ($cursor_ts, $cursor_id) ORDER BY created_at ASC, id ASC.

mediumLowFindings.title: Webhook listing only returns enabled webhooks, but the management API should show all
mediumLowFindings.description: The findByTenantId method always filters by 'enabled = true'. This is correct for event fan-out (findMatchingWebhooks), but it is also used by the webhook management API (GET /api/v1/webhooks). A user who disables a webhook via PATCH cannot see it in the listing anymore, making it impossible to re-enable or delete it through the list endpoint. The management listing should return all webhooks (enabled and disabled) while the event delivery path should only query enabled ones.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add an optional 'includeDisabled' parameter to findByTenantId, or create a separate method for the management API that does not filter by enabled. The route handler should call the version that shows all webhooks.

mediumLowFindings.title: In-memory rate-limit and SSE maps are module-level singletons that leak across tests and hot reloads
mediumLowFindings.description: The inMemoryWindows map in sliding-window-rate-limiter.ts (line 102) is a module-level global. While the SSE service creates its buffers map inside the factory function (correctly scoped), the rate limiter's fallback map persists across all createSlidingWindowLimiter calls. In test environments or hot-reload scenarios, stale entries accumulate across test runs. In production with a single process this is benign, but it violates the factory pattern used elsewhere and could cause test flakiness.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Move the inMemoryWindows map inside the createSlidingWindowLimiter factory function so each limiter instance has its own isolated map.

mediumLowFindings.title: Introspection query detector returns true for mixed queries containing both __schema and data fields
mediumLowFindings.description: The isIntrospectionQuery function returns true if ANY selection in any query operation is __schema or __type. This means a query like '{ __schema { types { name } } users { id } }' would be identified as an introspection query, causing the entire query to be handled by the introspection handler instead of executing the 'users' resolver. The user would receive only introspection data and silently lose the 'users' result.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Change the function to only return true when ALL selections in the operation are introspection fields (__schema or __type). Return false if any non-introspection field is present.

mediumLowFindings.title: GraphQL write scope check uses 'write' but the platform uses 'data:write' scopes
mediumLowFindings.description: The assertWritePermission function checks for scopes 'write' or 'admin' in the WRITE_SCOPES set. However, the data route handler (routes/data.ts line 43) checks for 'data:write' scope for mutating operations. This inconsistency means the GraphQL endpoint may grant write access to users with a bare 'write' scope while denying it to users with 'data:write', or vice versa. The webhook routes use 'webhooks:manage', lineage uses 'lineage:read' - the scoping pattern across the gateway is 'domain:action', not bare 'write'.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Change WRITE_SCOPES to check for 'data:write' and 'admin' to be consistent with the REST data routes. Also consider adding 'data:read' checks to assertReadPermission for consistency.

mediumLowFindings.title: MIME type allowlist mismatch between route and service causes silent rejection
mediumLowFindings.description: The uploads route has an ALLOWED_MIME_TYPES set containing 'application/x-ndjson' but NOT 'application/octet-stream'. The upload service (upload-service.ts line 113) has an ALLOWED_CONTENT_TYPES set containing 'application/octet-stream' but NOT 'application/x-ndjson'.
