When a user uploads an NDJSON file with content type 'application/x-ndjson', the route allows it through, but if the upload service's createUpload is called with that content type, it would throw UploadUnsupportedTypeError because 'application/x-ndjson' is not in the service's set. Conversely, 'application/octet-stream' passes the service but is rejected by the route. The route check runs first, so 'application/octet-stream' files are rejected at the route level even though the service would accept them.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Unify the two MIME type allowlists into a single shared constant. Both should include the same set of types: 'text/csv', 'application/json', 'text/tab-separated-values', 'application/x-ndjson', and 'application/octet-stream'.

mediumLowFindings.title: Upload uses uploadJob.id as connectorId fallback, creating orphaned raw tables
mediumLowFindings.description: When no connectorId is provided in the form data, the upload route passes it to createUpload without connectorId, so uploadJob.connector_id is null. Then on line 97, the fileParseQueue payload sets `connectorId: uploadJob.connector_id ?? uploadJob.id`. This means when there is no linked connector, the uploadJob's own UUID is used as the connectorId. The parse worker will then create a raw table named `raw_<uploadJobId>` and insert records into it. This raw table is never cleaned up by the retention service because there is no connector row with that ID. The table becomes an orphan that grows indefinitely.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Either require a connectorId for file uploads (reject if missing), or create a tracking mechanism for unlinked upload tables so the retention service can clean them up. At minimum, document this behavior and add cleanup logic for upload-created raw tables.

mediumLowFindings.title: Module-level BullMQ Queue reads OP_REDIS_URL at import time, ignoring runtime config
mediumLowFindings.description: The uploads route creates a module-level BullMQ Queue singleton that reads `process.env['OP_REDIS_URL']` at import time. This means the Queue is created before the service app is initialized, using whatever env var is set at module load time. If the Redis URL is configured differently at runtime (e.g., via loadConfig), or in tests where the env var is not set, the queue will connect to the wrong Redis instance (defaulting to localhost:6379). The same pattern exists in sync-service.ts and webhook-receive-service.ts. Additionally, this module-level Queue is never closed during graceful shutdown - the cleanup function in index.ts closes workers but not these standalone queues.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Pass the Redis URL from the injected config via UploadRouteDeps rather than reading process.env at module level. Create the Queue inside createUploadRoutes and ensure it is included in the cleanup function. Apply the same fix to the module-level queues in sync-service.ts and webhook-receive-service.ts.

mediumLowFindings.title: Cursor-based pagination returns wrong results when cursor ID is not found
mediumLowFindings.description: In listSyncs, the cursor pagination uses `findIndex` to locate the cursor position. If the cursor syncJobId is not found in the filtered array (e.g., the job was removed from BullMQ between pages), `findIndex` returns -1 and the calculation `cursorIdx = -1 + 1 = 0` silently restarts pagination from the beginning instead of returning an empty page or an error. This could cause clients to loop indefinitely, re-fetching the first page forever.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: When the cursor is not found in the result set, either return an empty page with no nextCursor (indicating the cursor has expired) or throw a validation error informing the client that the cursor is no longer valid.

mediumLowFindings.title: Double JSON serialization of records wastes CPU and memory on the hot path
mediumLowFindings.description: In processSyncJob, the records array is serialized to JSON twice on every batch: once for the 10 MB soft size guard (line 683: `JSON.stringify(records)`) and once for the 1 MB hard fail guard (line 698: `JSON.stringify(jobPayload)`, which contains the same records). For large batches near the threshold, this unnecessarily doubles CPU and memory pressure. The jobPayload serialization already includes the records, so checking it alone would cover both guards. Moreover, the 10 MB guard checks `records` alone but the 1 MB guard checks the full `jobPayload` which is always larger -- so the 10 MB guard on records alone is effectively unreachable for any batch that would fail the 1 MB payload guard.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Remove the separate records-only JSON.stringify and rely solely on the jobPayload size check. Adjust the warning threshold to apply to the full payload size, or compute serialized size once and reuse it for both checks.

mediumLowFindings.title: Schema inference off-by-one: schema only inferred when exactly SCHEMA_INFERENCE_ROWS records parsed
mediumLowFindings.description: The schema inference check on line 305 triggers only when `rowsParsed === SCHEMA_INFERENCE_ROWS` (i.e., exactly 200). If the file has fewer than 200 records, inferredSchema is never set and no schema is written to the upload job. For files with fewer than 200 records, users see a null inferredSchema even though there are records available for inference. The check should be `rowsParsed >= SCHEMA_INFERENCE_ROWS` or should trigger at end-of-file when rowsParsed < SCHEMA_INFERENCE_ROWS.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add a fallback after the main parsing loop: if !schemaInferred and batch has records, infer schema from whatever records are available. Change the condition to `rowsParsed >= SCHEMA_INFERENCE_ROWS && !schemaInferred` to handle edge cases.

mediumLowFindings.title: ForbiddenError leaks connector existence to cross-tenant users
mediumLowFindings.description: In requireConnectorForTenant, when a connector exists but belongs to a different tenant, the code throws ForbiddenError('You do not have access to connector X'). This is an information leak: a user in tenant A can probe connector IDs and distinguish between 'connector does not exist' (ConnectorNotFoundError) and 'connector exists but belongs to another tenant' (ForbiddenError) by observing the HTTP status code difference (404 vs 403). This violates the principle of not revealing resource existence to unauthorized users.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Change the ForbiddenError to a ConnectorNotFoundError when tenantId !== '*' and the connector belongs to a different tenant. This way, cross-tenant access attempts receive the same 404 response as non-existent connector lookups, preventing enumeration.

mediumLowFindings.title: Connector ID path parameter not validated as UUID before database lookup
mediumLowFindings.description: The `:id` path parameter in GET/PATCH/DELETE /:id routes is passed directly to connectorService.getConnector without any UUID format validation. While the pg driver will reject non-UUID strings with a database error, the error message will be a raw PostgreSQL error (e.g., 'invalid input syntax for type uuid') rather than a clean validation error. This affects all connector routes using c.req.param('id'), as well as webhook and upload routes.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add a UUID validation check for all :id path parameters before passing them to service methods. Use a shared middleware or helper that validates the format matches /^[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}$/i and throws a ValidationError with a user-friendly message.

mediumLowFindings.title: olderThanHours parameter is accepted but never used in query
mediumLowFindings.description: The findUnregisteredShadowTables method accepts an olderThanHours parameter (called with value 48 from cleanup-service.ts line 83), but the SQL query does not include any time-based filter. All unregistered shadow tables are returned regardless of age, meaning tables could be dropped immediately after creation rather than waiting the intended 48 hours. This could delete shadow tables that are still in active use by running migrations.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add a time-based filter to the query, for example: AND (SELECT MAX(obj_description(c.oid)) FROM pg_catalog.pg_class c WHERE c.relname = t.table_name) ... or more practically, compare against a creation-time proxy. Since information_schema.tables does not include creation time, consider joining against pg_stat_user_tables or pg_class to filter by table age, or register all shadow tables in the registry at creation time so the findActiveOrphans path handles them.

mediumLowFindings.title: Unsanitized non-string default value interpolated into migration view SQL
mediumLowFindings.description: In buildMigrationFieldSpec, when the default value is not a string, it is converted via String(f.defaultValue) and stored as defaultExpression. This expression is later interpolated directly into SQL in buildUnionViewDDL (ddl-builder.ts line 233). An attacker could supply a default value like an object with a custom toString() that returns malicious SQL, or a value like ["1); DROP TABLE x; --"] which when stringified produces unexpected SQL fragments.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Validate the default value type strictly: for number fields, ensure it is actually typeof 'number' and isFinite. For other types, use proper SQL escaping. Consider using parameterized queries or a whitelist approach for the default expression generation.

mediumLowFindings.title: List entities returns items.length as total instead of actual total count
mediumLowFindings.description: The GET /api/v1/ontology endpoint returns total: items.length which is the count of items in the current page, not the total number of entities across all pages. This misleads API consumers who expect 'total' to represent the full count, and breaks pagination UIs that show 'showing N of M' counts.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Either query for the actual total count from the database (e.g., SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ontology.entities WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL), or rename the field to 'count' or 'pageSize' to avoid confusion, or remove the field entirely since hasMore and nextCursor already provide pagination semantics.

mediumLowFindings.title: Stale pre-fetched run step statuses used for cancellation — already-completed steps may be re-cancelled
mediumLowFindings.description: The allRunStepRows array is fetched once before the step traversal loop at line 1481, but the statuses of individual steps change to 'running', 'completed', 'failed', etc. during the loop. When cancellation is detected at line 1487, the code filters allRunStepRows for status === 'pending' using the stale snapshot from before the loop started. Steps that were already completed during the traversal still appear as 'pending' in this stale list and will have their status overwritten to 'cancelled' — destroying the record that they actually completed.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Re-fetch the run steps from the database when cancellation is detected, or use the DB to conditionally update only steps that are still in 'pending' status: UPDATE ... SET status='cancelled' WHERE run_id=$1 AND status='pending'.

mediumLowFindings.title: SSRF blocklist regex does not match URLs without trailing path
mediumLowFindings.description: The SSRF_BLOCKED_PATTERNS regexes in pipeline-service.ts (lines 379-395) all require a trailing slash after the host/port (e.g., /^https?:\/\/localhost(:\d+)?\//) . A URL like 'http://localhost' or 'http://169.254.169.254' without a trailing slash will NOT be blocked, bypassing the SSRF protection at definition-save time. Note: the execution-engine.ts version at line 204 correctly uses (\/) or (\/|$) patterns.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Change all SSRF_BLOCKED_PATTERNS regexes in pipeline-service.ts to match URLs both with and without trailing slashes by using (\/|$) instead of \/ at the end, matching the pattern already used in execution-engine.ts.

mediumLowFindings.title: Promise.race in parallel step waitMode 'any' leaks unresolved branch promises and does not cancel losing branches
mediumLowFindings.description: When a parallel step has waitMode='any', Promise.race is used so the first branch to complete wins. However, the losing branches continue executing in the background indefinitely — they are never cancelled. This means: (1) side effects from losing branches (code execution, webhook calls, connector syncs) still happen, potentially producing duplicate or unwanted actions; (2) the branch promises remain pending in memory, holding references to their RunContext and step outputs until they eventually complete or the process restarts.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Use AbortController or a shared cancellation token to cancel losing branches when the first one completes. Alternatively, use Promise.allSettled with a first-completion flag, and document that waitMode='any' does not cancel other branches if that is intentional behavior.

mediumLowFindings.title: HTTP server response error not handled — promise rejection on arrayBuffer() silently swallowed
mediumLowFindings.description: In the HTTP server handler, the non-SSE response path calls `void response.arrayBuffer().then(...)` but never attaches a .catch() handler. If arrayBuffer() rejects (e.g., body stream interrupted), the rejection is swallowed by void, but the Node.js response object may remain open indefinitely since res.end() is never called. Additionally, if the response from app.fetch is a promise and it rejects, the `void responseOrPromise.then(handleResponse)` at line 469 also silently swallows the rejection.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add .catch() handlers to both promise chains: (1) response.arrayBuffer().then(...).catch(() => { if (!res.headersSent) res.writeHead(500); res.end(); }), and (2) responseOrPromise.then(handleResponse).catch(() => { res.writeHead(500); res.end(); }).

mediumLowFindings.title: Event trigger filter timeout uses resolve(undefined) instead of reject, conflating timeout with 'undefined' evaluation result
mediumLowFindings.description: The evaluateFilter function at line 93 races the JSONata evaluation against a 100ms timeout. On timeout, it resolves with `undefined` and treats `undefined` as a timeout (fail-open, returns true). However, if the JSONata expression legitimately evaluates to `undefined` (a valid JSONata result for unresolved paths), the function also incorrectly treats it as a timeout and returns true, potentially triggering pipeline runs that should have been filtered out. The timer is also never cleared on success.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Use a sentinel symbol or reject with a TimeoutError instead of resolving with undefined. For example: use a unique Symbol('timeout') as the sentinel value, or use new Promise<never>((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new TimeoutError()), 100)) and catch the timeout in the outer try/catch. Also clear the timer on success.

mediumLowFindings.title: deriveSlug can produce empty string or slugs shorter than minimum length
mediumLowFindings.description: The deriveSlug function strips all non-alphanumeric/hyphen characters, then trims leading/trailing hyphens. If the pipeline name is something like '---' or consists entirely of non-ASCII characters (e.g., Chinese, emoji), the function returns an empty string. The slug regex in the schema requires min 3 chars matching /^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9\-]{1,62}[a-z0-9]$/, so the derived slug would fail validation if it were re-validated — but it is not re-validated since deriveSlug is only called when no explicit slug is provided, and the result goes directly to the database.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: After deriving the slug, validate it against the same regex used in the schema. If it is empty or too short, either throw a validation error or fall back to a UUID-based slug (e.g., 'pipeline-' + uuid.slice(0, 8)).

mediumLowFindings.title: SSE log stream uses stale initial run status for terminal check — may close prematurely or miss final logs
mediumLowFindings.description: The SSE log stream handler fetches the run status once at line 54, then uses it to decide whether to close the stream at line 105. If the run transitions to terminal status between the initial fetch and the log retrieval, the stream may close before all final log entries are captured. Conversely, if the run is fetched as 'running' but becomes terminal between the status check and the follow-loop entry, the stream enters the poll loop and catches it on the next iteration — which is correct but shows the initial check is redundant in a racy way.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: After fetching initial logs, re-check the run status to ensure any terminal transition that happened during log retrieval is captured. Or simplify by always entering the poll loop and letting the terminal check inside the loop handle closure.

mediumLowFindings.title: buildAdjacencyMap does not recurse into parallel branch steps for cycle detection
mediumLowFindings.description: The buildAdjacencyMap function only processes top-level steps. When a parallel step contains branches with nested steps, only the entryStepId of each branch is added as a neighbor of the parallel step, but the steps inside the branches are not added to the adjacency map. This means cycles within parallel branches (e.g., a conditional step inside a branch that points back to the parallel step) would not be detected by hasCycle.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Recursively call buildAdjacencyMap on each branch's steps array and merge the resulting adjacency maps into the parent map, so that cycle detection covers nested branch graphs as well.

mediumLowFindings.title: SSRF bypass via IPv6 unspecified address :: and missing IPv4-mapped IPv6 handling
mediumLowFindings.description: The BLOCKED_IPV6_PREFIXES list checks for '::1' (loopback), 'fe80:' (link-local), 'fd' and 'fc' (ULA), but does not include '::' (the unspecified address, equivalent to 0.0.0.0 for IPv6) or '::ffff:' (IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses). A DNS record returning '::' or '::ffff:10.0.0.1' would bypass all IPv6 checks. Verified: `isIpv6Blocked('::')` returns false, `isIpv6Blocked('::ffff:127.0.0.1')` returns false.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add '::' to the prefix list for the unspecified address. Add '::ffff:' to catch IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses, and when a '::ffff:' address is detected, extract the embedded IPv4 address and run it through isIpv4Blocked() as well.

mediumLowFindings.title: Timer leak in routeToIsolatedVm creates unhandled promise rejections
mediumLowFindings.description: The timeout Promise created at line 287-292 uses a setTimeout that is never cleared when client.send() resolves successfully. When the normal (non-timeout) path completes, the timer continues running and eventually fires, rejecting the timeoutPromise. Since nobody is listening to this rejection (Promise.race already resolved with the send result), this produces an unhandled promise rejection. With max timeout of 300,000ms + 2,000ms buffer, these leaked timers accumulate across many concurrent executions.

mediumLowFindings.title: execution_date derived from log line timestamp instead of execution started_at, breaking co-partitioning
mediumLowFindings.description: The comment at lines 138-141 explicitly states 'execution_date must match the execution's started_at so the log row lands in the correct co-partitioned range' but the implementation uses `new Date(logLine.timestamp)` which is the log line's own timestamp, not the execution's started_at. If an execution starts at 23:59:59 on the last day of a month and log lines arrive in the next month, those log rows will be inserted into a different partition than the execution record. This causes co-partitioned queries to miss log lines and will fail with a partition routing error if the next month's log partition doesn't exist yet.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Look up the execution's started_at from the execution record (or cache it when the execution is created/dispatched) and use that value for execution_date. For example, maintain a Map<executionId, Date> populated during runExecution/runInternalExecution and use it in the onLogLine callback.

mediumLowFindings.title: Unhandled promise rejection in HTTP server when app.fetch rejects
mediumLowFindings.description: The HTTP server handler uses `void responseOrPromise.then(handleResponse)` without a .catch() handler. If app.fetch() throws asynchronously (e.g., middleware throws an unhandled exception), the rejection is silently discarded, and the client connection hangs forever since res.end() is never called. Similarly, `void response.arrayBuffer().then(...)` at line 399 lacks error handling.

mediumLowFindings.title: recordRun adds execution to inflightIds even when sandbox is DRAINING_OLD
mediumLowFindings.description: recordRun() unconditionally adds the executionId to primary.inflightIds and increments runCount without checking the sandbox state. If recordRun is called after getPrimary() returned successfully but triggerRecycle() ran in between (e.g., the recycle timer fired), the new execution is added to inflightIds while the drain is already in progress. The drain's waitForInflightDrain will then wait for or force-kill this execution that was just dispatched, causing unexpected execution failures.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Check `isDraining` in recordRun and throw ExecutionSandboxUnavailableError if the sandbox is draining, or guard the getPrimary -> recordRun sequence with a state check.

mediumLowFindings.title: Connector run uses empty string as code when plugin bundle fetch returns null
mediumLowFindings.description: In runConnectorExecution, if the plugin bundle cache returns null (bundle not found or fetch failed), the code falls through to execute with `bundle?.bundleBase64 ?? ''` (empty string). This sends an empty code payload to the sandbox which will either crash or produce a cryptic error, rather than failing fast with a clear 'plugin bundle not found' error.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Check for null bundle immediately after the pluginBundleCache.get() call and throw a descriptive error: `if (bundle === null) throw new Error('Plugin bundle not found for plugin ' + request.pluginId);`

mediumLowFindings.title: Rename file route validates toPath but not fromPath, allowing path traversal in source path
mediumLowFindings.description: In the POST /:id/files/rename route, validateFilePath() is called on parsed.data.toPath but not on parsed.data.fromPath. While the fromPath is used in a WHERE clause (so SQL injection is not a concern), the lack of validation means a fromPath like '/../../../etc/passwd' would be accepted. Although the DB query would simply not find such a path (returning null and a 409), the inconsistency could be exploited if the validation rules ever change or if the fromPath is logged/displayed without sanitization.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add validateFilePath(parsed.data.fromPath) before the rename operation, consistent with how all other file path inputs are validated.

mediumLowFindings.title: In-memory rate limit Map grows unboundedly as unique users accumulate
mediumLowFindings.description: The rateLimitBuckets Map stores one entry per userId that ever calls the embed token generation endpoint. When a bucket expires (now >= resetAt), it is replaced on next access, but buckets for users who never return are never cleaned up. In a system with many users creating embed tokens, this Map will grow without bound, causing a slow memory leak. The code comment acknowledges this: 'In a multi-replica deployment this should use Redis.'
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add a periodic cleanup that removes expired buckets (e.g., via setInterval every 5 minutes), or switch to a Redis-backed implementation as the comment suggests. Alternatively use a bounded LRU cache.

mediumLowFindings.title: Concurrent version creation can cause unique constraint violation resulting in unhandled 500 error
mediumLowFindings.description: The AppVersionRepository.create() method computes version_number via SELECT MAX(version_number) + 1 inside the INSERT statement. Two concurrent createVersion calls for the same app can both read the same MAX value and attempt to insert the same version_number. If there is a unique constraint on (app_id, version_number), one will fail with a Postgres unique violation error. This error propagates as an unhandled 500 to the API consumer rather than a proper conflict response. Unlike the builds table (which uses advisory locks), the app versions have no serialization mechanism.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Either: (1) use a Postgres advisory lock on the app_id before inserting (same pattern as build triggers), (2) wrap the insert in a retry loop that catches unique violation errors and re-attempts with the new MAX, or (3) use a sequence/serial column for version_number.

mediumLowFindings.title: Preview reload SSE stream only works for public apps, fails silently for platform-user apps
mediumLowFindings.description: The /apps/:slug/preview/reload-stream endpoint only looks up apps via appRepo.findPublicBySlug(slug), which filters by access_mode = 'public'. Platform-user apps (the default access mode) are never found by this query, so the endpoint always returns 404 for them. This means the preview hot-reload feature is broken for the majority of apps. Additionally, there is no authentication check, so anyone can subscribe to a public app's reload events.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add logic to also check for platform-user apps when a user session is available (same pattern as the main /apps/:slug/* route), and add auth checks for non-public apps to prevent unauthorized access to reload events.

mediumLowFindings.title: deleteRole does not verify role belongs to specified app - cross-app role deletion
mediumLowFindings.description: Same issue as updateRole: deleteRole calls assertAppAccess(tenantId, appId) then permRepo.deleteRole(roleId) where deleteRole SQL is 'DELETE FROM app.roles WHERE id = $1' without filtering by app_id. An authenticated user can delete any role they know the ID of, as long as they provide any valid appId they own for the access check.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Change permRepo.deleteRole to accept both roleId and appId, and modify the SQL to: DELETE FROM app.roles WHERE id = $1 AND app_id = $2

mediumLowFindings.title: validateFilePath rejects files without extensions despite .env.example being in allowed list
mediumLowFindings.description: The validateFilePath function extracts the extension using path.slice(path.lastIndexOf('.')). For the allowed extension '.env.example', a file at '/config/.env.example' would have lastIndexOf('.') point at '.example', yielding ext='.example' which is NOT in the allowed set. The intended extension '.env.example' can never be matched by this logic because lastIndexOf('.') only captures the last dot-delimited segment. Any file intended to use the '.env.example' extension would be rejected with an invalid path error.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Either remove '.env.example' from ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS (since it can never match), or change the extension extraction logic to check for compound extensions like '.env.example' by testing multiple suffixes.

mediumLowFindings.title: BullMQ Queue defaultJobOptions have no effect - created and immediately closed
mediumLowFindings.description: A BullMQ Queue instance is created with defaultJobOptions (attempts: 5, exponential backoff) and immediately closed on line 59. The code comment says 'Set retry defaults on the Queue so that jobs added by any producer inherit exponential backoff' but this is incorrect. BullMQ defaultJobOptions are instance-level settings, not persisted queue-level configuration. They only apply to jobs added through that specific Queue instance. Since this Queue is never used to add jobs and is immediately closed, the retry configuration has zero effect. Jobs added by other services (the actual producers) will use whatever options they specify, or BullMQ defaults (no retries).
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Remove the dead Queue instantiation. Instead, ensure that the producers (other services that add jobs to the 'audit' queue) specify the retry options when calling queue.add(). Alternatively, if the logging service should set retry policy, it would need to be enforced on the Worker side by implementing custom retry logic in the worker's error handler.

mediumLowFindings.title: CSV export produces malformed output when trace_id or service contain commas or newlines
mediumLowFindings.description: In the CSV export streaming handler, the trace_id (line 183) and service (line 184) fields are written without CSV quoting. The input validation schemas allow any characters in these fields (only length is constrained: service max 64 chars, traceId max 128 chars). If a log event has a trace_id or service containing commas, double quotes, or newlines, the CSV output will be malformed - fields will be misaligned and parsers will produce incorrect data.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Quote all string fields in the CSV output using proper RFC 4180 escaping. Apply the same quoting pattern used for message to trace_id and service: `"${row.trace_id.replace(/"/g, '""')}"` and `"${row.service.replace(/"/g, '""')}"`. Alternatively, create a helper function csvEscape(value: string) that wraps in quotes and escapes internal double-quotes, and apply it to all string fields.

mediumLowFindings.title: Missing UUID validation on log event ID path parameter causes 500 errors
mediumLowFindings.description: The GET /api/v1/logs/:id endpoint extracts the id path parameter and passes it directly to logEventRepository.findById() which uses it in a WHERE id = $1 query against a UUID column. If a caller passes a non-UUID string (e.g., /api/v1/logs/not-a-uuid), PostgreSQL will throw 'invalid input syntax for type uuid' which propagates as an unhandled 500 Internal Server Error instead of a proper 400 Bad Request. The OpenAPI metadata (openapi-meta.ts line 163) specifies z.string().uuid() for the parameter but this validation is not enforced in the actual route handler.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add UUID format validation before calling the repository: const idResult = z.string().uuid().safeParse(id); if (!idResult.success) throw new ValidationError('Invalid log event ID', idResult.error.issues);

mediumLowFindings.title: Upload temp directory never cleaned up
mediumLowFindings.description: The POST /api/v1/plugins route creates a temp directory at /tmp/oneplatform-plugins/<uuid> and writes the uploaded bundle file there. However, this directory is never cleaned up. The installPlugin service method only cleans up its own extractDir (a separate temp directory created inside extractAndValidateBundle). Each plugin install request leaves behind a directory on disk that is never removed, causing unbounded disk usage over time.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add a try/finally block around the installPlugin call in the route handler that removes tmpDir after the service call completes (or fails): try { ... await pluginService.installPlugin({...}); ... } finally { await rm(tmpDir, { recursive: true, force: true }).catch(() => {}); }

mediumLowFindings.title: Redis retryWithBackoff calls connect() on already-connected client
mediumLowFindings.description: The Redis client is created with lazyConnect: true. The retryWithBackoff function calls both redis.connect() and redis.ping() in sequence. If connect() succeeds but ping() fails (e.g., due to a transient timeout), the retry will call redis.connect() again on a client that is already in the 'connecting' or 'connected' state. ioredis throws 'Redis is already connecting/connected' in this case, which can cause startup to fail even though Redis becomes available.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Check the Redis client status before calling connect(): async () => { if (redis.status === 'wait') await redis.connect(); await redis.ping(); }. Alternatively, separate the connect and ping into two steps: await redis.connect(); await retryWithBackoff(() => redis.ping(), 'Redis', 30_000);

mediumLowFindings.title: Missing ROLLBACK in disableInstance hook-disable transaction
mediumLowFindings.description: In disableInstance, a database transaction is opened with BEGIN at line 236, but the try block has no catch clause. If hookRepo.updateStateByInstance throws (e.g., database connection error, constraint violation), the client is released back to the pool in the finally block with an uncommitted open transaction. This leaves the connection in a dirty state. The next consumer that acquires this connection from the pool will inherit the open transaction, potentially causing data integrity issues or confusing errors.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add a catch clause that rolls back before re-throwing: try { await client.query('BEGIN'); ... await client.query('COMMIT'); } catch (err) { await client.query('ROLLBACK').catch(() => undefined); throw err; } finally { client.release(); }

mediumLowFindings.title: patchInstance re-enables with stale instance data after config/displayName update
mediumLowFindings.description: When patchInstance receives both config/displayName changes AND enabled=true, the config and displayName are updated in the database first (lines 365, 368). Then enableInstance is called with the original instance object fetched before those updates (line 347). Inside enableInstance, connector registration uses instance.display_name (line 175 of enableInstance), which is the stale pre-update value. The connector in the Ingestion Service will be registered with the old display name instead of the newly provided one.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Re-fetch the instance from the database after applying config/displayName updates and before calling enableInstance: const freshInstance = await instanceRepo.findByIdAndTenant(instanceId, tenantId); if (freshInstance === null) throw ...; const result = await enableInstance(freshInstance, plugin.id);

mediumLowFindings.title: Upgrade config validation only checks 'required' fields, misses schema constraints
mediumLowFindings.description: The upgrade pre-flight config validation (B6 fix) at line 218 only checks whether required fields exist in the instance config using a simple 'key in config' test. It does not run full JSON Schema validation (Ajv). A new plugin version could introduce type changes, pattern constraints, enum restrictions, min/max limits, or additional nested property requirements that would not be detected by this shallow check. The instance service uses Ajv.compile() for proper validation at instance creation (line 307 of validateConfigAgainstSchema), but the upgrade service bypasses this. Instances could become silently invalid after upgrade.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Use the same validateConfigAgainstSchema function (Ajv-based) that the instance service uses: import or extract the validateConfigAgainstSchema function to a shared location and call it for each instance's config against the new configSchema during upgrade validation.

mediumLowFindings.title: Cache DELETE endpoint missing key validation present in GET/PUT
mediumLowFindings.description: The GET (line 178) and PUT (line 205) cache endpoints validate the key parameter with: key.length > 256 || !/^[\w\-.:]+$/.test(key). The DELETE endpoint at line 234 does not perform this validation, accepting any key value. While this is an internal endpoint protected by service token auth, the inconsistency means a malformed key could be injected into the Redis key string (plugin:cache:{tenantId}:{pluginId}:{key}). Although Redis key injection is limited in impact, it breaks the security-in-depth pattern the other endpoints follow.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add the same key validation as GET/PUT: if (key.length > 256 || !/^[\w\-.:]+$/.test(key)) { return c.json({ error: { code: 'VALIDATION_ERROR', message: 'key must be max 256 URL-safe chars.', requestId: c.var.requestId } }, 400); }

mediumLowFindings.title: In-memory rate limiter Map grows unboundedly
mediumLowFindings.description: The token bucket rate limiter stores an entry in a Map for every unique userId that makes a publish or rate request. These entries are never evicted. Over the lifetime of the process, the Map will grow without bound. With many users, this will consume increasing memory. The buckets Map is module-scoped and shared across all requests.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add periodic cleanup of stale entries (e.g., entries that haven't been accessed in 5+ minutes), or use an LRU cache with a max size. For example, use an interval timer to prune entries where (now - bucket.lastRefill) > 300_000.

mediumLowFindings.title: Ratings cursor pagination uses id > cursor with DESC ordering, producing incorrect results
mediumLowFindings.description: In findRatingsByPlugin, the cursor-based pagination uses 'AND id > $2' (line 295) as the cursor condition, but the ORDER BY is 'created_at DESC, id DESC' (line 296). For descending pagination, the cursor condition should use '<' (less than) to get the next page of results. Using '>' with DESC order will skip results or return results from the wrong direction, effectively showing unpredictable pages when the cursor is applied.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Change the cursor condition to use '<' for DESC ordering: 'AND id < $2' instead of 'AND id > $2'. This ensures the next page retrieves ratings with smaller IDs (i.e., earlier in the descending sort).

mediumLowFindings.title: CORS middleware treats wildcard '*' origin as a literal string, silently breaking dev environments
mediumLowFindings.description: The CORS middleware does a strict Set lookup (originSet.has(origin)) against configured origins. When OP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS contains '*', the middleware treats it as a literal origin string 'http://*' or '*'. Browsers never send Origin: * so all browser requests in development environments configured with wildcard origins will receive 403 ORIGIN_NOT_ALLOWED. The config schema's originsSchema (config.ts line 5-16) blocks '*' in production but allows it in non-production, suggesting wildcard is intended to work in development. The middleware should explicitly check for '*' and allow all origins when it is present.

mediumLowFindings.title: Public route prefix extraction strips all param segments, creating overly broad path matches
mediumLowFindings.description: When a publicRoute contains ':', the regex `normalized.replace(/\/:[^/]+/g, '')` strips ALL colon-prefixed segments, not just trailing ones. For a route like '/api/v1/users/:userId/profile/:section', the prefix becomes '/api/v1/users/profile' which is nonsensical and would never match any real URL. The comment says 'Strip the trailing /:paramName segment(s)' but the regex operates globally on any segment containing ':', including mid-path parameters. This could create false positives where paths matching the concatenated non-param segments are incorrectly treated as public, or false negatives where legitimate parameterized paths don't match because the extracted prefix is wrong.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix:
For routes with mid-path parameters, convert the pattern into a regex that matches any segment in param positions, rather than stripping them. For example:

const regexStr = normalized
  .split('/')
  .map(seg => seg.startsWith(':') ? '[^/]+' : seg)
  .join('/');
prefixPublicRoutes.push(new RegExp('^' + regexStr + '$'));

Alternatively, if only trailing params are intended, use slice to get the prefix up to the first param segment rather than a global replace.

mediumLowFindings.title: Service token callerService extracted from unverified JWT payload before signature check
mediumLowFindings.description: The serviceAuthMiddleware extracts callerService from the JWT payload (line 104) before verifying the token signature (line 131-132). The callerService value is then used to look up the public key and is included in error messages (line 121). While this is a common pattern for key selection in asymmetric JWT verification (you need to know which key to use), the unverified callerService is reflected directly into the error response message at line 121: `Unknown service: ${callerService}`. An attacker could craft a JWT with any arbitrary string in the 'sub' claim and have it reflected in the error response, potentially enabling response injection or log injection if the value contains special characters.

mediumLowFindings.title: Response envelope middleware skips wrapping any response containing a 'data' key, preventing routes from returning objects with 'data' as a domain field
mediumLowFindings.description: The middleware checks `"data" in (body as object)` to detect already-enveloped responses and skip double-wrapping. However, this means if a route handler returns a domain object that naturally has a 'data' field (e.g. { data: [...], metadata: {...} } or { data: 'raw content', format: 'csv' }), the middleware assumes it is already enveloped and does not wrap it. The consumer would receive { data: [...], metadata: {...} } instead of the expected { data: { data: [...], metadata: {...} } }. This is a semantic ambiguity that can cause subtle frontend breakage when domain models use 'data' as a field name.

mediumLowFindings.title: Token refresh race: concurrent callers may use stale token after refresh
mediumLowFindings.description: The `refresh()` method correctly deduplicates concurrent refresh calls by sharing `refreshInFlight`. However, when two requests fail with 401 simultaneously and both call `refresh()`, the first call sets `this.currentToken = newToken` at line 55. The second call awaits the same promise and gets the same newToken, but it also sets `this.currentToken = newToken` again (harmless in this case). The real issue is that `this.refreshInFlight` is set to null in the `.finally()` at line 40 BEFORE `this.currentToken` is updated at line 55. There is a window between `.finally()` running (setting refreshInFlight=null) and line 55 executing (setting currentToken). If a third request enters `refresh()` during that window, it would see `refreshInFlight === null`, trigger a NEW refresh call, and might get a DIFFERENT token than what's about to be set at line 55, causing a token mismatch.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Move the `this.refreshInFlight = null` cleanup to after `this.currentToken` has been updated. Replace the `.finally()` approach with a try/finally inside the refresh method that clears the in-flight promise only after the token has been stored: `this.refreshInFlight = this.refreshFn(); try { const newToken = await this.refreshInFlight; ... this.currentToken = newToken; } finally { this.refreshInFlight = null; }`

mediumLowFindings.title: destroy() mutates Set while iterating, then calls clear() on subscriptions that already removed themselves
mediumLowFindings.description: In the `destroy()` method, the code iterates over `activeSubscriptions` with a for-of loop and calls `sub.unsubscribe()` on each. But `unsubscribe()` was wrapped at line 257-259 to call `activeSubscriptions.delete(sub)` before calling `originalUnsubscribe()`. This means the Set is mutated during iteration. While JavaScript's Set iteration specification allows deletion of the current element during for-of without issues, the subsequent `activeSubscriptions.clear()` at line 291 is redundant and masks the design intent. More importantly, if any subscription's `unsubscribe()` throws, the remaining subscriptions are not cleaned up.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Wrap each unsubscribe call in a try-catch to ensure all subscriptions are cleaned up even if one throws: `for (const sub of activeSubscriptions) { try { sub.unsubscribe(); } catch { /* ignore */ } } activeSubscriptions.clear();`

mediumLowFindings.title: SSE parser uses trimStart() on data lines, corrupting data with leading whitespace
mediumLowFindings.description: At line 88, after extracting the data portion with `line.slice(5)`, the code calls `.trimStart()` which strips all leading whitespace. Per the SSE specification (W3C EventSource), the data field value should be the text after 'data:' with only a single leading space removed if present (i.e., 'data: foo' gives 'foo', but 'data:  foo' should give ' foo'). Using `.trimStart()` instead of removing at most one leading space corrupts data payloads that legitimately begin with whitespace, such as indented JSON fragments or formatted text.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Follow the SSE spec: remove exactly one leading space if present. Replace `.trimStart()` with a conditional slice: `const raw = line.slice(5); const chunk = raw.startsWith(' ') ? raw.slice(1) : raw;`

mediumLowFindings.title: SSE parser splits on \n only, missing \r\n and bare \r line endings
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix:
Split on all SSE-valid line endings. Replace `buffer.split('
')` with a regex split that handles all three: `buffer.split(/
||
/)`. This matches the SSE specification and handles all server line-ending conventions.

mediumLowFindings.title: Filter builder silently overwrites duplicate field+operator conditions
mediumLowFindings.description: The `toParams()` method builds a Record<string, string> using `params[key] = condition.value`. If the same field+operator combination is added multiple times (e.g., `filter('status').eq('active').and('status').eq('draft')`), the second condition silently overwrites the first in the output params. This is because the key `filter[status][eq]` is identical for both. The builder accumulates both conditions in the array but the serialization only keeps the last one, which is surprising and leads to data loss. The 'immutable builder' documentation suggests branching is safe, but reusing the same field+operator discards earlier conditions.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Either throw a ValidationError when a duplicate field+operator is detected in toParams(), or support multiple values for the same key by returning Record<string, string | string[]> and appending to an array. Alternatively, document the limitation clearly in the JSDoc.

mediumLowFindings.title: parseEntityData mutates supposedly-readonly Entity by caching parsed data on it
mediumLowFindings.description: The `parseEntityData` function caches the parsed JSON result by writing a `__parsedData` property directly onto the Entity instance via `entityAny[cacheKey] = parsed`. The Entity interface declares all fields as non-mutable plain strings, and Entity objects returned from gRPC calls may be frozen or shared across code paths. This mutation is unexpected and can cause issues: (1) If the entity is Object.freeze()'d, the assignment silently fails in sloppy mode or throws in strict mode. (2) The cached value is typed as T, but a subsequent call with a different generic T would return the previously cached value with the wrong type. (3) The mutation makes the function impure, violating the expectation set by its signature.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Use a WeakMap<Entity, unknown> for caching instead of mutating the entity object: `const parseCache = new WeakMap<Entity, unknown>(); export function parseEntityData<T>(entity: Entity): T { const cached = parseCache.get(entity); if (cached !== undefined) return cached as T; const parsed = JSON.parse(entity.dataJson) as T; parseCache.set(entity, parsed); return parsed; }`

mediumLowFindings.title: PKCE callback code/state extracted at module scope but never auto-processed
mediumLowFindings.description: At PKCE handler construction time (lines 243-252), the code extracts `code` and `state` from the current URL query params and strips them via `history.replaceState`. However, the extracted `callbackCode` and `callbackState` variables are never used -- they are local variables that are discarded. The caller must separately call `handleCallback(window.location.href)` to actually exchange the code. But by the time they call it, the code/state have already been stripped from the URL (line 250), so `handleCallback` will fail because the URL no longer contains the params. The caller would need to save the original URL before creating the client.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Either: (1) save the full URL before stripping and use it internally when handleCallback is called without arguments, or (2) do not strip the URL params at construction time -- let handleCallback do the stripping after successfully exchanging the code, or (3) auto-process the callback at construction and store the resulting tokens. The current approach strips the params but never processes them, creating a timing bug where the authorization code is lost.

mediumLowFindings.title: Default retry policy retries on NetworkError status codes but NetworkError has no statusCode
mediumLowFindings.description: In the transport's `request()` method (line 239), the retry logic uses `getStatusCode` which extracts `err.statusCode` from OnePlatformError instances. However, NetworkError sets statusCode to undefined (since the request never reached the server). The retry handler's `withRetry` at retry-handler.ts line 111 checks `if (status === undefined || !policy.retryableStatusCodes.includes(status))` -- when status is undefined, it throws immediately without retrying. This means timeout errors and connection failures (NetworkError with reason 'timeout' or 'fetch-failed') are NEVER retried, despite NetworkError having `retryable = true`. The retry mechanism only retries on HTTP status codes, not on network-level failures.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Modify the `getStatusCode` callback to return a synthetic retryable code for NetworkError instances, or modify `withRetry` to also check the error's `retryable` property when statusCode is undefined. For example: `(err) => { if (err instanceof NetworkError) return 503; return err instanceof OnePlatformError ? err.statusCode : undefined; }`

mediumLowFindings.title: PKCE URL stripping drops query parameters unrelated to auth callback
mediumLowFindings.description: When stripping the OAuth callback params from the URL, the code replaces the entire URL with just `pathname + hash`, discarding ALL query parameters -- not just `code` and `state`. If the application URL contained other query parameters (e.g., `?code=abc&state=xyz&tab=settings&view=dashboard`), the `tab` and `view` params are also lost. This can break application routing or state management that relies on query parameters.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Only remove the `code` and `state` parameters while preserving others: `const cleanParams = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search); cleanParams.delete('code'); cleanParams.delete('state'); const qs = cleanParams.toString(); const cleanUrl = window.location.pathname + (qs ? '?' + qs : '') + window.location.hash;`

mediumLowFindings.title: DataNamespace Proxy intercepts built-in property accesses, may break debugging tools
mediumLowFindings.description: The Proxy handler for `client.data` intercepts ALL string property accesses (line 235) and returns an EntityResource for any string property that is not 'entity'. This means accessing `client.data.then`, `client.data.toJSON`, `client.data.constructor`, or `client.data[Symbol.toStringTag]` all return EntityResource instances for entity types named 'then', 'toJSON', etc. This is particularly problematic for `.then` because it makes `client.data` look like a thenable to Promise.resolve() and await, causing unexpected behavior: `await client.data` would attempt to call `client.data.then()` which is an EntityResource object (not a function), causing a confusing error.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add a guard list for known built-in property names that should not be intercepted: `const RESERVED = new Set(['then', 'catch', 'finally', 'toJSON', 'toString', 'valueOf', 'constructor', 'inspect', Symbol.toPrimitive, Symbol.toStringTag]); ... if (typeof prop !== 'string' || RESERVED.has(prop)) return Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver);`

mediumLowFindings.title: Optimistic rollback uses stale previousValue after rapid successive writes
mediumLowFindings.description: The setValue callback captures the current 'value' state as 'previousValue' for rollback on failure. When multiple setValue calls are made in rapid succession, the second call's previousValue is the optimistically-set value from the first call (not the confirmed server value). If the second PUT fails, it rolls back to the first call's unconfirmed optimistic value rather than the true server-side state. For example: server state is 'X', call setValue('A') then immediately setValue('B'). If the PUT for 'B' fails, the state reverts to 'A' (the optimistic value), not 'X' (the actual server-confirmed value). This leaves the UI in a state that does not match the server.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Store the last server-confirmed value in a separate ref (e.g., confirmedValueRef) and update it only after a successful PUT. On rollback, revert to confirmedValueRef.current instead of the potentially-optimistic 'value' state. Alternatively, serialize writes through a queue (similar to useMutation's enqueue pattern) so each write completes before the next begins.

mediumLowFindings.title: faviconUrl set without URL protocol validation
mediumLowFindings.description: The applyFavicon function sets link.href = faviconUrl with no validation that the URL uses a safe protocol (http: or https:). While BffClient validates its bffBaseUrl protocol, the branding fetch response's faviconUrl is trusted unconditionally. A malicious or compromised tenant branding API response could supply a data: URI (for tracking) or other unexpected protocol. The same issue applies to logoUrl which is rendered as an attribute.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Validate that faviconUrl and logoUrl use http: or https: protocols before applying them. Reject data: URIs, blob: URIs, and javascript: URIs. Example: const parsed = new URL(faviconUrl); if (parsed.protocol !== 'http:' && parsed.protocol !== 'https:') return;

mediumLowFindings.title: Subscription registration reads filter/events only at mount time, silently ignoring dynamic changes
mediumLowFindings.description: When useSubscription registers with WebSocketManager, it reads optionsRef.current.filter and optionsRef.current.events at the time the effect runs (on [id, entity, wsManager] changes only). If the caller changes filter or events after mount, optionsRef is updated but the server-side subscription still uses the original values. The onEvent callback correctly uses optionsRef for the latest callback, but the server-side filter is stale. This means events that should be filtered out by the new filter will still arrive, and events that match only the new filter will not be subscribed. The JSDoc mentions this is a design trade-off, but callers who pass dynamic filters will silently receive incorrect event streams with no warning.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Either (a) include a serialized representation of filter and events in the effect's dependency array so the subscription is re-registered when they change, or (b) emit a console.warn in development mode when filter/events change after initial registration so callers learn they need to use a key prop to force remount, or (c) add an updateRegistration method to WebSocketManager that sends an updated subscribe message without unregister/re-register.

mediumLowFindings.title: 204 No Content returns undefined cast as T, hiding type errors for non-void callers
mediumLowFindings.description: When the BFF responds with 204 No Content, the request() method returns 'undefined as T'. This is correct for callers that expect void (like useMutation's remove()), but any caller that requests a concrete type T (e.g., request<User>(...)) will receive undefined at runtime while TypeScript believes it has a User. This is an unsafe cast that hides a runtime type violation. If a new BFF endpoint incorrectly returns 204 when it should return data, the caller will get undefined with no type-level protection.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Consider adding a generic constraint or overload that makes the 204 case type-safe. For example, add a separate requestVoid() method for endpoints that return no body, or use a conditional return type: when method is DELETE, return type is void. Alternatively, throw an AppSDKError when 204 is received but T is not void, though this requires runtime type information.

mediumLowFindings.title: QueryCache.invalidate() deletes entries while iterating over entries.keys()
mediumLowFindings.description: The invalidate() method iterates over this.entries.keys() and calls this.entries.delete(key) inside the loop. While the ES2015 Map spec guarantees that deleting the current key during iteration is safe and the iterator will not revisit deleted keys, this pattern depends on a subtle spec guarantee that is easy to break during refactoring. If someone were to change the iteration to use a cached array or different collection type, it could silently skip entries or throw.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Collect keys to delete first, then delete them in a separate loop: const toDelete = [...this.entries.keys()].filter(k => this.keyBelongsToEntity(k, entity)); for (const key of toDelete) { this.entries.delete(key); this.notifyListeners(key); }. This makes the intent explicit and is safe regardless of collection type.

mediumLowFindings.title: withRetry performs 4 total attempts but BFF_MAX_RETRIES=3 implies 3 total
mediumLowFindings.description: The retry loop condition is 'attempt <= BFF_MAX_RETRIES' with attempt starting at 0 and BFF_MAX_RETRIES=3, resulting in 4 total attempts (indices 0, 1, 2, 3). The constant name 'BFF_MAX_RETRIES' and the JSDoc 'up to BFF_MAX_RETRIES times' suggest the intent is 3 total attempts (1 initial + 2 retries), not 4 (1 initial + 3 retries). The exponential backoff delays are computed as 500ms, 1000ms, 2000ms which match 3 retries, but the loop actually allows a fourth attempt at 4000ms delay.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Change the loop condition to 'attempt < BFF_MAX_RETRIES' for 3 total attempts, or rename the constant to BFF_MAX_ATTEMPTS = 4 to match the actual behavior. Alternatively, add a comment clarifying that BFF_MAX_RETRIES means 3 retries plus 1 initial attempt = 4 total.

mediumLowFindings.title: AppProvider cleanup destroys WebSocketManager and PermissionCache but refs remain stale on remount
mediumLowFindings.description: The useEffect cleanup calls wsManager.destroy() and permissionCache.destroy(), which set internal 'destroyed' flags to true. However, the useProviderSingletons hook uses useRef to hold these instances and only creates them when the ref is null. On React Strict Mode double-mount (or retry via retryCount increment), the cleanup runs and destroys the instances, but the refs still hold the destroyed objects. The next effect run reuses the same destroyed instances because the refs are not null. The WebSocketManager.connect() checks 'if (this.destroyed) return' and will silently refuse to connect. The PermissionCache.refresh() also bails when destroyed. This means after a retry (setRetryCount(n => n+1)), the app may fail to establish WebSocket connections or refresh permissions.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Either (a) reset the 'destroyed' flag in connect()/seed() methods so destroyed instances can be reused, or (b) set the refs to null in the cleanup function so useProviderSingletons creates fresh instances on remount: bffClientRef.current = null; permissionCacheRef.current = null; wsManagerRef.current = null. Option (a) is simpler: add 'this.destroyed = false;' at the top of WebSocketManager.connect() and PermissionCache.seed().

mediumLowFindings.title: CONDITIONAL_METHODS map references feature flags and methods that do not exist in SDK interfaces
mediumLowFindings.description: The CONDITIONAL_METHODS map checks for feature flags like `supportsWebhook`, `supportsBatch`, `supportsDelete`, `supportsMfa`, `supportsResize` and expects methods like `fetchIncremental`, `handleWebhook`, `writeBatch`, `delete`, `initiateMfa`, `verifyMfa`, `onResize`. None of these flags or methods exist in any SDK type definition (connector.ts, transformer.ts, destination.ts, auth-provider.ts, widget.ts). The real optional methods use different naming (e.g., `subscribeToEvents` for connectors, `transformBatch` for transformers). This makes the conditional validation logic entirely non-functional -- it will never trigger because no plugin metadata() will ever return these non-existent flags.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Update the CONDITIONAL_METHODS map to reference actual SDK interface names. For connector: `supportsRealtime` should check for `subscribeToEvents`. For transformer: remove `supportsBatch` (there is no such metadata flag; `transformBatch` is always optional). For destination: `supportsStreaming` should check for `writeStream`. Remove entirely fabricated entries like auth-provider.supportsMfa and widget.supportsResize.

mediumLowFindings.title: Scaffolded auth-provider getAuthorizationUrl signature does not match AuthProvider interface
mediumLowFindings.description: The scaffold generates `getAuthorizationUrl(state: string, options: AuthOptions, config?: Record<string, unknown>): string` with 3 parameters, but the actual AuthProvider interface in types/auth-provider.ts defines `getAuthorizationUrl(state: string, options: AuthOptions): string` with only 2 parameters. The scaffolded code also generates corresponding tests that pass a third `config` argument. While TypeScript's structural typing allows extra parameters in some contexts, this teaches developers the wrong API signature and means the scaffolded tests use a non-standard calling convention.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Change the scaffold to generate `getAuthorizationUrl(state: string, options: AuthOptions): string` matching the actual interface. The clientId should be retrieved from the plugin instance configuration (available via the initialize() lifecycle hook or stored during initialization) rather than passed as a third parameter. Update the generated test code accordingly.

mediumLowFindings.title: HookPayloadDataMap maps before:pipeline.complete to PipelineCompleteData which documents itself as after-only
mediumLowFindings.description: PipelineCompleteData (line 224) has a JSDoc comment stating it is 'Available to `after:pipeline.complete` only -- at this point all steps have either succeeded or failed.' However, HookPayloadDataMap maps both `before:pipeline.complete` and `after:pipeline.complete` to PipelineCompleteData. The data shape includes `status`, `duration`, and `stepResults` which would not be available in the 'before' stage since the pipeline has not actually completed yet. This type mismatch could lead plugin authors to rely on fields like `status` in a before hook where they would not have meaningful values.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Either (1) create a separate `PipelinePreCompleteData` type for `before:pipeline.complete` that omits the fields only available after completion (status, duration, stepResults), or (2) update the PipelineCompleteData JSDoc to clarify that the before-stage receives partial data with these fields possibly undefined and make them optional in the interface.

mediumLowFindings.title: Widget scaffold template inserts user-controlled values into HTML without escaping
mediumLowFindings.description: The scaffolded widget render() method interpolates `title` (from data.config) and `data.user.id` directly into an HTML template string without HTML entity escaping. While the SDK docs mention DOMPurify is applied server-side, the scaffold teaches an unsafe pattern that developers may replicate when building real widgets. A malicious config title containing '<script>' or HTML entities could inject content if the server-side sanitization is ever bypassed or misconfigured.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add an HTML escaping utility function to the scaffold template (e.g., `function escapeHtml(s) { return s.replace(/&/g,'&').replace(/</g,'<').replace(/>/g,'>').replace(/"/g,'"'); }`) and use it to wrap all interpolated values in the rendered HTML. This teaches a defense-in-depth pattern even though the platform applies DOMPurify.

mediumLowFindings.title: Timeout timer in timedCall is never cleared when the actual call resolves first
mediumLowFindings.description: In the timedCall function, Promise.race is used between fn() and timeoutPromise(). When fn() resolves/rejects before the timeout, the setTimeout in timeoutPromise is never cleared. While unref() prevents it from keeping the process alive, the timer callback still fires after the timeout period, calling reject() on an already-settled promise. Over many fetchBatch iterations (up to maxBatches=100), this accumulates dangling timers.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Refactor timedCall to use an AbortController or return the timeout handle from timeoutPromise so it can be cleared with clearTimeout when the fn() resolves first. For example: wrap the race in a try/finally that clears the timer handle.

mediumLowFindings.title: Path traversal vulnerability in applyRemoteChange allows writing files outside localDir
mediumLowFindings.description: applyRemoteChange() constructs the local file path by joining localDir with event.path (received from the server via SSE). If event.path contains path traversal sequences like '../../.bashrc', join() will resolve them and write to arbitrary locations outside the project directory. The function should validate that the resolved path is within localDir before writing.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: After computing localPath, resolve both paths and verify containment: `const resolved = resolve(localPath); if (!resolved.startsWith(resolve(localDir) + sep) && resolved !== resolve(localDir)) throw new Error('path traversal detected');`

mediumLowFindings.title: SSE parser loses multi-line data fields -- only keeps the last data line
mediumLowFindings.description: Per the SSE specification (W3C EventSource), when multiple 'data:' lines appear before an empty line, their values should be concatenated with newlines. The current parser overwrites current.data on each 'data:' line (line 34: `current.data = line.slice(5).trimStart()`), so only the last data line is kept. This means multi-line SSE data payloads (which are common for JSON larger than a single line) will be silently truncated to just the final line.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Concatenate data lines per the SSE spec: `current.data = current.data !== undefined ? current.data + '\n' + line.slice(5).trimStart() : line.slice(5).trimStart();`

mediumLowFindings.title: URL construction silently drops path components from platformUrl
mediumLowFindings.description: buildUrl() uses `new URL(path, base)` where base is the platformUrl. The URL constructor's behavior when the base has a path component is counterintuitive: `new URL('/api/v1/data', 'https://example.com/platform/')` correctly produces `https://example.com/api/v1/data`, but it drops the `/platform/` prefix from the base. Users who configure platformUrl as something like `https://gateway.internal/oneplatform` will have all API calls silently routed to the wrong paths (e.g., `/api/v1/data` instead of `/oneplatform/api/v1/data`). The path portion of platformUrl is always discarded.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Concatenate the base path and the request path before constructing the URL: `const baseUrl = new URL(base.endsWith('/') ? base : base + '/'); const url = new URL(path.startsWith('/') ? path.slice(1) : path, baseUrl);` -- this preserves any path prefix in the platform URL.

mediumLowFindings.title: Division by zero crash in migration progress display when total is 0
mediumLowFindings.description: In migrateAction(), the progress display computes `Math.round(status.progress / status.total * 100)`. If the server returns total=0 (empty entity type or edge case), this produces NaN or Infinity, which then displays as 'NaN%' or 'Infinity%'. Additionally, if both progress and total are 0, the 'completed' status check may never trigger, leading to the timeout path even though no work was needed.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Guard against zero total: `const pct = status.total > 0 ? Math.round(status.progress / status.total * 100) : 0;` and use `pct` in the display string.

mediumLowFindings.title: Passphrase exposed in process memory after being passed on command line
mediumLowFindings.description: When --include-credentials is used and --passphrase is not provided, promptPassphrase() interactively collects the passphrase. However, if --passphrase is provided on the command line, the passphrase is visible in `process.argv`, in shell history, and in `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` on Linux. While the code correctly warns about using POST to avoid logging it in server access logs, the CLI-side exposure is also significant. The same issue affects `config import --passphrase`.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add a note in the help text that the passphrase will be prompted interactively if omitted, and recommend omitting it for security. Consider additionally reading from an env var (e.g., OP_CONFIG_PASSPHRASE) as a middle ground between CLI args and interactive prompts.

mediumLowFindings.title: Schedule 'get' subcommand missing from bash/zsh completion scripts
mediumLowFindings.description: The schedule command group registers a 'get' subcommand (line 119 of schedule/index.ts), but the bash completion script at completion/index.ts line 57 lists schedule subcommands as 'list create pause resume delete' -- missing 'get' and 'update'. The zsh and fish completions have the same omission. Users relying on tab completion will not discover these subcommands.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Update the schedule completion lists in all three shell scripts (bash, zsh, fish) to include 'get' and 'update': 'list get create update pause resume delete'.

mediumLowFindings.title: Mapping 'import' subcommand missing from completion scripts
mediumLowFindings.description: The mapping command group registers an 'import' subcommand (mapping/index.ts line 381), but the completion scripts at completion/index.ts list mapping subcommands as only 'list create update delete preview' -- missing 'import'. Users will not get tab completion for 'op mapping import'.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add 'import' to the mapping completion lists in all three shell scripts: 'list create update delete preview import'.

mediumLowFindings.title: DLQ replay-all subcommand missing from completion scripts
mediumLowFindings.description: The dlq command group registers 'replay-all' (dlq/index.ts line 114), but completion scripts list dlq subcommands as 'list replay discard' -- missing 'replay-all'. Tab completion will not suggest this bulk operation.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add 'replay-all' to the dlq completion lists in all three shell scripts: 'list replay replay-all discard'.

mediumLowFindings.title: parseConfigDocuments accepts any string as ResourceKind without validation
mediumLowFindings.description: The YAML parser casts d['kind'] directly to ResourceKind without validating it is one of the six known kinds (Role, Ontology, Connector, Pipeline, App, Webhook). If a user provides a YAML document with kind: 'Unknown', it will be accepted as a ConfigDocument but will have no dependency edges in DEPS and no priority in KIND_PRIORITY (defaulting to 99). This means invalid kinds silently pass through parsing and topological sort, only failing later at import time with a confusing server error.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Validate that d['kind'] is one of the valid ResourceKind values before pushing: `const validKinds = new Set(['Role','Ontology','Connector','Pipeline','App','Webhook']); if (!validKinds.has(d['kind'] as string)) throw new Error('Unknown resource kind: ' + d['kind']);`

mediumLowFindings.title: Interactive login sends credentials using the old profile's HTTP client (without auth or with wrong platform URL)
mediumLowFindings.description: In loginAction's interactive mode (no --key), the email/password POST is made via ctx.http which was constructed by the preAction hook using the current profile's credentials and platform URL. If the user has not yet logged in (credentials are null), the HTTP client has no auth header -- which is correct for a login endpoint. However, if the user provides --platform to override the URL, ctx.http still points at the OLD platformUrl (from the pre-action hook's resolution), not the overridden URL. The --platform override is applied to opts.platform (line 31) but only used for key-based login (line 41-51); the interactive path at line 59 uses ctx.http which was constructed before the override.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: For interactive login, build a temporary HTTP client using the resolved platformUrl (just as is done for the --key path), so that --platform overrides work correctly in both login modes.

mediumLowFindings.title: user get renders a single object through render() with columns, which expects an array
mediumLowFindings.description: In getAction, ctx.renderer.render(user, USER_COLUMNS) is called with a single user object (not wrapped in an array). The render() method checks Array.isArray(data) to decide on table/tsv rendering (output.ts lines 161-174). Since a single object is not an array, it will always fall through to renderJson() regardless of the output format. Meanwhile, the connectors and pipelines get commands correctly wrap in an array: `ctx.renderer.render([connector], CONNECTOR_COLUMNS)`. This inconsistency means `op user get <id> -o table` always outputs JSON.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Wrap the single user object in an array: `ctx.renderer.render([user], USER_COLUMNS);`

mediumLowFindings.title: Plugin rollback ignores --yes flag, always prompts for confirmation
mediumLowFindings.description: rollbackAction checks `if (!ctx.yes)` and then calls confirmDestructive with `false` as the yes parameter (line 194). This means even when `--yes` is passed globally, the confirmation prompt still appears because the hardcoded `false` overrides ctx.yes. The correct pattern (used elsewhere, e.g., dlq discard) is to pass ctx.yes to confirmDestructive.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Remove the outer `if (!ctx.yes)` check and pass ctx.yes to confirmDestructive: `await confirmDestructive('Roll back plugin ...?', ctx.yes);`

mediumLowFindings.title: Plugin install ignores --yes flag, always prompts non-dev installations
mediumLowFindings.description: installAction checks `ctx.yes` on line 126 and prints a warning, but the else branch on line 129 calls `confirmDestructive('Install plugin ...?', false)` with a hardcoded `false`, ignoring ctx.yes. This means --yes does produce a warning but the prompt still appears because confirmDestructive receives false. The auto-approve message on line 127 is misleading since confirmation is not actually bypassed.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Change the else branch to pass ctx.yes: `await confirmDestructive('Install plugin ...?', ctx.yes);` and remove the separate ctx.yes check branch, or restructure to: `if (!opts.dev) await confirmDestructive('Install plugin ...?', ctx.yes);`

mediumLowFindings.title: Plugin upgrade ignores --yes flag, always prompts for confirmation
mediumLowFindings.description: upgradeAction checks `if (!ctx.yes)` and then calls confirmDestructive with `false` as the yes parameter. Same issue as the rollback command -- even with --yes, the prompt still appears because confirmDestructive receives false.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Remove the outer if check and pass ctx.yes: `await confirmDestructive('Upgrade plugin?...', ctx.yes);`

mediumLowFindings.title: Retry-After header parsed as integer fails for HTTP-date format, causing immediate retry with no delay
mediumLowFindings.description: The HTTP Retry-After header has two valid formats: a number of seconds (e.g. '120') or an HTTP-date (e.g. 'Wed, 21 Oct 2015 07:28:00 GMT'). The code uses parseInt(retryAfterHeader, 10) which returns NaN for date strings. NaN * 1000 = NaN, and setTimeout(fn, NaN) fires immediately with no delay, defeating the purpose of rate-limit backoff. This means if the server sends a Retry-After with a date value, the client will retry immediately, potentially hammering the server.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: After parseInt, check for NaN and fall back to the default: const parsed = parseInt(retryAfterHeader, 10); const retryAfterMs = !isNaN(parsed) ? parsed * 1000 : 1000; -- optionally also handle the HTTP-date format by trying new Date(retryAfterHeader).getTime() - Date.now().

mediumLowFindings.title: formatBytes crashes with NaN output for negative byte values
mediumLowFindings.description: formatBytes(bytes) only guards against bytes === 0 but not negative values. Math.log(negative) returns NaN, so Math.floor(NaN) is NaN, and sizes[NaN] is undefined. The function returns 'NaN undefined' as a string. Negative values can occur from delta calculations (e.g. showing storage change where current < previous), or from backend errors returning -1 as a sentinel.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add a guard for negative values at the top of the function: if (bytes < 0) return `-${formatBytes(-bytes, decimals)}`; -- or if negative values should not occur, add: if (bytes < 0) return '0 B';

mediumLowFindings.title: ErrorBoundary 'Sign in' button navigates to non-existent route /auth/login instead of /login
mediumLowFindings.description: When the ErrorBoundary classifies an error as a permission error, the 'Sign in' button navigates to '/auth/login'. However, the router defines the login route at '/login' (router.tsx line 49). The '/auth/login' path does not exist and will hit the 404 catch-all route, leaving the user on a Not Found page instead of the login form. Every other auth redirect in the codebase correctly uses '/login'.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Change the URL to '/login': onClick={() => { window.location.href = "/login"; }}

mediumLowFindings.title: Auto-layout BFS assigns incorrect layer to nodes reachable from multiple paths
mediumLowFindings.description: The applyAutoLayout function uses BFS to assign layers but adds nodes with visited-check. The comment on line 285 says 'use the maximum layer to avoid overlaps' but the code uses a visited set that prevents re-processing. If node B is reachable via A->B (layer 1) and also via A->C->B (layer 2), whichever path BFS discovers first wins. If A->B is discovered first, B gets layer 1 instead of the correct layer 2, causing B to overlap with C on the canvas.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Instead of using a visited set, allow re-processing nodes when a longer path is found. Replace the visited guard with a comparison: if the new layer is greater than the existing layer, update and re-enqueue. Or use a simpler approach: compute all layers first via repeated relaxation (like Bellman-Ford for longest path in a DAG), then assign positions.

mediumLowFindings.title: JSON.stringify(eventFilter) in useCallback deps causes re-creation on every render when caller provides inline array
mediumLowFindings.description: The useCallback for onEvent includes JSON.stringify(eventFilter) in its dependency array. If the caller passes an inline array literal like ['pipeline.*'], a new array reference is created every render, so JSON.stringify produces the same string -- but the useCallback still runs JSON.stringify every render to compare.
