More critically, if eventFilter reference changes but content is the same, the callback is recreated, triggering useSSEStream to disconnect and reconnect the SSE connection (since onEvent is passed via a ref, the reconnection does not happen -- but it does cause unnecessary garbage). However, the real issue is when eventFilter content actually changes: the SSE connection URL never changes, so the new filter is silently applied to the existing stream without reconnection, which is correct behavior. The performance cost of serializing on every render is minor but the pattern is an anti-pattern.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Memoize the eventFilter in the caller or use useRef for the filter, or move eventFilter to a useRef inside the hook and compare via JSON.stringify outside the deps array, similar to how onEventRef is used.

mediumLowFindings.title: Debounced auto-save closes over stale editorStore and client references
mediumLowFindings.description: The debouncedSave is memoized with [appId] as the only dependency. However, it captures `client` and `editorStore` from the render scope closure. Since useEditorStore() returns a new object reference each render (Zustand store selector), and client comes from useApiClient(), these could theoretically become stale. More practically, `editorStore.markSaved` inside the debounced callback uses the editorStore reference from the render when debouncedSave was created, not the current one. While Zustand actions are typically stable references, this relies on an implementation detail. If client or store instance changes (e.g., during hot module replacement), the debounced save will use stale references.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Use refs for client and editorStore to avoid stale closures: const clientRef = useRef(client); clientRef.current = client; const storeRef = useRef(editorStore); storeRef.current = editorStore; Then use clientRef.current and storeRef.current inside the debounced function.

mediumLowFindings.title: Webhook URL validation rejects valid HTTPS URLs that contain 'http://' as a substring
mediumLowFindings.description: The webhook URL validation uses z.string().url() followed by .refine(val => !val.startsWith('http://'), ...). The .url() validator accepts any valid URL including http:// URLs. The refine then rejects URLs starting with 'http://'. However, the error message says 'Webhook URLs must use HTTPS' but the validation does not positively check for https:// -- it only rejects http://. This means non-http, non-https schemes like ftp://, file://, or custom schemes would pass validation but likely fail at delivery time.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Replace the negative check with a positive one: .refine((val) => val.startsWith('https://'), 'Webhook URLs must use HTTPS.') -- this rejects http://, ftp://, and any other non-HTTPS scheme.

mediumLowFindings.title: describeCron produces incorrect ordinal suffixes for days 11-13 and 21-23
mediumLowFindings.description: The describeCron function generates ordinal suffixes for day-of-month values but only handles '1st', '2nd', '3rd' explicitly and uses 'th' for everything else. This works for most numbers but produces wrong output for '21st' (shows '21th'), '22nd' (shows '22th'), '23rd' (shows '23th'), and correctly handles 11th/12th/13th by accident (since they are not 1/2/3). For days 21, 22, 23, 31 the output is grammatically incorrect.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Implement a proper ordinal function: function ordinal(n: string) { const num = parseInt(n, 10); if (num % 100 >= 11 && num % 100 <= 13) return `${n}th`; if (num % 10 === 1) return `${n}st`; if (num % 10 === 2) return `${n}nd`; if (num % 10 === 3) return `${n}rd`; return `${n}th`; }

mediumLowFindings.title: Incremental sync 'since' parameter is lost across pagination within the same run
mediumLowFindings.description: When incrementalField is configured along with offset or cursor pagination, the 'since' value from the decoded cursor is only set on the first fetchBatch call that has it. However, the computeNextCursor() method at lines 697-719 constructs the next cursor for offset/cursor pagination without preserving the 'since' value from the previous cursor. For example, in offset pagination, encodeCursor({ offset: nextOffset }) drops any 'since' value. This means on page 2+, the incremental filter disappears and the connector fetches unfiltered data, potentially re-ingesting records that were already synced.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Preserve the 'since' value when encoding the next cursor. For offset pagination: `encodeCursor({ offset: nextOffset, since: previousCursor?.since })`. Apply the same fix in the cursor pagination case: `encodeCursor({ token: nextToken, since: previousCursor?.since })`. And for link pagination: `encodeCursor({ nextUrl, since: previousCursor?.since })`.

mediumLowFindings.title: User-supplied headers object values not validated, enabling header injection
mediumLowFindings.description: The parseConfig function casts rawHeaders to Record<string, string> without validating that every value is actually a string. If a tenant passes headers with non-string values (e.g., `{ "Authorization": 123 }` or `{ "X-Custom": { "nested": true } }`), the cast at line 150 silently allows them through. When these are passed to the fetch API, behavior is implementation-defined -- non-string values may be stringified as '[object Object]' or cause a runtime crash. Additionally, there is no check preventing the user from overriding security-sensitive headers like 'Authorization' or 'X-API-Key' via the static headers config, which would conflict with or override the credential-based auth headers.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Iterate over the entries of rawHeaders and validate that every value is a string, filtering or throwing on non-string values. Also consider rejecting or warning when static headers contain 'Authorization' or 'X-API-Key' keys, since those are managed by the auth resolution logic.

mediumLowFindings.title: Unsafe property access on potentially non-object values in extractCursorToken crashes the host
mediumLowFindings.description: In extractCursorToken(), lines 770-772 access nested properties like `(obj["meta"] as Record<string, unknown> | undefined)?.next_cursor`. If obj["meta"] is a non-null primitive (e.g., a number or string), the `as Record<string, unknown>` cast will not actually convert it, and accessing `?.next_cursor` on a primitive may not crash but produces undefined. However, the same pattern is more dangerous if obj["pagination"] or obj["paging"] happen to be arrays or other non-plain-object types -- the cast is unsafe. More critically, if the API returns a body where any of these fields is a string, number, or boolean, the cast suppresses the type error and could produce unexpected behavior in edge cases.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add a typeof guard before accessing nested properties: `const meta = obj["meta"]; const metaCursor = (meta && typeof meta === "object" && !Array.isArray(meta)) ? (meta as Record<string, unknown>)["next_cursor"] : undefined;` Apply the same pattern for pagination and paging fields.

mediumLowFindings.title: Retry-After header with HTTP-date format is silently ignored
mediumLowFindings.description: The parseRetryAfter function only handles the integer-seconds format of the Retry-After header. Per RFC 7231, the Retry-After header can also contain an HTTP-date (e.g., 'Wed, 21 Oct 2015 07:28:00 GMT'). When the API sends an HTTP-date, parseInt() returns NaN and the function returns undefined, causing the platform to fall back to its default backoff strategy instead of respecting the server's requested wait time. This could lead to the connector retrying too aggressively and getting banned.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Parse the HTTP-date format as a fallback: `const seconds = parseInt(value, 10); if (!isNaN(seconds)) return seconds; const date = new Date(value); if (!isNaN(date.getTime())) { const delta = Math.max(0, Math.ceil((date.getTime() - Date.now()) / 1000)); return delta; } return undefined;`

mediumLowFindings.title: Link header parser breaks on URLs containing commas
mediumLowFindings.description: The parseNextLinkHeader function splits the Link header on commas (line 374). However, RFC 8288 allows the URL portion to contain commas (e.g., `<https://api.example.com/items?filter=a,b>; rel="next"`). Splitting on comma will break the URL into two fragments, causing the parser to fail to find the next link. The URL `<https://api.example.com/items?filter=a` becomes one part and `b>; rel="next"` becomes another, neither of which matches the expected pattern.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Use a regex-based parser that handles commas inside angle brackets. For example: `const linkRegex = /<([^>]*)>\s*;\s*rel=["']?([^"',;]*)["']?/g; let match; while ((match = linkRegex.exec(linkHeader)) !== null) { if (match[2] === 'next') return match[1]; } return null;`

mediumLowFindings.title: Invalid cursor logged in error message may leak sensitive pagination state
mediumLowFindings.description: When decodeCursor fails, the error message includes the raw cursor string value. In some API integrations, cursor tokens may contain sensitive information (session tokens, internal IDs, or encoded query parameters). Including the raw cursor in the error message means it will be logged by the platform's error handling, potentially exposing sensitive data to anyone with log access.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Truncate the cursor value in the error message and avoid exposing the full string: `throw new PluginConfigError('Invalid cursor value — cannot decode pagination state (length: ' + cursor.length + ')', 'cursor');`

mediumLowFindings.title: POST requests never send a request body
mediumLowFindings.description: The connector supports method: 'POST' but the fetch call at line 557 never includes a body in the request. Many REST APIs that use POST for querying expect a JSON body with filter/pagination parameters. The connector only passes parameters as URL query strings regardless of the HTTP method. For APIs that expect POST with a JSON body (e.g., Elasticsearch _search, GraphQL endpoints), the connector will send an empty-body POST which will likely return an error or default unfiltered results.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: When meta.method is 'POST', pass pagination and incremental parameters as a JSON body instead of (or in addition to) query parameters. Add a Content-Type: application/json header and construct a body from the params: `const fetchInit: RequestInit = { method: meta.method, headers }; if (meta.method === 'POST') { fetchInit.body = JSON.stringify(params); headers['Content-Type'] = 'application/json'; }`. This may require refactoring buildRequestUrl to also return the params object separately.

mediumLowFindings.title: Unguarded response.json() throws untyped SyntaxError on non-JSON proxy responses
mediumLowFindings.description: In parseRowsResponse (line 796) and fetchTableSchema (line 518), response.json() is called without a try-catch. If the proxy returns a 200 status with a non-JSON body (e.g., an HTML error page from a reverse proxy like Nginx, or a plain-text message), response.json() throws a raw SyntaxError. This untyped error bypasses the plugin error taxonomy -- the Execution Service would treat it as an unrecoverable error with no useful context, rather than a PluginDataError with diagnostic information about what the proxy returned.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Wrap response.json() in a try-catch and throw a PluginDataError on parse failure, including a truncated snippet of the response body for debugging. For example: try { json = await response.json(); } catch { const text = await response.text(); throw new PluginDataError('Proxy returned non-JSON response', { body: text.slice(0, 500) }); }. Note: you must clone the response or read it as text first, since calling both .json() and .text() on the same Response body is not allowed.

mediumLowFindings.title: handleToConfig lacks validation for proxyUrl, producing cryptic TypeError on corrupted metadata
mediumLowFindings.description: In handleToConfig (line 765), proxyUrl is extracted with a bare type assertion: 'm["proxyUrl"] as string'. Unlike every other field in the function, it has no nullish coalescing fallback. If handle.metadata is corrupted or missing proxyUrl (e.g., due to a serialization/deserialization bug in the platform's checkpoint system), proxyUrl becomes undefined. When buildUrl is subsequently called with 'undefined' as the base, 'new URL("undefined/rows")' throws a TypeError('Invalid URL') -- an untyped error that provides no indication that the issue is a missing proxyUrl in the handle metadata.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add a validation guard after rehydration: if typeof proxyUrl is not 'string' or proxyUrl is empty, throw a PluginConfigError('Handle metadata is missing proxyUrl -- the connector handle may be corrupted'). This provides a clear, actionable error message.

mediumLowFindings.title: handleToConfig nullish coalescing allows batchSize=0 to pass through unchecked
mediumLowFindings.description: The batchSize rehydration uses nullish coalescing: '(m["batchSize"] as number) ?? DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE'. The ?? operator only catches null/undefined, not 0. If handle.metadata contains batchSize=0 (due to corruption or manual manipulation), it passes through as 0. This results in 'limit=0' being sent to the proxy, which could return all rows (unbounded query) or zero rows depending on proxy implementation, creating either a performance bomb or silent data loss.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Use a logical OR or explicit validation: 'batchSize: (typeof m["batchSize"] === "number" && m["batchSize"] > 0) ? m["batchSize"] : DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE'. Alternatively, validate the full rehydrated config the same way parseConfig validates the initial config.

mediumLowFindings.title: Empty requiredExternalUrls will block all fetch calls to the MySQL proxy in production
mediumLowFindings.description: The manifest declares 'requiredExternalUrls: []' (empty array). The FetchProxy interface documentation states: 'Only URLs declared in manifest.requiredExternalUrls are permitted.' The proxyUrl is a user-configured URL that varies per deployment. With an empty allowlist, all calls to context.fetch.fetch(proxyUrl, ...) will be rejected with PluginAuthError in production. This works in tests because the mock context does not enforce the URL allowlist. The Postgres connector may not have this problem because it uses a different proxy pattern (platform-managed proxy URLs), but the MySQL connector sends requests to an arbitrary user-configured proxyUrl.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Either add a glob/wildcard pattern to requiredExternalUrls that matches allowed proxy hosts (e.g., 'https://*.internal.example.com/*'), or document that the platform admin must configure the URL allowlist at deployment time. If the platform supports dynamic URL approval based on config values, use that mechanism instead. At minimum, add a comment explaining why this is empty and how it is expected to work in production.

mediumLowFindings.title: customQuery ignores table and incrementalColumn without warning, leading to silent misconfiguration
mediumLowFindings.description: When customQuery is provided, the connector silently ignores the table and incrementalColumn settings. The manifest description mentions 'Ignored when customQuery is set' for the table field, but the code does not warn or reject this combination. More critically, if incrementalColumn is set alongside customQuery, the connector stores incrementalColumn in handle metadata (line 666) and later uses it in findHighWaterMark (line 748), but buildCustomQuery (line 495) does not add a WHERE clause for the incremental filter. This means the cursor's 'since' field is tracked but never applied to the query, creating the illusion of incremental sync without actually filtering rows.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Reject the configuration when both customQuery and incrementalColumn are set, similar to the Postgres connector (line 225): 'incrementalColumn cannot be used together with customQuery'. Alternatively, warn and set incrementalColumn to null when customQuery is present.

mediumLowFindings.title: Database and table names interpolated into SQL string despite backtick quoting can be bypassed
mediumLowFindings.description: The parseConfig function rejects backtick characters in database and table names (line 198), but this check is insufficient. MySQL identifiers quoted with backticks can be broken with other character sequences. For example, a table name containing a backslash followed by a backtick in certain MySQL configurations (NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES off) could potentially break out of the backtick quoting. Additionally, the check does not reject newline characters, null bytes, or other control characters that could alter SQL parsing behavior depending on the proxy's MySQL driver configuration.

mediumLowFindings.title: configSchema in metadata() does not list proxyUrl as required, contradicting runtime validation
mediumLowFindings.description: The configSchema returned by metadata() lists 'required: ["database", "table"]' but omits 'proxyUrl'. However, parseConfig() throws PluginConfigError if proxyUrl is missing (line 250-254). This means the JSON Schema validation at install time will accept configs without proxyUrl, but the connector will fail at runtime when connect() is called. The manifest (plugin.manifest.json) also does not list proxyUrl as required. This mismatch between schema declaration and runtime behavior causes confusing errors -- the admin submits a config that passes schema validation, only for it to fail at connect time.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix:
Add 'proxyUrl' to the required array in both the metadata() configSchema and the plugin.manifest.json:

required: ["database", "table", "proxyUrl"]

mediumLowFindings.title: IPv4 regex capture groups mapped via .map(Number) includes the full match, producing NaN comparison
mediumLowFindings.description: The destructuring 'const [, a, b] = ipv4Match.map(Number)' maps the entire match array through Number(), including ipv4Match[0] which is the full match string (e.g., '192.168.1.1'). Number('192.168.1.1') returns NaN. This is harmless because the destructuring skips index 0 via the leading comma, but it is misleading code. More importantly, for the check 'b !== undefined' on line 166, b can never be undefined because the regex has 4 capture groups and will always produce indices 0-4. The check is dead code that obscures a potential issue: b could theoretically be NaN if the regex matched a non-numeric octet, though the \d+ pattern prevents that.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Parse only the capture groups you need: const a = Number(ipv4Match[1]); const b = Number(ipv4Match[2]); and remove the 'b !== undefined' check which is always true.

mediumLowFindings.title: Config validation accepts http:// URLs that the FetchProxy will always reject
mediumLowFindings.description: extractConfig() allows URLs starting with http:// (line 232), and the code comment (line 11-12) says 'http:// URLs are supported in config (user intent)'. However, the manifest's requiredExternalUrls only declares ['https://**']. The FetchProxy enforces this allowlist and its documentation states 'Protocol must match exactly (https:// required; http:// is blocked)'. Any http:// URL will be accepted by config validation, pass the HEAD check... which then throws a PluginAuthError from FetchProxy. The user sees a confusing authentication error instead of a clear 'http not supported' message.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Either (a) reject http:// URLs in extractConfig with a clear error message: 'Only https:// URLs are supported. The platform does not allow unencrypted HTTP connections.' or (b) add 'http://**' to requiredExternalUrls in the manifest if http support is truly intended. Option (a) is recommended for security.

mediumLowFindings.title: Encoding config is accepted but never applied; non-UTF-8 files will produce garbled data
mediumLowFindings.description: The encoding config option is extracted (line 247-249), stored in CsvConfig and handle.metadata, and documented in the configSchema (line 305). However, it is never actually used when decoding the response body. The response is decoded via response.text() (line 430), which per the Fetch API specification always uses UTF-8. If a user configures encoding: 'latin1' or 'windows-1252' for a file that uses that encoding, the file will be silently decoded as UTF-8, producing garbled characters for any byte > 127. The user has no indication that the setting is being ignored.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Either (a) use response.arrayBuffer() and decode with new TextDecoder(encoding) to honor the config: const buf = await response.arrayBuffer(); const text = new TextDecoder(encoding).decode(buf); or (b) remove the encoding config option entirely and document that only UTF-8 is supported, to avoid misleading users.

mediumLowFindings.title: disconnect() does not clear cached parsed CSV data; up to 100MB can remain in cache for 24 hours
mediumLowFindings.description: The comment on line 458 claims 'the cache is cleared on disconnect via key expiry' but disconnect() (line 513-520) does not call context.cache.delete(). The parsed CSV data (which for a 100MB file can be significantly larger as a JSON structure of string arrays) remains in the cache (likely Redis) for the full 24-hour TTL. For a connector with maxFileSizeMb=100, the parsed JSON representation could be 200-400MB. The cache accessor has a delete() method available. The Connector interface contract also says 'Resources to release: HTTP connections, open file handles' in disconnect -- cached data is an analogous resource.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add cache cleanup in disconnect(): try { await context.cache.delete(rowsCacheKey(_handle.connectionId)); } catch (err) { context.logger.warn('Failed to clear CSV cache', { error: err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err) }); }. Wrap in try/catch because the Connector interface contract says disconnect() must not throw.

mediumLowFindings.title: Multi-character delimiters silently accepted but cause incorrect parsing
mediumLowFindings.description: The delimiter config is validated only as a non-empty string (line 240). The parser compares single characters against the delimiter via text[pos] === delimiter (lines 149, 164, 171). In JavaScript, text[pos] returns a single character; comparing it to a multi-character string with === always returns false. A multi-character delimiter like '||' or '::' will never be detected: all fields merge into one giant field per row. The data is silently corrupted with no error reported.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add validation in extractConfig() to reject multi-character delimiters: if (delimiter.length !== 1) { throw new PluginConfigError('config.delimiter must be a single character', 'delimiter'); }. This matches RFC 4180 which defines a single-character separator.

mediumLowFindings.title: All fetch exceptions misclassified as PluginTimeoutError, including permanent failures
mediumLowFindings.description: When context.fetch.fetch() throws during the GET request in fetchBatch (line 401-403), every exception is wrapped as PluginTimeoutError. PluginTimeoutError has isRetryable=true, meaning the platform will retry these failures with backoff. However, many fetch exceptions are permanent (e.g., PluginAuthError from FetchProxy for disallowed URLs, DNS resolution failures for misspelled domains, SSL certificate errors). Wrapping them all as retryable timeout errors causes the platform to pointlessly retry failures that will never succeed, wasting ingestion worker time and delaying error surfacing.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Preserve the original error type if it is already a PluginError subclass, and only wrap unknown errors: catch (err) { if (err instanceof PluginError) throw err; const message = err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err); throw new PluginTimeoutError(`CSV fetch failed: ${message}`); }. This preserves PluginAuthError (non-retryable) from the FetchProxy while still wrapping genuine network timeouts.

mediumLowFindings.title: Mapping failure throws PluginDataError halting entire batch, inconsistent with skip-on-error design
mediumLowFindings.description: When mapPayloadToRecord throws (lines 594-599), the error is caught and re-thrown as PluginDataError, which is a non-retryable error that halts the entire batch and routes to the DLQ. This is inconsistent with the connector's own design principle stated at line 569: 'one malformed delivery must not block the rest of the queue'. HMAC verification failures are gracefully skipped with a warning log (lines 573-585), but a mapping failure kills the entire batch, abandoning all remaining payloads in the page. While mapPayloadToRecord currently handles most edge cases internally, a future change could introduce a throwing path, and the contract mismatch between 'skip bad records' for auth and 'halt everything' for data would cause operational issues.

mediumLowFindings.title: O(n*m) filtering of processed IDs using Array.includes on unsorted list
mediumLowFindings.description: On line 604, remainingIds is computed by filtering allIds against processedIds using Array.prototype.includes, which is O(m) per element where m is the number of processed IDs. With allIds of length n and processedIds of length m (up to batchSize=1000), this is O(n*m). If the pending index grows large (thousands of queued webhooks during a burst), this becomes a significant bottleneck. Additionally, on line 608, individual cache.delete calls are issued sequentially in a for loop rather than in parallel, adding unnecessary latency proportional to the number of processed payloads.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Convert processedIds to a Set for O(1) lookup: 'const processedSet = new Set(processedIds); const remainingIds = allIds.filter(id => !processedSet.has(id));'. For the sequential deletes, use Promise.all to issue them concurrently: 'await Promise.all(processedIds.map(id => context.cache.delete(pendingPayloadKey(instanceId, id))));'.

mediumLowFindings.title: timingSafeEqual leaks length information via early return on length mismatch
mediumLowFindings.description: The timingSafeEqual function returns false immediately when the two strings have different lengths (line 212). While HMAC hex digests for a given algorithm always have a fixed length (64 chars for SHA-256, 40 chars for SHA-1), the attacker controls the received signature value from the HTTP header. After the prefix stripping on line 248 (which removes 'sha256=' or 'sha1=' if present), a malformed prefix (e.g., 'sha256 =' with a space, or 'SHA256=' uppercase) would not be stripped, leaving the raw signature at a different length than the expected hex digest. The early return on length mismatch then reveals that the comparison failed on length rather than content, which is a minor timing side-channel. More practically, the prefix stripping is case-sensitive (line 246: 'const prefix = `${algorithm}=`'), so a sender using uppercase 'SHA256=abc...' would not have the prefix stripped, causing a length mismatch rather than a proper constant-time comparison.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Normalize the received signature before comparison. Lowercase and trim the received signature value, and handle common prefix variations (e.g., case-insensitive prefix matching). For the length check, pad the shorter string to match the longer one's length so the XOR loop always runs in full: 'const maxLen = Math.max(a.length, b.length); let mismatch = a.length !== b.length ? 1 : 0; for (let i = 0; i < maxLen; i++) { mismatch |= (a.charCodeAt(i) || 0) ^ (b.charCodeAt(i) || 0); } return mismatch === 0;'.

mediumLowFindings.title: estimatedTotal reports stale count that does not account for skipped/removed payloads
mediumLowFindings.description: The estimatedTotal field on line 635 is set to allIds.length, which is the count from the initial snapshot before any processing. After the batch completes, the actual remaining count is remainingIds.length (computed on line 605), which may be significantly smaller because processed IDs (including skipped ones) were removed. The estimatedTotal is documented as advisory (connector.ts line 50: 'The platform never makes correctness decisions based on this value'), but it would show misleading progress in the UI -- e.g., showing 100 total when only 3 remain after processing 97 in a previous batch.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Use remainingIds.length (computed on line 605) as the estimatedTotal, since it reflects the actual number of payloads remaining after this batch: 'estimatedTotal: processedIds.length > 0 ? remainingIds.length + records.length : allIds.length'. Move the estimatedTotal calculation after the index update block.

mediumLowFindings.title: Concurrent refresh cache key is not user-scoped, causing cross-user token leakage
mediumLowFindings.description: When a concurrent refresh request finds the lock held, it falls back to reading a cached TokenPair from the key 'oidc:refreshed:token' (line 688). However, this cache key is global to the plugin instance, not scoped per user or per refresh token. If User A's refresh completes and caches the result, then User B's concurrent refresh finds the lock held (for a different token), User B receives User A's access token. The lock key is correctly per-token (uses hashString(refreshToken)), but the fallback cache read uses a global key.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Scope the cached refresh result key to include the refresh token hash, e.g., `oidc:refreshed:token:${hashString(refreshToken)}`. This ensures the fallback cache lookup only returns a result for the same user/token that was being refreshed.

mediumLowFindings.title: RSA-PSS salt length is hardcoded to 32 for all PS variants, incorrect for PS384 and PS512
mediumLowFindings.description: The RSA-PSS salt length is hardcoded to 32 bytes for all PS256/PS384/PS512 algorithms. Per RFC 7518 Section 3.5, the salt length MUST equal the hash output length: 32 bytes for PS256 (SHA-256), 48 bytes for PS384 (SHA-384), and 64 bytes for PS512 (SHA-512). Using the wrong salt length will cause signature verification to fail for PS384 and PS512 tokens, or worse, Web Crypto may reject the verify call entirely.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Derive the salt length from the algorithm's hash. For example: `const hashSize = { 'SHA-256': 32, 'SHA-384': 48, 'SHA-512': 64 }; const saltLength = hashSize[(cryptoKey.algorithm as RsaHashedKeyAlgorithm).hash.name] ?? 32;`

mediumLowFindings.title: Default algorithm inference for EC keys always assumes ES256, incorrect for P-384 and P-521 curves
mediumLowFindings.description: When a JWK lacks an 'alg' field, the code defaults EC keys to 'ES256' regardless of the actual curve. If the key uses curve P-384 (should be ES384) or P-521 (should be ES512), importJwk will attempt to import the key with namedCurve 'P-256' (from the ES256 algorithm params), which will fail silently (caught and returns null). This means tokens signed with P-384 or P-521 keys that omit the 'alg' field in JWKS will always fail verification.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Derive the algorithm from the curve when the alg field is absent: `const alg = jwk.alg ?? (jwk.kty === 'EC' ? (jwk.crv === 'P-384' ? 'ES384' : jwk.crv === 'P-521' ? 'ES512' : 'ES256') : 'RS256');`

mediumLowFindings.title: atob-based base64url decoding silently produces corrupt output for multi-byte UTF-8 characters
mediumLowFindings.description: In the decodeJwtPayloadUnsafe function's atob() fallback path (used when Buffer is unavailable), the decoded binary string from atob() is not processed through a TextDecoder. For JWT payloads containing multi-byte UTF-8 characters (e.g., non-ASCII names, internationalized email addresses), atob() returns a latin-1 string where each byte becomes a separate character. Passing this directly to JSON.parse will produce mojibake or parse errors for payloads containing characters outside the ASCII range.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Apply TextDecoder to the atob output to correctly handle multi-byte UTF-8: `const binaryString = atob(payloadPart.replace(/-/g, '+').replace(/_/g, '/')); const bytes = new Uint8Array(binaryString.length); for (let i = 0; i < binaryString.length; i++) bytes[i] = binaryString.charCodeAt(i); const json = new TextDecoder().decode(bytes);`

mediumLowFindings.title: In-memory redirectUriByState Map is not safe across horizontally scaled instances
mediumLowFindings.description: The redirect_uri is stored in an in-memory Map keyed by the OAuth state parameter during getAuthorizationUrl(). When handleCallback() runs, it looks up the state in this same Map. In a horizontally scaled deployment (multiple pod replicas), the getAuthorizationUrl() call may land on instance A while handleCallback() lands on instance B. Instance B's Map will not contain the entry, causing a fallback to tenant config which may contain a stale or missing redirect_uri, leading to 'redirect_uri_mismatch' errors from the identity provider.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Use the distributed cache (context.cache) to store the redirect_uri keyed by state, instead of an in-memory Map. Since getAuthorizationUrl() is synchronous and cannot use async cache, either make it async (requires interface change) or use the REDIRECT_URI_CACHE_PREFIX constant that is already defined but never used (line 318) by caching the URI asynchronously in a wrapper called by the Auth Service.

mediumLowFindings.title: additionalParams can override security-critical OAuth parameters
mediumLowFindings.description: The additionalParams from AuthOptions are applied via params.set() after all security-critical parameters (response_type, client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state) are set. Since URLSearchParams.set() replaces existing keys, a caller passing additionalParams with keys like 'response_type', 'client_id', 'redirect_uri', or 'state' can override the secure defaults. For example, setting response_type to 'token' would switch to the implicit flow, bypassing PKCE/code-exchange security.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add a blocklist check before setting additional params: `const BLOCKED_PARAMS = new Set(['response_type', 'response_mode', 'client_id', 'redirect_uri', 'scope', 'state']); for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(options.additionalParams)) { if (!BLOCKED_PARAMS.has(key)) params.set(key, value); }`

mediumLowFindings.title: djb2 hash function uses signed 32-bit arithmetic, producing negative intermediate values
mediumLowFindings.description: The hashString function uses the djb2 algorithm with bitwise operators. In JavaScript, `hash << 5` operates on signed 32-bit integers, and the XOR with charCodeAt can produce negative values. While `hash >>> 0` at the end converts to unsigned, the intermediate signed overflow behavior means that hash values wrap around at 2^31 rather than 2^32 during computation. This does not cause a crash but means the hash distribution is slightly different from the canonical unsigned djb2, and for very long strings the intermediate values could produce collisions that the unsigned variant would not.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Use `hash = (((hash << 5) + hash) ^ value.charCodeAt(i)) >>> 0;` inside the loop to keep the value unsigned at each step, matching the canonical djb2 distribution.

mediumLowFindings.title: buildSearchBase false-positive detection of full DNs causes incorrect search base construction
mediumLowFindings.description: buildSearchBase checks if the searchBase contains 'dc=', 'o=', or 'c=' (case-insensitive) to decide whether it is already a full DN. This heuristic produces false positives for legitimate OU names that happen to contain these substrings. For example, an OU named 'ou=production' matches 'o=' (substring of 'production'), and 'ou=advocacy' also matches. In these cases the baseDN is NOT appended, producing a malformed search base like 'ou=production' instead of 'ou=production,dc=example,dc=com'. The substring match on 'o=' is especially problematic because 'o' is extremely common in English words.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Use a regex that matches these as RDN components (preceded by start-of-string or comma) rather than substring matching. For example: /(?:^|,)\s*(dc|o|c)\s*=/i.test(searchBase). This ensures that 'ou=production' does not falsely match the 'o=' pattern.

mediumLowFindings.title: groupMapping values not validated -- non-string values cause silent type corruption
mediumLowFindings.description: The groupMapping config is validated as an object (not null, not array) but is then cast to Record<string, string> without verifying that all values are actually strings. If a tenant admin provides groupMapping with numeric, boolean, or nested-object values (e.g., {"Admins": 42} or {"Admins": true}), these non-string values pass through unchecked. The mapGroupsToRoles method pushes these values into the platformRoles array, which the AuthResult interface declares as string[]. Downstream platform RBAC code expecting string role names will receive numbers or booleans, leading to authorization failures or type errors.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Iterate over the object entries and filter/validate that every value is a string. For example: Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(rawGroupMapping).filter(([_, v]) => typeof v === 'string')). Alternatively, throw a PluginConfigError if any value is not a string.

mediumLowFindings.title: extractMemberOfGroups ignores groups where the first RDN attribute does not match groupNameAttribute
mediumLowFindings.description: The extractMemberOfGroups method only extracts a group name when the FIRST RDN component of the memberOf DN matches the groupNameAttribute. In Active Directory, group DNs typically start with 'cn=' (e.g., 'cn=Developers,ou=groups,...'). However, if groupNameAttribute is set to a non-cn attribute (e.g., 'sAMAccountName' or 'name'), the method will never find a match because it only looks at the first RDN and expects it to start with that attribute. The method silently returns an empty group list, causing all users to have no roles. This is especially confusing because the explicit group search path (searchGroupsExplicitly) correctly fetches the requested attribute from the group entries.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: When using the memberOf fallback path, always extract from the first RDN (typically 'cn=') regardless of groupNameAttribute, since the DN's first RDN attribute is fixed by the directory schema and is independent of the attribute the admin wants to use for display names. Alternatively, document that groupNameAttribute must be 'cn' when groupSearchBase is not set, and validate this in parseConfig.

mediumLowFindings.title: Service-account bind DN and error reason logged and included in error details on bind failure
mediumLowFindings.description: When proxyBind fails, the PluginAuthError is thrown with the bindDN and failure reason included both in the error message string and in the structured details object: `throw new PluginAuthError('LDAP bind failed for ${params.bindDN}: ${reason}', { bindDN: params.bindDN, reason })`. During the initialize() probe bind, this exposes the service account's full DN in error responses. While the handleCallback caller catches and re-throws with a sanitized message for user binds, the initialize() probe bind failure propagates this error directly to the platform, where it may be surfaced in admin dashboards or error logs that could be visible to lower-privileged tenant admins.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Avoid including the full bindDN in the error message. Use a generic message like 'LDAP service account bind failed' and move the bindDN to debug-level logging only (which is already done on line 349). The details object should omit or redact the bindDN.

mediumLowFindings.title: configSchema in metadata() marks bindCredentialKey as required but parseConfig provides a default
mediumLowFindings.description: The configSchema in metadata() lists 'bindCredentialKey' in the 'required' array (line 528), which means the platform's JSON Schema validation will reject any configuration that omits this field. However, parseConfig (line 135) provides a default value of 'ldap_bind_password' when bindCredentialKey is missing or empty. This creates an inconsistency: the schema validation will reject configs before parseConfig ever gets a chance to apply its default. The manifest (plugin.manifest.json line 15) also lists it as required. Either the default in parseConfig is dead code, or the schema should not mark it as required.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Remove 'bindCredentialKey' from the required array in both metadata().configSchema and plugin.manifest.json to allow the parseConfig default to take effect, or remove the default from parseConfig and require it to always be provided explicitly.

mediumLowFindings.title: Grafana admin password defaults to 'admin' with no production override
mediumLowFindings.description: The Grafana container uses GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD: ${OP_GRAFANA_PASSWORD:-admin}, defaulting to 'admin'. The docker-compose.prod.yml file does NOT override or enforce a strong Grafana password (it has no grafana section). While Grafana is bound to 127.0.0.1:3100, any user with local access to the host or SSH tunneling capability can access the Grafana dashboard with admin/admin credentials. Grafana provides access to Jaeger traces, which may contain sensitive request metadata.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add a grafana section to docker-compose.prod.yml that requires OP_GRAFANA_PASSWORD with the ${OP_GRAFANA_PASSWORD:?Must set OP_GRAFANA_PASSWORD} syntax, similar to how POSTGRES_PASSWORD is handled. Alternatively, generate the Grafana password in op-init.

mediumLowFindings.title: Gateway API key validation call to auth service uses Bearer token instead of X-Service-Token
mediumLowFindings.description: When the gateway validates API keys, it calls the auth service's /internal/auth/validate-api-key endpoint with an Authorization: Bearer header containing config.serviceToken (a plain string from OP_SERVICE_TOKEN env var). However, /internal/* routes are protected by serviceAuthMiddleware which expects an X-Service-Token header containing an Ed25519-signed JWT. Using Authorization: Bearer sends the token to the auth middleware layer instead, which would treat it as a user JWT. If OP_SERVICE_TOKEN is not set, the gateway sends the request without any service authentication header, relying solely on Docker network isolation for access control to the /internal/ endpoint.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Use the Ed25519 service token signer (createServiceTokenSigner) to generate a proper X-Service-Token header for service-to-service calls, matching what serviceAuthMiddleware expects on /internal/* routes.

mediumLowFindings.title: EdDSA JWT public key (jwtPublicKey) is never passed to authMiddleware by createApp
mediumLowFindings.description: The authMiddleware supports EdDSA token verification when jwtPublicKey is provided, but the createApp function's CreateAppConfig interface does not include a jwtPublicKey field, and createApp never passes it to authMiddleware. This means EdDSA user-facing tokens will always be rejected with 'EdDSA token received but no public key is configured' across all services. While this is not an active vulnerability (tokens are rejected rather than accepted), it indicates a broken feature path that could lead to confusion or workarounds that weaken security.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Add jwtPublicKey as an optional field to CreateAppConfig and pass it through to authMiddleware. Services should load the JWT Ed25519 public key and include it in the createApp config.

mediumLowFindings.title: Gateway service has unrestricted wildcard RBAC permissions to all internal endpoints
mediumLowFindings.description: The service RBAC matrix grants gateway-service a blanket wildcard rule: { target: "*", method: "*", pathPattern: "*" }. This means the gateway can call any internal endpoint on any service with any HTTP method. If the gateway is compromised (e.g., via SSRF or an upstream dependency vulnerability), the attacker gains unrestricted access to every internal service endpoint, including sensitive operations like credential decryption, user deletion, and plugin execution. A more restrictive set of permissions following the principle of least privilege would limit blast radius.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Replace the wildcard rule with an explicit allowlist of the specific internal endpoints the gateway actually needs to call, such as /internal/auth/validate-api-key. This limits the blast radius of a gateway compromise.

mediumLowFindings.title: Postgres superuser password has a weak dev default that is not generated by op-init on first run
mediumLowFindings.description: The PostgreSQL container has POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-dev_postgres_superuser}. While op-init generates a strong password file (db_password_postgres_superuser.txt), this is only used by set-passwords.sh to ALTER ROLE. The initial POSTGRES_PASSWORD env var used during postgres container initialization still defaults to the weak 'dev_postgres_superuser' string unless the operator manually sets POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env. The prod compose file does enforce this, but the base compose with the weak default could be mistakenly used in production.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Have op-init write the superuser password to a file, then use the set-passwords.sh script to change it on first boot, or document prominently that POSTGRES_PASSWORD must be set in .env even for development.

mediumLowFindings.title: Docker socket proxy enables POST and DELETE capabilities for container management
mediumLowFindings.description: The docker-socket-proxy has CONTAINERS=1, IMAGES=1, POST=1, DELETE=1, and LOG=1 enabled. While this is necessary for the execution service to manage sandbox containers, the POST and DELETE permissions combined with CONTAINERS access allow creating and deleting arbitrary containers. If the execution service or sandbox network is compromised, an attacker could create privileged containers or delete other services' containers. The proxy lacks fine-grained path filtering to restrict operations to sandbox containers only.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Consider using a more restrictive Docker socket proxy that supports path-based filtering (e.g., only allowing operations on containers with specific labels or name prefixes). Alternatively, document this as an accepted risk with monitoring for unexpected container operations.

mediumLowFindings.title: Init script writes secret files with world-readable permissions (0444)
mediumLowFindings.description: All secret files (master key, JWT secret, database passwords, Ed25519 private keys) are written with chmod 0444 (world-readable). The comment explains this is necessary because service containers run as UID 1001 and postgres as UID 70, and the volume is mounted :ro. However, 0444 means any process in any container that mounts init-data can read every secret file, not just its own. A compromised app-service container could read the auth-service's database password, the master encryption key, and all Ed25519 private keys.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Consider per-service secret directories with tighter permissions (e.g., each service's secrets in a directory owned by its UID), or use Docker secrets with per-service targeting instead of a shared volume. At minimum, restrict private key files to 0400 with ownership matching the service UID.

mediumLowFindings.title: Gateway readyz uses "error" for failed checks while all other services use "fail"
mediumLowFindings.description: The gateway's readyz endpoint sets check values to "error" on failure, while all other services (and the core package) use either "fail" (custom health routes) or "error" (core health.ts). The core health.ts actually uses type `CheckResult = "ok" | "error"` matching the gateway, but all custom health routes type their checks as `Record<string, "ok" | "fail">`. Any monitoring dashboard or alerting tool that parses individual check statuses will have to handle both "error" and "fail" as failure indicators.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Standardize check failure values. Either update the gateway to use "fail" to match the 5 other custom health routes, or update all to use "error" to match the core health.ts pattern.

mediumLowFindings.title: Gateway healthz returns status "alive" while all other services return "ok"
mediumLowFindings.description: The gateway's /healthz endpoint returns status: "alive" while the core health.ts returns status: "ok" and all other custom health routes also return status: "ok". Any health monitoring system that checks the status field for a specific value will behave inconsistently for the gateway.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Change the gateway healthz status from "alive" to "ok" to match all other services.

mediumLowFindings.title: Plugin service readyz uses check key "database" while all other services use "postgres"
mediumLowFindings.description: The plugin service names its Postgres check as checks["database"] while all other services (app, execution, gateway, ingestion, pipeline) and the core health.ts use checks["postgres"]. A unified monitoring dashboard that aggregates readyz responses across services will see inconsistent check names.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Change the plugin service check key from "database" to "postgres" to match all other services.

mediumLowFindings.title: Plugin service reads OP_SERVICE_TOKEN_SECRET while gateway and execution read OP_SERVICE_TOKEN
mediumLowFindings.description: The plugin service reads process.env["OP_SERVICE_TOKEN_SECRET"] and fatally exits if it is empty. The gateway reads process.env["OP_SERVICE_TOKEN"] (no _SECRET suffix) and the execution service also reads process.env["OP_SERVICE_TOKEN"]. Neither variable is set in docker-compose.yml. If an operator sets OP_SERVICE_TOKEN for the gateway, the plugin service will not see it (it looks for OP_SERVICE_TOKEN_SECRET) and will crash on startup.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Standardize on a single env var name (either OP_SERVICE_TOKEN or OP_SERVICE_TOKEN_SECRET) across all services, and add it to docker-compose.yml.

mediumLowFindings.title: Inline error responses bypass error handler and omit requestId field
mediumLowFindings.description: Seven inline error responses in pipeline/executions.ts and app/embed.ts return error JSON directly via c.json() instead of throwing AppError subclasses. These responses omit the requestId field that the core error handler always includes (via AppError.toApiError(requestId)). API clients following the spec's error format (which includes requestId for support correlation) will not find it in these responses. This makes it harder to trace errors in production.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Replace inline c.json error returns with throw new ValidationError("Missing pipelineId path parameter.") to go through the error handler which properly includes requestId. The same applies to pipeline/executions.ts lines 53, 93, 152 and app/embed.ts lines 213, 244, 250 and app/index.ts line 660.

mediumLowFindings.title: Three duplicate ontology:map Queue instances created at module level with no retry config and no consumer
mediumLowFindings.description: The ingestion service creates three separate BullMQ Queue instances for the "ontology:map" queue (in sync-service.ts:288, upload-service.ts:165, and webhook-receive-service.ts:180), each at module level. None of these have defaultJobOptions (no retry config), unlike other queues which use exponential backoff. More critically, there is no Worker anywhere in the codebase that consumes from the "ontology:map" queue -- jobs enqueued here will accumulate in Redis indefinitely with no processing.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Either implement a Worker for the ontology:map queue in the ontology service, or if the queue processing is not yet implemented, add a TODO and ensure the queues have retry configuration matching the platform standard (5 attempts, exponential backoff). Also consolidate the three Queue instances into a single shared instance.

mediumLowFindings.title: Module-level BullMQ Queue bypasses validated config and uses different retry settings
mediumLowFindings.description: The uploads route creates a module-level Queue with attempts: 3 and delay: 5000ms, while the core createQueue() helper uses attempts: 5 and delay: 1000ms. Additionally, the core createWorker() sets removeOnComplete: { count: 0 } and removeOnFail: { count: 100 }, but the uploads route uses removeOnComplete: { age: 86_400 } and removeOnFail: { age: 604_800 }. This means the file-parse queue has inconsistent retry/retention behavior compared to queues created through the standard pattern.
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Use createQueue() from @oneplatform/core to ensure consistent retry policy, or document why this queue intentionally differs. The module-level instantiation also reads process.env["OP_REDIS_URL"] directly instead of receiving the validated config URL.

mediumLowFindings.title: executeAtomicSwap does BEGIN/COMMIT without try/catch ROLLBACK
mediumLowFindings.description: The executeAtomicSwap function calls client.query("BEGIN") and later client.query("COMMIT"), but if any query between BEGIN and COMMIT throws, there is no explicit ROLLBACK. While the calling code uses try/finally with client.release(), and pg.Pool does issue an implicit ROLLBACK when releasing a client with a pending transaction, relying on this implicit behavior is fragile and inconsistent with other transaction patterns in the codebase (e.g., migration files use explicit BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK in try/catch/finally).
mediumLowFindings.suggestedFix: Wrap the transaction body in a try/catch that explicitly calls client.query("ROLLBACK") on error, consistent with the pattern used in all migration files across the codebase.
